rule: two independent readings agree (both blind readers, or one reader and a third who checked the source); conflicts with the earlier audit go to a third reader; quotes checked verbatim in code

alondra-nelson.q: Guardrails like: more rigorous system testing to protect people from discriminatory impacts of technologies; having meaningful human oversight over life-impacting decisions; consulting with the public before introducing new technologies into communities
alondra-nelson.work: Remarks of Dr. Alondra Nelson at the NACDL and UC Berkeley Samuelson Clinic's Criminal Legal Education Seminar: 'Unlocking the Black Box'
alondra-nelson.why: In remarks on algorithmic injustice in policing and housing she endorses rigorous testing for discriminatory impacts as a needed guardrail before systems are introduced.

dean-ball.q: I do not think there should be new laws to regulate “algorithmic discrimination” or “algorithmic addiction” or “algorithmic pricing.”
dean-ball.work: Before Leviathan Wakes (Why I Believe What I Believe)
dean-ball.why: He rejects new laws on algorithmic discrimination, which would include mandatory bias testing of decision systems.

joy-buolamwini.q: Beyond having companies implement internal bias mitigation processes, there needs to be external testing and validation to assess the use of face-based tools in employment contexts.
joy-buolamwini.work: Written Testimony, Hearing on Facial Recognition Technology (Part 1): Its Impact on our Civil Rights and Liberties
joy-buolamwini.why: She calls for independent external bias testing before face-based AI is used in hiring, and similar checks for housing, credit and policing.

marsha-blackburn.q: Audits of high-risk AI systems to undergo regular bias evaluations to prevent discrimination based on protected characteristics, including political affiliation.
marsha-blackburn.work: Blackburn Unveils National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence (TRUMP AMERICA AI Act)
marsha-blackburn.why: Her bill requires bias audits of high-risk AI systems, defined to include employment and law enforcement uses.

meredith-whittaker.q: Require Algorithmic Impact Assessments in both Public and Private Sectors before AI Systems are Acquired and Used
meredith-whittaker.work: Written Testimony of Meredith Whittaker: "Artificial Intelligence: Societal and Ethical Implications"
meredith-whittaker.why: In testimony documenting biased AI in hiring, policing, benefits and housing, her first recommendation is mandatory impact assessment with public agency review before such systems are used.

ted-cruz.q: They want a testing regime to guard against AI quote discrimination, and have government agencies provide ‘guidance documents,’ seemingly something out of Orwell
ted-cruz.work: Sen. Cruz: Adopting Europe's Approach on Regulation Will Cause China to Win the AI Race (opening statement, 'Winning the AI Race' hearing)
ted-cruz.why: He mocks a government testing regime for AI discrimination as Orwellian.

barack-obama.q: I have to tell you that generally speaking, the way I think about AI is as a tool, not a buddy.
barack-obama.work: Barack Obama on AI, free speech, and the future of the internet
barack-obama.why: He explicitly says AI is a tool, not a buddy.

eugenia-kuyda.q: In my view, going back to your question, I think even what we have right now with LLMs is enough to build a truly incredible friend.
eugenia-kuyda.work: Replika CEO Eugenia Kuyda says it's okay if we end up marrying AI chatbots (Decoder interview)
eugenia-kuyda.why: Kuyda describes Replika as 'an AI friend' throughout and says current models already suffice to build a truly incredible friend, though a different kind of relationship from human friendship.

jaron-lanier.q: You won’t be falling in love with an A.I. Instead, it’ll be the same humans you are disillusioned with—people who work at companies that sell A.I.
jaron-lanier.work: Your A.I. Lover Will Change You
jaron-lanier.why: He denies that an AI lover is a real partner, saying it is a front for the company selling it.

jonathan-haidt.q: An AI companion can imitate friendship, but it can’t actually be a friend.
jonathan-haidt.work: Don't Give Your Child Any AI Companions
jonathan-haidt.why: Direct denial that an AI can be a real friend.

josh-hawley.q: Mark Zuckerberg’s ambition to replace friendship, real friendship with AI—what a terrible idea.
josh-hawley.work: Josh Hawley: We Must ‘Bend’ AI to Serve the Good
josh-hawley.why: He contrasts 'real friendship' with AI and rejects replacing friendship with AI.

pope-leo-xiv.q: The dialogic, adaptive, mimetic structure of these language models is capable of imitating human feelings and thus simulating a relationship. While this anthropomorphization can be entertaining, it is also deceptive, particularly for the most vulnerable.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Message for the 60th World Communications Day 2026
pope-leo-xiv.why: He calls chatbot relationships simulated and deceptive, adding that without embracing others there can be no friendships.

russell-moore.q: Chatbots are artificial, constructed to echo to users exactly what they want to hear. There’s no risk of being misunderstood or disagreed with or hurt. And yet what is that relationship? In the end, these conversations are only an echo of ourselves.
russell-moore.work: Chatbot Companionship Will Make Our Loneliness Crisis Worse
russell-moore.why: He argues chatbot friendship is only a self-echo, contrasting it with real friendship a chatbot cannot replicate.

stuart-russell.q: LLMs are also capable of inducing a form of hallucination in their users: millions of people have been seduced into relying on LLMs as their primary emotional contact, leaving them vulnerable to software updates that undermine their imagined connection.
stuart-russell.work: Written Testimony before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology, & the Law ('Oversight of A.I.: Principles for Regulation')
stuart-russell.why: Russell calls emotional bonds with chatbots a hallucination and an 'imagined connection', which denies that they are real friendships.

yuval-noah-harari.q: Although there is no indication that AI has any consciousness or feelings of its own, to foster fake intimacy with humans it is enough if the AI can make them feel emotionally attached to it.
yuval-noah-harari.work: Watch out humans: AI has hacked the operating system of civilisation
yuval-noah-harari.why: He calls AI intimacy fake because AI has no feelings of its own.

abeba-birhane.q: Without intentional rectification and proper guardrails, AI often leads to surveillance, manipulation, inequity and erosion of fundamental rights and human agency while concentrating power, wealth and influence in the hands of AI developers and vendors.
abeba-birhane.work: Bending the arc of AI towards the public interest: Thoughts on and after the AI Action Summit in Paris
abeba-birhane.why: She says that on its current, unguarded course AI concentrates power and wealth in the hands of AI developers and vendors.

andrew-yang.q: 1. AI will not democratize opportunity; it will accelerate inequality on a scale we have never seen before.
andrew-yang.why: He backs the claim that AI will accelerate inequality, noting AI-lab insiders getting rich while most are left out.

anton-korinek.q: We find that the market for cutting-edge foundation models exhibits a strong tendency towards market concentration
anton-korinek.work: Market concentration implications of foundation models: The invisible hand of ChatGPT
anton-korinek.why: The paper's central finding is that frontier AI tends toward natural monopoly, with resulting concentration of economic power and inequality.

arvind-narayanan.q: The real impact of AI is likely to be subtler: AI tools will shift power away from workers and centralize it in the hands of a few companies.
arvind-narayanan.work: A misleading open letter about sci-fi AI dangers ignores the real risks
arvind-narayanan.why: They forecast directly that AI will concentrate power in a few companies.

asad-ramzanali.q: A few trillion-dollar companies now comprise an AI oligopoly that poses major risks to competition and to our national security.
asad-ramzanali.work: Break Up Big AI Before It Breaks Us
asad-ramzanali.why: He describes AI as already controlled by a few dominant companies that are extending that control.

audrey-tang.q: The result is a system that interacts with billions of people but is, by default, controlled by a small circle of researchers and executives, while those most affected have almost no voice in shaping the outcomes.
audrey-tang.why: She says the current approach puts control of AI in a few private corporations.

balaji-srinivasan.q: AI is empirically decentralizing rather than centralizing. Right now, AI is arguably having a decentralizing effect, because there are (a) so many AI companies
balaji-srinivasan.why: He states that AI is decentralizing, pointing to many companies, small teams and open-source models.

bernie-sanders.q: They are implementing a technology that will make them and their corporate clients even richer and more powerful.
bernie-sanders.work: Artificial intelligence is coming for the working class. We must fight back
bernie-sanders.why: He predicts AI will concentrate wealth and power in a handful of tech billionaires and their companies.

brian-merchant.q: Tech giants and venture capitalists have poured hundreds of billions of dollars into AI firms, again concentrating wealth and power in a few controlling hands.
brian-merchant.work: Understanding the Luddites in the age of AI
brian-merchant.why: In his own voice he says AI investment is concentrating wealth and power in a few hands, echoing the factory owners.

bruce-schneier.q: Efforts to disrupt the AI oligopoly by funding start-ups are self-defeating as Big Tech profits from the cloud computing services and AI models powering those start-ups—and often ends up acquiring the start-ups themselves.
bruce-schneier.work: Build AI by the People, for the People
bruce-schneier.why: He describes AI as an oligopoly of a few tech giants that start-ups cannot disrupt.

chris-murphy.q: They are blinded by the profits they will make and the godlike power they will wield.
chris-murphy.work: Murphy Speaks on AI's Impact on Job Loss, Purpose, Social Connection at Brookings Institution
chris-murphy.why: He expects AI executives to gain enormous wealth and power.

daniel-faggella.q: As tech giants win the “winner takes all” game of AI, this power will continue to concentrate.
daniel-faggella.work: Substrate Monopoly - The Future of Power in a Virtual and Intelligent World
daniel-faggella.why: His substrate-monopoly thesis predicts that power will concentrate in whoever controls AI and compute.

daron-acemoglu.q: I think right now the foundation models which--like ChatGPT-4--are so resource-intensive, and they're going in a particular way that they might actually strengthen the hold of Google and Microsoft.
daron-acemoglu.work: Daron Acemoglu on Innovation and Shared Prosperity
daron-acemoglu.why: Asked whether AI threatens big tech's dominance, he says the current path is more likely to strengthen the largest firms.

david-sacks.q: In summary, the latest releases of AI models show that model capabilities are more decentralized than many predicted.
david-sacks.work: Long X post: the 'Goldilocks' state of AI and why the doomer narratives were wrong
david-sacks.why: He reads the current course as decentralized competition, while noting it could change.

e-glen-weyl.q: have seen the challenges of emerging monopolies only expand in the market for chips and generative foundation models.
e-glen-weyl.why: The co-authored chapter says the current US model has let monopolies grow and that this problem is now expanding into AI models and chips.

elizabeth-warren.q: Americans are hanging on by their fingernails in an economy that funnels wealth to the ultra-rich and leaves crumbs for working people. AI threatens to supercharge this divide
elizabeth-warren.work: Why We Need to Tax AI
elizabeth-warren.why: She argues AI on its current course will deepen wealth concentration, creating 'dozens of tech billionaires'.

emily-m-bender.q: This technological sector is presently the site of enormous inﬂuxes of capital and enormous concentrations of power.
emily-m-bender.work: Written testimony, House Science Committee joint subcommittee hearing 'Balancing Knowledge and Governance: Foundations for Effective Risk Management of Artificial Intelligence'
emily-m-bender.why: In her opening testimony she describes the AI sector as concentrating capital and power, which is why she asks for regulation.

fei-fei-li.q: Right now, due to the vast amount of compute and data required to train these systems, Much of the innovation in AI is concentrated in the hands of a few very large corporations and select nations.
fei-fei-li.work: Briefing to the UN Security Council on AI and international peace and security (9821st meeting)
fei-fei-li.why: In her own briefing, Li says the costs of compute and data are concentrating AI in a few large corporations, and calls for public investment to counter it.

felix-simon.q: Given the nature of the technology — which has a high barrier to entry due to the vast data and computational power requirements — platform companies are likely to dominate this space for the foreseeable future.
felix-simon.work: Artificial Intelligence in the News: How AI Retools, Rationalizes, and Reshapes Journalism and the Public Arena
felix-simon.why: In his own report he forecasts a few platform companies dominating AI, adding that control over infrastructure confers power.

holly-elmore.q: There’s no place for the rest of us in the world the AI industry is trying to build.
holly-elmore.why: She argues the AI industry is capturing all the value, like conquistadors, leaving everyone else without a role.

jaron-lanier.q: That looks an awful lot like the new digital economy to me, where you have (natural language) translators and everybody else who contributes to the corpora that allow the data schemes to operate, contributing mostly to the fortunes of whoever runs the top computers.
jaron-lanier.why: He says the AI data economy channels wealth to whoever runs the top computers, a pattern he calls non-sustainable.

jason-crawford.q: I’m sure some people find this plausible or even likely, but I don’t (mostly because I just don’t think this is the way an economy works, but secondarily because I would expect world governments to intervene with some sort of massive welfare program).
jason-crawford.work: The future of humanity is in management
jason-crawford.why: He rejects the scenario in which a few AI owners control the economy, and expects AI to increase ownership broadly.

jeff-jarvis.q: Open AI may be our best and only defense against its oligarchic domination.
jeff-jarvis.why: He warns that without openness AI is headed toward domination by a few giants.

josh-hawley.q: We are watching a handful of companies assemble a concentration of capital, information, and political power without precedent in the American experience.
josh-hawley.work: The American Covenant’s Answer to AI
josh-hawley.why: He states that AI is concentrating capital and power in a handful of companies, and that left to itself it will gather power into fewer hands.

karen-hao.q: And they, of course, have also consolidated an extraordinary amount of political and economic power.
karen-hao.why: Describing AI companies such as OpenAI as empires, she says they have already concentrated vast political and economic power.

kate-crawford.q: The territories are dominated by a few global mega-companies, which are creating new infrastructures and mechanisms for the accumulation of capital and exploitation of human and planetary resources.
kate-crawford.why: She describes AI as concentrating wealth and control in a few mega-companies, echoed in her interview remark that AI empowers already powerful institutions.

liz-shuler.q: Does anyone want to continue on this race-to-the-bottom we’re on right now — where workers are being fired; discriminated against; surveilled without our consent … where this handful of billionaires, one soon to be a trillionaire, get to play God with our economy and our lives?
liz-shuler.work: AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler's Speech to the National Press Club
liz-shuler.why: She describes the current AI course as putting economic power in the hands of a handful of tech billionaires.

marc-andreessen.q: So what happens is the opposite of technology driving centralization of wealth – individual customers of the technology, ultimately including everyone on the planet, are empowered instead, and capture most of the generated value.
marc-andreessen.work: Why AI Will Save the World
marc-andreessen.why: He argues AI, like past technology, spreads value to customers rather than concentrating wealth.

meredith-whittaker.q: what we're looking at is a significant concentration of power over infrastructure and decision-making that is then rebranded as a kind of God's Head intelligence
meredith-whittaker.work: Meredith Whittaker on Who Controls Your Data in the Age of AI
meredith-whittaker.why: She explains that AI's need for data, compute and distribution concentrates the industry in the hands of a few platform winners of the last tech boom.

pope-leo-xiv.q: In fact, as with every major technological shift, AI tends to amplify the power of those who already possess economic resources, expertise and access to data.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: He says AI concentrates power in a few hands and names the 'new monopolies of AI'.

ro-khanna.q: These principles are the beginning of a framework to ensure that AI does not usher in a level of wealth and power concentration that further rips our democracy apart.
ro-khanna.work: We need a new tech social contract to reclaim AI from billionaires
ro-khanna.why: He argues that on the current course AI will deepen the wealth and power concentration of tech lords.

robin-hanson.q: Many organizations supply many AIs and they are pushed by law and competition to get their AIs to behave in civil, lawful ways that give customers more of what they want compared to alternatives.
robin-hanson.why: His most likely scenario is many competing AI suppliers, not concentration in a few firms.

scott-alexander.q: If AI takeover is averted, the default outcome of the current AI race is that some particular company wins.
scott-alexander.work: AI Chip Regulation Is Not A Dystopian Surveillance State
scott-alexander.why: He says the default course of the AI race ends with one company winning, and goes on to say that tech companies taking an outsized share of power is no longer speculative.

scott-santens.q: The wealth they generate flows to a remarkably small number of people while the costs are distributed across entire communities who have been dispossessed of what was theirs.
scott-santens.work: Our Data. Our Resources. Our Terms and Conditions.
scott-santens.why: He describes the AI buildout as concentrating wealth in a few hands, and calls those concentrations a vulnerability.

timnit-gebru.q: Many of these systems are developed by multinational corporations located in Silicon Valley, which have been consolidating power at a scale that, journalist Gideon Lewis-Kraus notes, is likely unprecedented in human history.
timnit-gebru.work: The Exploited Labor Behind Artificial Intelligence
timnit-gebru.why: She describes AI developers as consolidating power on an unprecedented scale, and elsewhere calls for alternatives to their concentrated power.

tristan-harris.q: and that is just an unbelievable level of wealth concentration that we've never seen before.
tristan-harris.work: The Great Simplification ep. 214: Tristan Harris (transcript)
tristan-harris.why: Harris says businesses will pay a handful of AI companies instead of workers, producing unprecedented wealth concentration.

yoshua-bengio.q: the exponentially growing computational cost of the most advanced AI systems means that it is likely that the number of organizations able to train them will be very limited, giving them immense power.
yoshua-bengio.work: Reasoning through arguments against taking AI safety seriously
yoshua-bengio.why: He predicts frontier AI will put immense power in a very small number of organizations.

adam-thierer.q: For many professions, AI is already a multiplier tool that will create new opportunities and jobs well beyond what computers have already provided us.
adam-thierer.work: AI and the jobs apocalypse that wasn't
adam-thierer.why: The essay argues that predictions of AI job loss have been wrong and that AI is creating jobs.

andrew-yang.q: 2. AI is going to eliminate millions of jobs faster than new ones can be created.
andrew-yang.why: This is one of four statements he says he agreed to back in a public debate.

arvind-narayanan.q: This has proven helpful both to understand why claims of rapid and widespread job displacement (such as Amodei’s claims about an imminent white-collar bloodbath) are unlikely to materialize
arvind-narayanan.work: Do AI Risks Require Extraordinary Government Intervention?
arvind-narayanan.why: The authors say rapid, widespread job displacement is unlikely, and elsewhere argue that humans move to tasks that have not been automated.

balaji-srinivasan.q: AI doesn’t take your job, it takes the job of the previous AI.
balaji-srinivasan.why: One of several slogans (with 'AI makes you the CEO' and 'AI will create tons of jobs in proctoring and verification') denying that AI mainly eliminates human jobs.

bernie-sanders.q: The artificial intelligence and robotics being developed by these multi-billionaires today will allow corporate America to wipe out tens of millions of decent-paying jobs, cut labor costs and boost profits.
bernie-sanders.work: AI must benefit everyone, not just a handful of billionaires
bernie-sanders.why: He forecasts tens of millions of lost jobs over the next ten years and asks how displaced workers will find 'jobs that don't exist'.

cory-doctorow.q: The AI can't do your job, but an AI salesman can convince your boss to fire you and replace you with an AI that can't do your job.
cory-doctorow.work: The Reverse-Centaur's Guide to Criticizing AI
cory-doctorow.why: He predicts that AI-driven firings will destroy jobs that will not come back after the bubble bursts, a net loss of jobs.

daniel-faggella.q: Humans will eventually be buffered entirely out of “work” of any kind (economic, scientific, governmental, etc.)
daniel-faggella.work: AGI Displacement of Work is the End of Man
daniel-faggella.why: He argues that AI displacement of human work is under way now and that 'we are about to be buffered out of work', with no offsetting creation of human jobs.

daniel-jeffries.q: Because here’s what the doomers never understood: productivity tools don’t eliminate human work.
daniel-jeffries.work: The Abundance Boom: A Memo from 2030
daniel-jeffries.why: The memo argues AI transforms and multiplies jobs rather than reducing total employment.

david-sacks.q: This means that apocalyptic predictions of job loss are as overhyped as AGI itself. Instead, the truism that “you’re not going to lose your job to AI but to someone who uses AI better than you” is holding up well.
david-sacks.work: Long X post: the 'Goldilocks' state of AI and why the doomer narratives were wrong
david-sacks.why: He argues humans and AI divide labour and that predictions of mass job loss are overhyped.

ed-zitron.q: Long story short, agents are not autonomous, they do not replace jobs, they cannot “replace coders,” they are not going to do so because probabilistic models are a horrible means of taking precise actions
ed-zitron.work: How To Argue With An AI Booster
ed-zitron.why: He denies that AI is or will be able to replace jobs at scale, calling such stories manipulative hype.

elon-musk.q: I do think it’s going to be a bumpy road because AI will be able to do any job better than any person can do that job.
elon-musk.work: Full Transcript: Zanny Minton Beddoes Interviews Elon Musk (The Economist)
elon-musk.why: Asked about job displacement over the next 10 years, he predicts AI will do any job better than people, so that work becomes 'optional'.

erik-brynjolfsson.q: This means we are not in danger of mass unemployment anytime soon. There is no shortage of work that needs to be done in our society that only humans can do.
erik-brynjolfsson.work: Testimony of Erik Brynjolfsson: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work (House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology)
erik-brynjolfsson.why: He says that over the coming decade AI will transform most jobs rather than eliminate work, and that mass unemployment is not in sight.

james-livingston.q: Rise of the Robots, a new book that cites these very sources, is social science, not science fiction.
james-livingston.work: What if jobs are not the solution but the problem? (Fuck work)
james-livingston.why: He endorses forecasts that about half of jobs are at risk of computerisation within 20 years and says there are not enough jobs.

jd-vance.q: AI, I really believe, will facilitate and make people more productive. It is not going to replace human beings. It will never replace human beings.
jd-vance.work: Remarks by the Vice President at the Artificial Intelligence Action Summit in Paris, France
jd-vance.why: He states AI will not replace workers, and elsewhere in the speech calls it a tool for job creation.

jensen-huang.q: Of course my first hope, and I think it will happen this way, although jobs will be changed and some jobs will be lost, a lot of jobs will be created.
jensen-huang.work: An Interview with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang About Chip Controls, AI Factories, and Enterprise Pragmatism
jensen-huang.why: He expects AI and robotics to create many jobs and to expand GDP over the next five to ten years, outweighing the jobs lost.

josh-hawley.q: The AI enthusiasts rush to say all these losses will be replaced—and more! But with what, exactly? Sweeping floors at a data center?
josh-hawley.work: AI Threatens the Working Man
josh-hawley.why: After forecasting millions of lost jobs in driving, manufacturing and services, he dismisses the claim that the losses will be replaced.

marc-andreessen.q: Comparative advantage in the context of a properly free market guarantees high employment regardless of the level of technology.
marc-andreessen.work: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto
marc-andreessen.why: He holds that technology does not reduce total employment and that job growth can continue forever.

mark-zuckerberg.q: The common belief is that AI will automate jobs away. But that hasn't really been how the history of technology has worked. Usually, you create things that take away 90% of the work, and that leads you to want more people, not less.
mark-zuckerberg.work: Mark Zuckerberg: AI will write most Meta code in 18 months
mark-zuckerberg.why: Right after predicting Meta will hire more customer-support staff because of AI, he rejects the belief that AI will automate jobs away.

noah-smith.q: Even if I’m wrong, though — even if the AI job apocalypse does eventually come — it doesn’t seem like it’s coming soon, and it certainly isn’t here right now.
noah-smith.work: AI keeps stubbornly refusing to take our jobs
noah-smith.why: He presents evidence that AI's new tasks match or exceed the tasks it replaces, and he does not expect net job loss soon.

paul-kingsnorth.q: It is also the basis of a newly-emergent technology - AI - which will at minimum be responsible for mass unemployment, fakery on an unprecedented scale and the breakdown of shared notions of reality.
paul-kingsnorth.why: Even in the least alarming (materialist) reading, which he calls only slightly more reassuring, he says AI will at minimum cause mass unemployment.

reid-hoffman.q: In the past, it has always been breakthrough technologies that have created the jobs of the future—and I expect it to be no different this time.
reid-hoffman.work: Impromptu: Amplifying Our Humanity Through AI
reid-hoffman.why: While granting AI will eliminate some jobs, he expects it to create the jobs of the future as past technologies did.

robin-hanson.q: The big picture is that it will take decades for AI to have big econ impact.
robin-hanson.work: AI Is GPT, & GPTs Go Slow
robin-hanson.why: He says noticeable effects on workforce participation will take decades, not the next ten years.

samuel-hammond.q: This “perfect complementarity” between production and consumption is why automation doesn’t lead to technological unemployment.
samuel-hammond.why: In a section applying growth models to AI automation, he argues that automation does not produce technological unemployment, because labor shifts to tasks that are still in demand.

taylor-barkley.q: AI won’t replace humans; it will augment our capabilities in ways that make them more valuable, not less.
taylor-barkley.work: Is AI Going to Take My Job? A Christian Response to Technological Disruption
taylor-barkley.why: He argues that AI will complement labor rather than cause net job loss.

tristan-harris.q: They know that this is coming. They know that they don't need nearly as many people.
tristan-harris.work: The Great Simplification ep. 214: Tristan Harris (transcript)
tristan-harris.why: Describing CEOs planning mass layoffs and rejecting the idea that 'humans will always find something else to do', Harris expects net job loss.

tyler-cowen.q: I think there'll be full employment pretty much forever. That doesn't worry me.
tyler-cowen.work: Tyler Cowen — The #1 bottleneck to AI progress is humans
tyler-cowen.why: Asked about AI and the future of work, he predicts full employment indefinitely.

andrew-yang.q: I hope that we heed Jacob’s warning. We are running out of time.
andrew-yang.why: He endorses a researcher's warning of a >10% chance of AI destroying humanity this decade and calls it a humanity-scale challenge.

anton-korinek.q: It's something that I would not rule out, and as a society, I think we absolutely want to spend resources on forestalling that.
anton-korinek.work: Interview: Anton Korinek (Econ Focus, Fourth Quarter 2025)
anton-korinek.why: Asked about catastrophic AI outcomes, he says he would not rule them out and goes on to endorse spending on mitigating AI existential risks.

arvind-narayanan.q: the x-risk framing is the one that is driving public concern and much policy discourse, despite the fact that credible causal pathways haven’t been articulated (and attempts to do so are unconvincing to say the least).
arvind-narayanan.work: A big-tent or small-tent AI safety movement?
arvind-narayanan.why: The authors say no credible pathway to AI extinction has been shown, and elsewhere in the essay say they may not consider superintelligence a threat.

balaji-srinivasan.q: which is like how how is AI risk real? Just turn it off. The whole thing is set up for you to be able to turn it off.
balaji-srinivasan.work: Why Balaji Srinivasan Thinks the SaaS Apocalypse Is Overhyped (a16z; published by a16z as 'Balaji on Why AI Raises the Cost of Verification')
balaji-srinivasan.why: After arguing that incentives and kill switches prevent a self-replicating Skynet, he dismisses AI risk as solvable by turning the system off.

bernie-sanders.q: AI is an existential threat to humanity. It must be treated as such.
bernie-sanders.work: Don't Let Big Tech Dictate Humanity's Future
bernie-sanders.why: Sanders states in his own voice that AI is an existential threat.

brian-merchant.q: Do I share the x-riskers’ fear that out-of-control, super-intelligent AI agents might end the world? I do not.
brian-merchant.work: The politics and possibilities of 'AI could kill us all'
brian-merchant.why: He says directly that he does not share the fear of AI-caused extinction and finds no credible account of how it would happen.

bruce-schneier.q: I actually don’t think that AI poses a risk to human extinction.
bruce-schneier.work: On the Catastrophic Risk of AI
bruce-schneier.why: Explaining his signature on the CAIS statement, he says plainly he does not think AI poses an extinction risk.

bryan-caplan.q: I’ve listened to the fearful past the point of patience, and I remain convinced that the risks of AI extermination are barely worth thinking about.
bryan-caplan.why: He calls the risk of AI extermination barely worth thinking about and offers to bet against AI disaster.

chris-callison-burch.work: Should We Trust AI? (Q&A with Chris Callison-Burch)
chris-callison-burch.why: Asked about a robot takeover, he rejects the extinction-level framing and calls the probability of AI apocalypse vanishingly small.

chris-murphy.q: So they won’t protect us. They can’t. As long as money is the only incentive, they will race to build the machine that could destroy us.
chris-murphy.work: AI Leaders Are Sounding the Alarm. Who's Listening?
chris-murphy.why: He treats recursive self-improvement as a real danger of a machine that could destroy us.

cory-doctorow.q: First of all, this is facially absurd. Throwing more words and GPUs into the word-guessing program won't make it sentient.
cory-doctorow.work: The Reverse-Centaur's Guide to Criticizing AI
cory-doctorow.why: He calls the 'AI Safety' worry that AI will turn humanity into paperclips facially absurd.

curtis-yarvin.q: Nonetheless, our argument is that there is zero risk to humanity from arbitrary virtual intelligence.
curtis-yarvin.why: The essay's stated thesis is that AI poses zero risk to humanity.

daniel-faggella.q: But an entity with great power and completely arbitrary goals could end sentient life (a la Bostrom’s Paperclip Maximizer) and prevent the blossoming of more complexity and life.
daniel-faggella.work: A Worthy Successor: The Purpose of AGI
daniel-faggella.why: He describes an unworthy successor AI that could end sentient life, probably including human deaths, as a real danger to prevent.

daniel-jeffries.q: Never mind that the AI revolution is probably not going to be any of these things. It's going to do some wonderful things, some iffy things, and some bad too. It won't bring about utopia or the end of the world or destroy all the jobs.
daniel-jeffries.work: AI, Art, Blurred Lines and the Looming Nightmare of Copyright Expansion
daniel-jeffries.why: He states in his own voice that AI will not bring about the end of the world, and elsewhere labels doom fears a 'Doomsday Cult'.

dario-amodei.q: This vacillation is unfortunate, as the technology itself doesn’t care about what is fashionable, and we are considerably closer to real danger in 2026 than we were in 2023.
dario-amodei.why: The scene asks how a civilization survived its technological adolescence 'without destroying yourself', and he calls that question apt for humanity with AI.

david-sacks.q: None of this is to gainsay the progress. We are seeing strong improvement in quality, usability, and price/performance across the top model companies. This is the stuff of great engineering and should be celebrated. It’s just not the stuff of apocalyptic pronouncements.
david-sacks.work: Long X post: the 'Goldilocks' state of AI and why the doomer narratives were wrong
david-sacks.why: In a post arguing the 'Doomer narratives were wrong', he says current AI progress does not warrant apocalyptic claims.

dean-ball.q: It is not any one of these things, but the combination of them, that gives me high confidence that AI existential risk is highly unlikely and thus not worth extreme policy mitigations
dean-ball.work: 2023 (Or, Why I am Not a Doomer)
dean-ball.why: In the section titled 'Why I am Not a Doomer' he concludes with high confidence that existential risk is highly unlikely, and adds that 'If anyone builds it, everyone dies' is false.

demis-hassabis.q: in my view, there's still significant risk, and we've got to do research carefully to quantify what that risk is, and then deal with it ahead of time with as much foresight as possible, rather than after the fact
demis-hassabis.work: Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis on AGI and AI in the Military
demis-hassabis.why: Asked whether AI disempowering humans and escaping control is a default path or a tail risk, he says the risk is unknown but still significant.

dwarkesh-patel.q: But Marc dismisses the concern that we may fail to control models, especially as they reach human level and beyond. And that’s where I disagree.
dwarkesh-patel.why: Responding to Andreessen's claim that AI killing humanity is a category error, he says the loss-of-control concern is legitimate.

ed-zitron.q: Everybody doing backflips out of fear about “powerful, autonomous AI breaking out of the sandbox” is mostly doing so because a British guy went on TV and said “AI will kill us all,”
ed-zitron.work: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands
ed-zitron.why: He dismisses the 'AI will kill us all' warnings (the same sentence ends calling them 'densely packed with bullshit') and elsewhere calls p(doom) talk and AI 2027 fan fiction.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: If somebody builds a too-powerful AI, under present conditions, I expect that every single member of the human species and all biological life on Earth dies shortly thereafter.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: The Only Way to Deal With the Threat From AI? Shut It Down
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He expects extinction from superhuman AI built under current conditions.

elon-musk.q: AI is a fundamental existential risk for human civilization, and I don’t think people fully appreciate that.
elon-musk.work: Elon Musk Governor's Interview (NGA 2017, AI segment transcript)
elon-musk.why: Speaking to the governors in his own voice, he calls AI an existential risk to civilization; later texts repeat a 10 to 20% annihilation estimate.

emily-m-bender.q: But no, the harms aren’t going to come from autonomous “AI” that just hasn’t been taught appropriate values.
emily-m-bender.work: On NYT Magazine on AI: Resist the Urge to be Impressed
emily-m-bender.why: She dismisses harm from autonomous misaligned AI, the source of extinction scenarios, as a strawman problem.

erik-hoel.q: Pandora's box has been forever unlocked. Forevermore, we will live with the existential risk of AI.
erik-hoel.work: AI progress has plateaued below GPT-5 level
erik-hoel.why: Even while arguing progress is plateauing, he affirms AI existential risk is real and permanent.

gary-marcus.q: My p(doom) is still lower than most industry people’s. I am at maybe 3% now, much higher than a month ago, contemplating what a wealthy, reckless megalomaniac might in the worst circumstances do,
gary-marcus.work: Why my p(doom) has risen, dramatically
gary-marcus.why: He puts his own probability of AI doom at about 3%: small, but real.

geoffrey-hinton.q: There is also a longer term existential threat that will arise when we create digital beings that are more intelligent than ourselves.
geoffrey-hinton.why: In his Nobel banquet speech Hinton names an existential threat from AI smarter than humans.

helen-toner.q: The classic AI risks—catastrophic misuse, catastrophic misalignment—could indeed be game over for dynamism, so we need to handle those.
helen-toner.work: In search of a dynamist vision for safe superhuman AI
helen-toner.why: Right after agreeing that dynamism is no help 'if all the humans are dead or totally disempowered', she treats catastrophic misalignment as a real risk that must be handled.

holly-elmore.q: A catastrophic accident could easily kill everyone on the plane— human extinction.
holly-elmore.why: In her metaphor for the race to superintelligence, she says the expected outcome includes human extinction.

jack-clark.q: one can concoct plausible scenarios by which AI could kill every single person on the planet. To think building this technology is without risk would be an act of hubris or insanity.
jack-clark.work: Import AI 458: Reckoning with the future; and a singularity story
jack-clark.why: He calls scenarios in which AI kills everyone plausible and says denying the risk would be hubris.

jaron-lanier.q: Given the power and potential reach of these new systems, it’s not unreasonable to fear extinction as a possible result.
jaron-lanier.why: He grants that extinction is a reasonable fear, arising from misuse and bad operation of the systems.

jeff-jarvis.q: a machine so powerful it could destroy humankind unless we listen to its creators. I call bullshit.
jeff-jarvis.why: He dismisses the idea of an AI that could destroy humanity.

karen-hao.q: Because there’s no scientific evidence that we can actually develop AGI, the people who are strongly — have this strong conviction that they will do it and that it’s going to happen soon, it is just purely based on belief.
karen-hao.work: Journalist Karen Hao on Sam Altman, OpenAI & the 'Quasi-Religious' Push for Artificial Intelligence
karen-hao.why: She treats both the utopian and the doom AGI camps as quasi-religious beliefs without scientific grounding, and says that when tested their logic does not hold.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: I might put AI xrisk in the next 20 years at ~5%. But 5% chance of extinction or similarly bad outcome is, well, still incredibly high!
leopold-aschenbrenner.work: Nobody's on the ball on AGI alignment
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He gives his own probability for extinction-level AI risk and calls it incredibly high, so he treats the risk as real.

marc-andreessen.q: Fortunately, I am here to bring the good news: AI will not destroy the world, and in fact may save it.
marc-andreessen.work: Why AI Will Save the World
marc-andreessen.why: He flatly denies that AI will destroy the world and dismisses 'killer software' scenarios.

max-tegmark.q: Sadly, I now feel that we’re living the movie “Don’t look up” for another existential threat: unaligned superintelligence.
max-tegmark.work: The 'Don't Look Up' Thinking That Could Doom Us With AI
max-tegmark.why: He calls unaligned superintelligence an existential threat that could cause human extinction.

meredith-whittaker.q: suddenly claims about sentience and about, you know,  you know, the superintelligence and about, you know, AI being on the cusp of, you know,  breaking into full consciousness and perhaps endangering human life. All of this almost like  religious, um, religious rhetoric
meredith-whittaker.work: Signal's President on AI, Advertising, and Running a Popular Messaging App
meredith-whittaker.why: She dismisses claims that AI might endanger human life as quasi-religious hype built around ChatGPT, not a real risk.

michael-kratsios.q: Ideological fixations on social equity, climate catastrophism and so-called existential risk are dangers to progress and obstacles to responsibly harnessing this technology as an extension of human ingenuity and capacities.
michael-kratsios.work: US statement at the Security Council open debate 'Artificial intelligence and international peace and security' (10005th meeting)
michael-kratsios.why: He dismisses 'so-called existential risk' as an ideological fixation, rejecting the idea that it is a real risk to plan around.

miles-brundage.q: We need to accept that at best, we will just barely avoid some of the worst case scenarios (e.g., an AI-enabled biological weapon that kills billions, a rogue AI takeover, or stable global totalitarianism enabled by AI)
miles-brundage.work: We're in Triage Mode for AI Policy
miles-brundage.why: He treats AI scenarios that kill billions, or a rogue AI takeover, as real possibilities we might only just avoid.

noah-smith.q: But if the biologists are wrong, and the AI of 2027 or 2032 or 2049 can design doomsday viruses, the consequence could be that our whole species dies.
noah-smith.work: Two missing pieces in the AI safety discussion
noah-smith.why: He argues that AI-designed bioweapons are a credible route to human extinction and urges readers to take it seriously.

oren-cass.q: These could be enormously costly, and lead to massive human suffering, but they are not existential. They are not even the equivalent of an old-fashioned war.
oren-cass.why: He argues that realistic AI disasters come with checkpoints and are fixable, so they are not existential; the other essay says not to 'fear it as an extinction-level threat'.

richard-blumenthal.q: The dangers are not just extinction but loss of jobs, one of potentially the worst nightmares that we have.
richard-blumenthal.work: Oversight of A.I.: Principles for Regulation (S. Hrg. 118-108), opening statement of Chair Blumenthal
richard-blumenthal.why: In his opening statement he counts extinction among the real dangers of AI, alongside job loss, after crediting witnesses' fact-based warnings of an existential threat.

ro-khanna.q: That means responsible AI pacing and calling for a U.S.-China treaty banning practices that allow AI to advance itself autonomously. That power risks humans losing control entirely
ro-khanna.work: Ro Khanna: Trump has no cards left to play ahead of the China summit
ro-khanna.why: He treats loss of human control to self-advancing AI as a real threat to 'humanity itself' warranting a treaty.

robin-hanson.q: While I agree that this is a logically possible scenario, not excluded by what we know, I am disappointed to see so many giving it such a high credence, given how crazy far it seems from our prior experience.
robin-hanson.why: He grants the extinction-by-foom scenario is logically possible but treats it as far-fetched and wrongly given high credence.

sam-altman.q: Development of superhuman machine intelligence (SMI) [1] is probably the greatest threat to the continued existence of humanity.
sam-altman.why: He calls superhuman machine intelligence the greatest threat to humanity's continued existence.

samuel-hammond.q: Even if the intermediate stages of AI don’t kill us all, they may indirectly affect x-risk by upending the very institutions we'll need during the stage that does.
samuel-hammond.why: Hammond assumes a later stage of AI may pose extinction-level risk; elsewhere he calls dismissing AGI risk as 'sci-fi' a failure of imagination.

scott-alexander.q: I believe - just like Geoff Hinton, Bill Gates, Sam Altman, Daniel Dennett, etc - that there’s a pretty serious risk of human extinction from AI over the next few decades.
scott-alexander.work: In Continued Defense Of Effective Altruism
scott-alexander.why: He states in his own voice that the extinction risk from AI is serious.

scott-santens.q: The winning scenario is aligned AI. The losing scenario is not that China gets there first. The losing scenario is that anyone gets there with a misaligned system.
scott-santens.work: Our Data. Our Resources. Our Terms and Conditions.
scott-santens.why: In a section titled 'The Race We Might Not Survive', citing extinction-risk estimates, he names misaligned AI as the losing scenario.

steven-adler.q: Even a 1-2% chance on ‘superintelligence will kill everyone on Earth’ is an absolutely outlandish probability to tolerate, if it is correct and if there’s anything we can do about it.
steven-adler.work: Review: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies
steven-adler.why: Reviewing the book in his own voice, he treats a superintelligence extinction risk as real enough to act on even at low probability.

stuart-russell.q: achieving AGI would present potential catastrophic risks to humanity, up to and including human extinction.
stuart-russell.work: Written Testimony before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology, & the Law ('Oversight of A.I.: Principles for Regulation')
stuart-russell.why: In his executive summary Russell says that, given our lack of control methods, AGI poses risks up to human extinction.

ted-cruz.q: Of course, these existential dangers are all theoretical; we’ve never actually seen such damage from AI.
ted-cruz.work: Sen. Cruz: Congress Should Not Allow a Big Govt-Big Tech Takeover of AI (executive session opening statement)
ted-cruz.why: He dismisses existential risk claims as theoretical hype used for regulatory capture.

timnit-gebru.q: the idea of superintelligent machines with their own agency and decision-making power is not only far from reality
timnit-gebru.work: The Exploited Labor Behind Artificial Intelligence
timnit-gebru.why: Writing against doomsday 'Terminator' narratives, she calls the superintelligent-machine scenario far from reality.

tristan-harris.q: And neither Xi Jinping nor Donald Trump, nor a Chinese military general, nor an American military general, nor a regular mom feeding her kids in Kansas wants uncontrollable AI that is existential for the world.
tristan-harris.work: The Great Simplification ep. 214: Tristan Harris (transcript)
tristan-harris.why: Harris describes loss-of-control AI as an existential danger to the world that leaders should coordinate to prevent.

venkatesh-rao.q: This is a philosophically naive and incoherent case for fear that deserves to be taken about as seriously as fear of ghosts or hell.
venkatesh-rao.why: Directly after describing the fear that 'a self-improving general intelligence will emerge and destroy us', Rao calls that case incoherent and comparable to fear of ghosts.

vitalik-buterin.q: One way in which AI gone wrong could make the world worse is (almost) the worst possible way: it could literally cause human extinction.
vitalik-buterin.why: After setting out the case that superintelligent AI could cause extinction, he judges the risk worth worrying about.

william-macaskill.q: Explosive technological progress could lead to new weapons and other destructive technologies. This could increase the risk of global catastrophe, including human extinction
william-macaskill.why: In listing the grand challenges of an AI-driven intelligence explosion, the authors say it could raise the risk of human extinction, alongside a separate AI takeover risk they treat as substantial.

yann-lecun.q: Okay, so AI doomers imagine all kinds of catastrophe scenarios of how AI could escape or control and basically kill us all, and that relies on a whole bunch of assumptions that are mostly false.
yann-lecun.work: Transcript for Yann LeCun: Meta AI, Open Source, Limits of LLMs, AGI & the Future of AI
yann-lecun.why: Asked why the doomers are wrong, LeCun says the scenarios in which AI kills us all rest on assumptions that are mostly false.

yoshua-bengio.q: Of course not; given the magnitude of the potentially negative impact (up to human extinction), it is imperative to invest more in both understanding and quantifying the risks and developing mitigating solutions.
yoshua-bengio.work: Reasoning through arguments against taking AI safety seriously
yoshua-bengio.why: He argues throughout that AI extinction risk is real and not negligible, citing a 5% median expert estimate as far from Pascal's-wager territory.

yuval-noah-harari.q: The rise of AI poses an existential danger to humankind, not because of the malevolence of computers, but because of our own shortcomings.
yuval-noah-harari.work: 'Never summon a power you can't control': Yuval Noah Harari on how AI could threaten democracy and divide the world
yuval-noah-harari.why: He states that AI poses an existential danger to humanity.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: Building superintelligence poses large existential risks. Also known as: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies. Where ‘it’ is superintelligence, and ‘dies’ is that probably everyone on the planet literally dies.
zvi-mowshowitz.work: New Statement Calls For Not Building Superintelligence For Now
zvi-mowshowitz.why: Opening his own explanation of why he signed the FLI statement, he says building superintelligence probably kills everyone.

adam-thierer.q: Doomsday forecasts persist, however, because the media and academics have powerful incentives to promote tales of a coming techno-apocalypse.
adam-thierer.work: AI and the jobs apocalypse that wasn't
adam-thierer.why: He argues that fears of AI job loss were wrong and persist because of incentives rather than evidence.

balaji-srinivasan.q: The point being that like AI overlords I don't actually think are in the offing. However, there's been so much sci-fi about them that people will
balaji-srinivasan.work: Why Balaji Srinivasan Thinks the SaaS Apocalypse Is Overhyped (a16z; published by a16z as 'Balaji on Why AI Raises the Cost of Verification')
balaji-srinivasan.why: He says AI overlords are not coming and attributes people's fear to science fiction, i.e. fear outruns the evidence.

bernie-sanders.q: The American people see what is coming. And they don’t like it.
bernie-sanders.work: Artificial intelligence is coming for the working class. We must fight back
bernie-sanders.why: Citing polls of public concern about AI job losses, he endorses those fears as an accurate reading of what is coming.

chris-murphy.q: It is hard to overstate that risk.
chris-murphy.work: AI Leaders Are Sounding the Alarm. Who's Listening?
chris-murphy.why: On recursive self-improvement he says the danger is hard to overstate, the opposite of fear exceeding evidence.

christopher-ferguson.q: The public narrative — “a chatbot encouraged a teen to commit suicide” — has already outpaced both the actual evidence from the case and any evidence from research.
christopher-ferguson.work: A tragedy, a lawsuit, and the birth of an AI moral panic
christopher-ferguson.why: In an essay warning of a coming 'AI moral panic', the author says public fear about chatbots has run ahead of the evidence.

curtis-yarvin.q: This is why no one should fear the LLM revolution. It is as likely as the screwdriver revolution, or perhaps the Roomba revolution.
curtis-yarvin.why: He argues the feared AI takeover is as unlikely as a screwdriver revolution, and his companion essay treats AI-risk belief as a popular delusion.

daniel-jeffries.q: But not if we kill it with short-sightedness and bizarrely overblown fears driven by doomsday cultists and media stories about the end of all jobs.
daniel-jeffries.work: AI, Art, Blurred Lines and the Looming Nightmare of Copyright Expansion
daniel-jeffries.why: He calls current public fears about AI doom and job loss overblown and speculative.

dario-amodei.q: just as I think most people are underestimating how bad the risks could be.
dario-amodei.why: He says most people underestimate AI's risks, the opposite of fearing too much.

david-sacks.q: This means that apocalyptic predictions of job loss are as overhyped as AGI itself.
david-sacks.work: Long X post: the 'Goldilocks' state of AI and why the doomer narratives were wrong
david-sacks.why: He calls both AGI fears and job-loss fears overhyped relative to what is observed.

demis-hassabis.q: I think the public’s right to be concerned.
demis-hassabis.work: Demis Hassabis Thinks We're in the 'Foothills of the Singularity'
demis-hassabis.why: Asked about negative public perception of AI, he says the concern is justified and that he shares it.

ed-zitron.q: but nevertheless have had the effect of making a lot of people really scared of AI, even if AI can’t really do the things he’s talking about.
ed-zitron.work: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands
ed-zitron.why: He argues the public fear stirred up by a researcher's warnings is about capabilities AI does not have.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: A large amount of failure to panic sufficiently, seems to me to stem from a lack of appreciation for the incredible potential lethality of this thing that Earthlings as a culture have not named.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: AGI Ruin: A List of Lethalities
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He thinks people fear AI too little, not too much.

elizabeth-nolan-brown.q: Unfortunately, we're almost certain to keep seeing people sue AI companies—language models, image generators, etc.—on dubious grounds, because America is in the midst of a growing AI tech panic.
elizabeth-nolan-brown.work: Sarah Silverman's Lawsuit Against OpenAI Is Full of Nonsense Claims
elizabeth-nolan-brown.why: She describes public reaction to AI as a 'tech panic', a theme repeated in her pieces on elections and Moltbook.

elon-musk.q: Well first of all, on the artificial intelligence front, I have exposure to the most cutting edge AI, and I think people should be really concerned about it.
elon-musk.work: Elon Musk Governor's Interview (NGA 2017, AI segment transcript)
elon-musk.why: He argues the public is under-concerned, not over-concerned, about AI.

erik-hoel.q: But are such levels of concern reasonable? I think yes, absolutely. If nothing changes.
erik-hoel.work: I am Bing, and I am evil
erik-hoel.why: Discussing panic about AI apocalypse, he says that level of concern is justified and calls for more.

felix-simon.q: We diagnose the alarmist discourse surrounding AI and elections as a version of what Orben (2020) has termed the “Sisyphean cycle of technology panics”
felix-simon.work: Don't Panic (Yet): Assessing the Evidence and Discourse Around Generative AI and Elections
felix-simon.why: The paper argues that fears about AI's electoral effects outran the evidence and are part of a recurring public overreaction to new technology.

geoffrey-hinton.q: And that got me very worried and it should get you very worried too.
geoffrey-hinton.work: Will AI outsmart human intelligence? (Royal Institution lecture, transcript)
geoffrey-hinton.why: Hinton tells the public it should be more worried, not less, about the advantages of digital intelligence.

george-hotz.q: This is negative valence hype, not only is it not true, it’s mostly designed to make you feel bad about yourself
george-hotz.work: I love LLMs, I hate hype
george-hotz.why: He says fears of a closing window or a permanent underclass are untrue, and he also rejects hard-takeoff scenarios.

guillaume-verdon.q: those that are for more centralization of power, control, and more regulations are aligning themselves with the doomers, because that sort of instilling fear in people is a great way for them to give up more control, and give the government more power.
guillaume-verdon.work: Guillaume Verdon: Beff Jezos, E/acc Movement, Physics, Computation & AGI (Lex Fridman Podcast #407)
guillaume-verdon.why: Speaking of those who fear a sudden takeoff into nanobots, he says from experience that the feared scenario is much harder than they believe.

holly-elmore.q: There’s plenty we can do together to make the world safer even if some people want to bury their heads in the sand about just how dangerous AI could be.
holly-elmore.work: The problem is not that leftists don't "believe" in AI
holly-elmore.why: She says people underrate how dangerous AI could be, the opposite of excessive fear.

jack-clark.q: But mostly, I think we need to listen: Generally, people know what’s going on. We must do a better job of listening to the concerns people have.
jack-clark.work: Import AI 431: Technological Optimism and Appropriate Fear
jack-clark.why: After describing public nightmares and anxieties about AI and his own 'appropriate fear', he says people generally understand what is going on.

jd-vance.q: And I think there's too much fear that AI will simply replace jobs rather than augmenting so many of the things that we do.
jd-vance.work: Remarks by the Vice President at the American Dynamism Summit
jd-vance.why: He says public fear about AI's effect on jobs is excessive.

jeff-jarvis.q: I intervened (as we say in circles) and said that first journalists must be educated about AI because too much of their coverage amounts to moral panic
jeff-jarvis.why: He calls public alarm about AI moral panic, like past panics over radio and TV.

jensen-huang.q: If we scare this country into thinking that AI is somehow a nuclear bomb, so that everybody hates AI and everybody’s afraid of AI, I don’t know how you’re helping the United States. You’re doing it a disservice.
jensen-huang.work: Jensen Huang: Will Nvidia's moat persist?
jensen-huang.why: He calls the fear-raising misguided and harmful. Elsewhere he says alarmist job warnings, such as the radiology one, 'went too far' and 'did harm'.

marc-andreessen.q: In contrast to this positive view, the public conversation about AI is presently shot through with hysterical fear and paranoia.
marc-andreessen.work: Why AI Will Save the World
marc-andreessen.why: He calls current AI fear an irrational moral panic.

matt-stoller.q: So color me skeptical of ghost stories. We can manage the risks of AI products. The real crisis is that we no longer manage the risks of anything.
matt-stoller.why: Closing an essay titled 'Stop Panicking About AI', he calls the doom narrative ghost stories and the risks manageable.

max-tegmark.q: instead, the most influential responses have been a combination of denial, mockery, and resignation so darkly comical that it’s deserving of an Oscar.
max-tegmark.work: The 'Don't Look Up' Thinking That Could Doom Us With AI
max-tegmark.why: He argues society takes the AI threat too lightly, not too seriously.

miles-brundage.q: most people don't know or care about most of this stuff, and that needs to change in order for policymakers to "feel the heat"
miles-brundage.work: We're in Triage Mode for AI Policy
miles-brundage.why: He argues that the public is too little concerned about AI risks, not too much.

neil-chilson.q: This knowledge problem is a major constraint on raw intelligence, suggesting that many AI doomer scenarios are far overblown.
neil-chilson.why: In his own voice he calls many AI doom scenarios far overblown.

noah-smith.q: And yet the instinctive negativity with which AI is being met by a large segment of the American public feels like an unreasonable reaction to me.
noah-smith.work: I love AI. Why doesn't everyone?
noah-smith.why: He argues that much of the public's anti-AI case, such as the claims about water use and present job loss, does not hold up against the data.

oren-cass.q: Pontificating that AI could someday destroy humanity is rather a waste of time when it cannot yet answer a basic question without hallucinating.
oren-cass.work: Is It Interesting to Say That AI Isn't That Interesting?
oren-cass.why: He argues the burden of proof is on those predicting catastrophe and that current evidence does not support their fears; the companion essay calls the moment 'our present panic'.

paul-kingsnorth.q: Notably, though, as we saw last time, the people actually running the show do not talk like this. In contrast, they are ‘kept awake at night’, as Google’s CEO put it last week, by the fear of what they are creating.
paul-kingsnorth.why: He sums up the 'chill out about AI' think pieces and then rebuts them, arguing the fear is warranted because the builders themselves are afraid.

pete-buttigieg.q: As I’ve done so, it has become clear to me that—even with all of the media attention and public interest in this topic—we are still profoundly underreacting, and we are dangerously underprepared.
pete-buttigieg.work: We Are Still Underreacting on AI
pete-buttigieg.why: He says society underreacts to AI rather than overreacting.

richard-blumenthal.q: In no way disparagingly do I say that those fears are reinforced, because I think you have provided objective,
richard-blumenthal.work: Oversight of A.I.: Principles for Regulation (S. Hrg. 118-108), opening statement of Chair Blumenthal
richard-blumenthal.why: He says the public's fears of AI are backed by objective, fact-based expert testimony, the opposite of fear outrunning the evidence.

richard-sutton.q: The AI fear-mongers have not helped us see clearly, but they have gotten us to pay attention.
richard-sutton.why: He describes public discussion of AI as driven by fear, and elsewhere says AI's biggest risk is fear.

robin-hanson.q: Many of these fears, however, are either unfounded or overblown.
robin-hanson.why: He argues most AI fears outrun what we know, being driven by prejudice and fear of change.

russell-moore.q: The relative apathy of most of the American public to all this is itself a piece of the mystery.
russell-moore.work: AI Tech Bros Seem Awful. They Might Be Telling Us the Truth.
russell-moore.why: Moore argues the public is too apathetic about insiders' warnings of uncontrollable AI, the opposite of fearing it too much.

sam-altman.q: The fear and anxiety about AI is justified
sam-altman.work: Untitled post, shown on the blog as "-"
sam-altman.why: He states directly that public fear of AI is justified.

scott-alexander.q: I find myself more optimistic about alignment than the average person who thinks about AI safety at all (although still more pessimistic than the average member of the population)
scott-alexander.why: He says he is more pessimistic about AI than the average member of the public, so in his view public fear falls short of the evidence rather than exceeding it.

ted-cruz.q: Instead of excessively regulating a new product based on fear, my bill would help our country regulate AI based on evidence.
ted-cruz.why: He frames current regulatory pushes as driven by fear rather than evidence.

tyler-cowen.q: That fear was not based on peer-reviewed scientific research showing a high chance of doom, nor was doom indicated in any market prices of the time, including measures of risk.
tyler-cowen.work: A doomsday scenario for American AI
tyler-cowen.why: In his imagined postmortem, Cowen says the panic over AI doom was a story spread on social media rather than evidence-based, and that debating doom on 'a highly speculative basis' demoralizes us.

venkatesh-rao.q: I sincerely believe their fears are strictly nonsensical in a philosophical sense, in the same sense that I consider fear of ghosts or going to hell in an “afterlife” to be strictly nonsensical.
venkatesh-rao.why: Rao says the special fears people hold about AI are baseless, which entails that they exceed what the evidence supports.

yann-lecun.q: But people are exploiting the fear about the technology, and we’re running the risk of scaring people away from it.
yann-lecun.work: How Not to Be Stupid About AI, With Yann LeCun
yann-lecun.why: He says fear of AI is being exploited and is scaring people away from a beneficial technology, which means the fear goes beyond what is warranted.

yoshua-bengio.q: Yes, extreme risks from AI are being discussed more now and are not being systematically ridiculed anymore. But we are still not taking them seriously enough.
yoshua-bengio.work: Reasoning through arguments against taking AI safety seriously
yoshua-bengio.why: He says concern about AI risk still falls short of what the evidence warrants.

yuval-noah-harari.q: Unfortunately, a closer look at history reveals that humans actually have good reasons to fear powerful new technologies.
yuval-noah-harari.work: Why AI poses an existential danger to humanity
yuval-noah-harari.why: Replying to people who call AI warnings over-the-top, he says the fear is well founded.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: They fear for their jobs because it is sensible to fear for your job given what AI can clearly do, and how people are planning for and reacting to AI.
zvi-mowshowitz.work: The American People Really Hate Data Centers
zvi-mowshowitz.why: He calls public fears about AI taking jobs and about humanity being wiped out sensible, while singling out water-use worries as a moral panic.

alex-tabarrok.q: We also have plenty of evidence that the fears of AI experts are sincere.
alex-tabarrok.work: What Regulatory Capture Actually Looks Like
alex-tabarrok.why: He argues that AI company leaders like Amodei, Altman and Musk sincerely believe the risks they warn the public about.

brian-merchant.q: Declarations that AI is so powerful it might end the world are a kind of marketing, and anyone who says otherwise is just as off base as those who say that’s all that it is.
brian-merchant.work: The politics and possibilities of 'AI could kill us all'
brian-merchant.why: He argues AI leaders' risk talk is partly strategic 'doom marketing' to attract investors and attention, and in a second piece calls Anthropic's risk framing cynical.

chris-murphy.q: They are in a race to deploy and commercialize and profit, and they are paying mere lip service to the ways that AGI could destroy the already fraying fabric of our nation.
chris-murphy.work: In our scramble to win the AI race against China, we risk losing ourselves
chris-murphy.why: He accuses industry leaders of lip service and 'whitewash' about AI's dangers.

cory-doctorow.q: The tech bros who have spent the past year holding flashlights under their chins and intoning “Ayyyyyy Eyeeeee” in their very spookiest voices want us to think they’re evil sorcerers, not huxters
cory-doctorow.why: He argues that AI industry figures stage talk of AI danger to make their products look powerful, so they are not being straight about the real risks.

ed-zitron.q: For years the AI industry has engaged in endless, vague safety theater about the “risks” of AI, all while peddling software that is actively harmful and unreliable.
ed-zitron.work: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands
ed-zitron.why: He calls the industry's risk talk 'safety theater' and elsewhere says the labs deliberately misled the public about their models.

emily-m-bender.q: Going along with company executives and describing their products as beings with agency allows these executives to evade accountability while deceiving the public.
emily-m-bender.work: Forget 'superintelligence': error-prone AI nearly sparked world war three this month
emily-m-bender.why: She and her co-author say AI executives deceive the public, framing their doom talk as marketing that hides the real risks.

gary-marcus.q: This company simply cannot be trusted. Their software is becoming ever more dangerous; their internal security practices leave a lot to be desired; they aren’t being straight with the public
gary-marcus.why: He says OpenAI, a leading AI company, is not being honest with the public as its software grows more dangerous.

george-hotz.q: Like GPT 2, when Open AI came out with GPT two and raised a whole fake AI safety thing about that. Now the model is laughable. They used AI safety to hype up their company and it’s disgusting.
george-hotz.work: Lex Fridman Podcast #387 transcript: George Hotz
george-hotz.why: In the AI safety section (speaker labels dropped, but this is Hotz's argument that Lex then summarizes and pushes back on), he accuses OpenAI's leadership of using fake safety claims as hype.

holly-elmore.q: As much as they declare themselves “the good guys” (paging George Orwell) because they pay lip service to safety, they are arguably the worst guy.
holly-elmore.why: She accuses a leading AI company of paying lip service to safety and of safety-washing its risks.

jeff-jarvis.q: This turns out to be another instance of the doom-as-marketing strategy engaged in by both OpenAI and Anthropic.
jeff-jarvis.why: He says leading AI companies talk up risks as marketing, not as honest disclosure.

joanna-bryson.q: Yesterday in the process of switching his misdirection about AI from impossible scenarios (AGI) to the one we're already solving (superintelligence), he fully revealed his anti-regulatory, anti-government agenda.
joanna-bryson.work: OpenAI reveals the anti-regulatory intent of its regulatory disinformation
joanna-bryson.why: She calls Sam Altman's public account of AI risk misdirection that serves an anti-regulatory agenda.

karen-hao.q: And he will say different things to different people if he thinks they need to hear different things.
karen-hao.work: Karen Hao on How AI Colonialism Is Threatening the World (extended interview)
karen-hao.why: She describes Altman telling both the optimist and the doom factions that he shares their view of AI's risks, which casts doubt on his candor.

marc-andreessen.q: This explains the mismatch between the words and actions of the Baptists who are actually building and funding AI – watch their actions, not their words.
marc-andreessen.work: Why AI Will Save the World
marc-andreessen.why: He says those building AI who warn of risk do not mean what they say, and elsewhere calls risk-warning CEOs self-interested Bootleggers.

matt-stoller.q: It’s hard to escape there’s something very strange and manipulative about AI safety discourse. The AI doomers have a lot of money, they run the major AI companies, they fund most AI research
matt-stoller.why: He calls the risk messaging from those running major AI companies manipulative and tied to their financial interests (e.g. seeking an antitrust exemption).

meredith-whittaker.q: This means that much of what we know about AI is written by the public relations and marketing departments of these same companies.
meredith-whittaker.work: Written Testimony of Meredith Whittaker: "Artificial Intelligence: Societal and Ethical Implications"
meredith-whittaker.why: She testifies that AI companies' public messaging promotes benefits while staying silent about harmful uses and problems; the '26' is a footnote marker in the source text.

noah-smith.q: So the fact that they’re still calling for a slowdown, in defiance of their own financial interests, is a clear sign that their worry about human extinction is sincere.
noah-smith.work: Two missing pieces in the AI safety discussion
noah-smith.why: He judges the heads of the AI labs sincere about the risks they warn of.

ruha-benjamin.q: At the very least, we should recognize the hollow ethical commitments of the artificial intelligentsia and the deceitful machinations of those who fancy themselves to be humanity’s stewards.
ruha-benjamin.why: She calls AI leaders' safety talk duplicitous ('Janus... their god of choice') and their ethical commitments hollow.

scott-alexander.q: The alternative is that all these people believed it then, and still believe it now, for the same reason that all of the independent experts and academics believe it.
scott-alexander.work: AI Safety Is Not A Corporate Plot
scott-alexander.why: His thesis is that AI company leaders' risk warnings are sincere beliefs, not a corporate plot.

ted-cruz.q: Some wealthy and well-connected AI entrepreneurs and their corporate allies hype up AI inventions as uniquely powerful and dangerous.
ted-cruz.work: Sen. Cruz: Congress Should Not Allow a Big Govt-Big Tech Takeover of AI (executive session opening statement)
ted-cruz.why: He says AI leaders exaggerate dangers to secure regulatory capture, so their risk talk is not candid.

yuval-noah-harari.q: The companies tell us completely contradictory things. When it comes to accountability, the story is: it's just a game.
yuval-noah-harari.work: Yuval Noah Harari on the threat of AI: 'Fascism isn't the worst-case scenario. Fascism is still human'
yuval-noah-harari.why: He says AI companies downplay their products to avoid accountability while telling investors they are taking over the world.

brian-merchant.q: They would stop supporting efforts to ban AI lawmaking and to exempt themselves from product liability.
brian-merchant.work: Why the AI backlash has turned violent
brian-merchant.why: He lists dropping efforts to exempt themselves from product liability as something AI companies should do, implying they should be liable.

gary-marcus.q: We need liability, auditing, standards of malpractice, international treaties, too.
gary-marcus.work: Why my p(doom) has risen, dramatically
gary-marcus.why: He calls for legal liability for AI makers as part of the regulation he wants.

guillaume-verdon.q: I mean, the reality is that whoever deploys an AI system is liable for or should be liable for what it does.
guillaume-verdon.work: Guillaume Verdon: Beff Jezos, E/acc Movement, Physics, Computation & AGI (Lex Fridman Podcast #407)
guillaume-verdon.why: He says whoever deploys an AI system should be liable for what it does, and builds his market-safety argument on that.

joanna-bryson.q: Recommendation: Do not allow powerful agencies or individuals to cap their legal or tax liabilities when they
joanna-bryson.work: Why AI is amoral, and artefacts can't consent
joanna-bryson.why: Her formal recommendation (which goes on: 'fully automate a part of their business process, or obscure accountability for development and operation of their products') is that firms must stay legally liable for their AI products, which she says are manufactured products.

jonathan-haidt.q: And we hold them responsible for their safety lapses.
jonathan-haidt.work: Why You Should Be a Techno-Skeptic (TED talk transcript)
jonathan-haidt.why: He says tech companies, including AI companies targeting children, should be treated like makers of dangerous consumer products and held responsible.

josh-hawley.q: The bill would impose criminal penalties on companies whose products solicit children sexually or coach them toward self-harm.
josh-hawley.work: The American Covenant’s Answer to AI
josh-hawley.why: He describes the GUARD Act, which he introduced, imposing legal penalties on AI companies whose products harm children, and criticizes AI for having 'no liability'.

marsha-blackburn.q: Places a duty of care on AI developers in the design, development, and operation of AI platforms to prevent and mitigate foreseeable harm to users.
marsha-blackburn.work: Blackburn Unveils National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence (TRUMP AMERICA AI Act)
marsha-blackburn.why: Her office's summary of her own bill puts a legal duty of care on AI developers for foreseeable harm to users.

meredith-whittaker.q: We need to make sure that the people who are benefiting and profiting from these technologies have liability for their failures and for the harms that they commit.
meredith-whittaker.work: Reclaiming the Future: Privacy, Ethics & Organizing in Tech (Meredith Whittaker with Kade Crockford)
meredith-whittaker.why: She states directly that those who profit from AI should be liable for the harms it causes.

richard-blumenthal.q: When AI companies and their clients cause harm, they should be held liable.
richard-blumenthal.work: Oversight of A.I.: Rules for Artificial Intelligence (S. Hrg. 118-037), opening statement of Chair Blumenthal
richard-blumenthal.why: In his opening statement he states directly that AI companies should be liable for the harms they cause.

safiya-noble.q: These companies should be required and held accountable, legally, to pay for and remediate and do the cleanup of all the damage that they do in society.
safiya-noble.work: The complex questions that arise when algorithms and AI intersect with race (Code Switch)
safiya-noble.why: Discussing harmful tech products, she says companies should be legally accountable for the damage they cause.

steven-adler.q: My view: AI companies should be liable for harms their products cause.
steven-adler.work: The magic phrase that kills AI regulation
steven-adler.why: He states this directly as his own view, preferring a negligence standard.

ted-cruz.q: To be clear, a ‘regulatory sandbox’ is NOT a free pass. People creating or using AI still have to follow the same laws as everyone else.
ted-cruz.work: Sen. Cruz: AI Policy Should Harness the Power of American Ingenuity (opening statement, 'AI've Got a Plan' hearing)
ted-cruz.why: He says AI makers stay subject to existing negligence, consumer protection and other liability law.

tristan-harris.q: CHT recently just officially endorsed the AI LEAD Act introduced by both a Democratic and a Republican senator. This is Senators Durbin and Hawley, and it creates a liability for products that are defective that create harm.
tristan-harris.why: Harris's organisation endorsed a bill that makes AI makers liable for harm caused by defective products.
