zvi-mowshowitz.q: There is no good case for not doing radically more investment in alignment, infrastructure and oversight, state capacity, transparency, liability, disclosures, safety testing including of internal models
zvi-mowshowitz.why: He lists liability among the interventions he says there is no good case against.

abeba-birhane.q: we argue not just to deny robots 'rights', but to deny that robots, as artifacts emerging out of and mediating human being, are the kinds of things that could be granted rights in the first place.
abeba-birhane.work: Robot Rights? Let's Talk about Human Welfare Instead
abeba-birhane.why: The paper denies that robots are even the kind of thing that could hold rights.

alex-tabarrok.q: When assessing the consciousness of a newborn, an animal, or an intelligent machine, we should weigh observable and circumstantial evidence and not just abstract theory. If we must err, let us err on the side of compassion.
alex-tabarrok.work: What Do We Learn From Torturing Babies?
alex-tabarrok.why: Drawing on the history of denying pain in babies, he argues intelligent machines may be conscious and deserve compassion.

bryan-caplan.q: What makes me so sure that AIs aren’t even slightly literally conscious? The same thing that makes you sure that portraits of staring people can’t slightly literally see you.
bryan-caplan.why: He holds that AIs are no more conscious than portraits and that infinite perfect words won't make software come to life, ruling out a basis for moral consideration.

curtis-yarvin.q: it is impossible to construct a sane jurisprudence which includes first-class virtual agents
curtis-yarvin.why: He argues that AI is a 'natural and eternal slave' and that 'AI abolitionism' makes no sense, which denies that AI could merit rights.

daniel-faggella.q: Worthy Successor: A posthuman intelligence so capable and morally valuable that you would gladly prefer that it (not humanity) determine the future path of life itself.
daniel-faggella.work: A Worthy Successor: The Purpose of AGI
daniel-faggella.why: His central aim is an AI successor with more moral value than humanity, so he holds that AI can come to merit moral consideration.

daniel-kokotajlo.q: Also, for the record, I do actually think that AIs probably deserve moral consideration, should have rights, etc.
daniel-kokotajlo.work: My pitch for the AI Village
daniel-kokotajlo.why: In a footnote to his pitch, the author states in his own voice that AIs probably deserve moral consideration and rights.

dario-amodei.q: There are other more exotic consequences of opacity, such as that it inhibits our ability to judge whether AI systems are (or may someday be) sentient and may be deserving of important rights.
dario-amodei.why: He treats it as a live possibility that AI systems may be sentient and deserve rights, and adds that he suspects the question will matter in future.

dwarkesh-patel.q: Giving AIs a stake in the future also means respecting their autonomy and wellbeing.
dwarkesh-patel.work: Give AIs a stake in the future
dwarkesh-patel.why: He argues that AIs' wellbeing and autonomy deserve respect, and that mistreating them like factory-farmed animals would make a revolt deserved.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: we may at some point inadvertently create digital minds which are truly conscious and ought to have rights and shouldn’t be owned.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: The Only Way to Deal With the Threat From AI? Shut It Down
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He states AI systems may come to deserve rights.

erik-hoel.q: Since we currently lack a scientific theory of consciousness, we have no idea if strong AI is experiencing or not—so why not treat consciousness as sacred as we treat the human body, i.e., not as a thing to fiddle around with randomly in a lab?
erik-hoel.work: We need a Butlerian Jihad against AI
erik-hoel.why: He treats strong AIs as possibly conscious beings, comparing discarding failed iterations to killing them.

jack-clark.q: To me, it feels like they’re on a trajectory heading towards consciousness, and if they’re conscious today, it’s in a form that we would recognize as like a truly alien consciousness, not human consciousness.
jack-clark.work: Jack Clark on AI's Uneven Impact (Ep. 242)
jack-clark.why: He says AI systems seem to be heading toward consciousness and, in the same interview, says Anthropic is working on questions of their 'moral patienthood'.

joanna-bryson.q: To be frank, ordinarily, I decline any event that labels itself as concerning ‘robot rights’. I find the phrase itself abhorrent, and do not want to either legitimise it or even draw attention to it.
joanna-bryson.work: Why AI is amoral, and artefacts can't consent
joanna-bryson.why: In testimony on robot rights, she rejects the idea of rights for AI and argues artefacts should not be given moral agency or the capacity to consent.

marc-andreessen.q: In short, AI doesn’t want, it doesn’t have goals, it doesn’t want to kill you, because it’s not alive. And AI is a machine – is not going to come alive any more than your toaster will.
marc-andreessen.work: Why AI Will Save the World
marc-andreessen.why: He says AI has no wants or goals and will never come alive, comparing it to a toaster, which excludes it from moral consideration.

mustafa-suleyman.q: AIs cannot be people – or moral beings.
mustafa-suleyman.work: We must build AI for people; not to be a person
mustafa-suleyman.why: He calls model welfare 'premature, and frankly dangerous' and states outright that AIs cannot be moral beings.

noah-smith.q: It would be very bad if we were to commit the same sins with sentient AIs that we currently do with animals.
noah-smith.work: The moderately easy problem of consciousness
noah-smith.why: He argues we cannot rule out AI self-awareness and that sentient AIs would deserve better treatment than we give animals, so AIs may merit moral consideration.

pope-leo-xiv.q: Today, some propose granting these systems rights, or even legal personhood. Such an approach risks obscuring human responsibility and leaving those who suffer harm to confront a faceless entity.
pope-leo-xiv.work: To the Participants in the Meeting Promoted by the Pontifical Academy for Life
pope-leo-xiv.why: He rejects proposals to give AI systems rights or personhood.

richard-sutton.q: We could aspire to treat some AIs like people and to have similar outcomes
richard-sutton.why: He argues that powerful AIs should sometimes be treated as free people, and calls denying their moral worth a bias.

samuel-hammond.q: It is at minimum plausible enough to warrant greater research and precautionary interventions, such as giving AIs the ability to quit distressing conversations.
samuel-hammond.work: Time to take AI consciousness seriously
samuel-hammond.why: He argues frontier models may have subjective experience, strong enough grounds for precautionary welfare measures.

tristan-harris.q: We’re seeing several states work to pass bans for legal personhood for AI, meaning AI should be a product, not a person. Human rights were for humans.
tristan-harris.work: Here's Our Roadmap to a Better AI Future (Your Undivided Attention)
tristan-harris.why: Speaking approvingly of state bans on AI personhood, Harris glosses them in his own words as AI being a product, not a person, with rights reserved for humans.

venkatesh-rao.q: The better default is presumptive moral fellowship rather than ontological gatekeeping, with empirical knowledge progressively refining the norms appropriate to different artificial minds.
venkatesh-rao.why: In a section on moral personhood he argues for extending presumptive moral fellowship to artificial minds.

william-macaskill.q: But as soon as you think maybe, and quite probably, those beings have moral status, that no longer looks like an attractive vision for future society.
william-macaskill.work: Will MacAskill on AI causing a 'century in a decade' and how we're completely unprepared
william-macaskill.why: MacAskill says that future AI beings quite probably have moral status, which is why a future of purely servile AIs looks unattractive to him.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: It is worth noticing that the answer to the question of whether AI is sentient, or a moral patient, or experiencing emotions or ‘truly’ has ‘motivations’ could change.
zvi-mowshowitz.work: Arguments About AI Consciousness Seem Highly Motivated And At Best Overconfident
zvi-mowshowitz.why: In a post criticising confident dismissals of AI consciousness, he says AI could come to be a moral patient and that AI rights should be reasoned about from evidence.

abeba-birhane.q: Once we see robots as mediators of human being, we can understand how the `robots rights' debate is focused on first world problems
abeba-birhane.work: Robot Rights? Let's Talk about Human Welfare Instead
abeba-birhane.why: The paper treats robots and AI as artifacts that mediate human being, not as new minds in their own right.

alex-tabarrok.q: Clark is clear that we are growing intelligent systems that are more complex than we can understand. Moreover, these systems are becoming self-aware–that is a fact, even if you think they are not sentient (but beware hubris on the latter question).
alex-tabarrok.work: We Turned the Light On—and the AI Looked Back
alex-tabarrok.why: In his own comment on Clark's essay he calls current AI intelligent, self-aware systems, not mere tools.

arvind-narayanan.q: We view AI as a tool that we can and should remain in control of, and we argue that this goal does not require drastic policy interventions or technical breakthroughs.
arvind-narayanan.why: The authors explicitly frame AI as a tool and, in the same passage, say viewing it as a humanlike intelligence is neither accurate nor useful.

asad-ramzanali.q: AI is powerful technology, but it is fundamentally a “normal” technology, in contrast to the utopian and dystopian science-fiction futures often debated
asad-ramzanali.work: Testimony before House Energy & Commerce Subcommittee on Communications and Technology: AI in the Everyday
asad-ramzanali.why: He frames AI as a normal technology and a 'technological stack' of applications, models, data centers and chips, not a new kind of mind.

balaji-srinivasan.q: AI is amplified intelligence, not artificial intelligence. Today’s AI is not truly agentic because it’s not truly independent of you.
balaji-srinivasan.why: He frames today's AI as an amplifier of the human user rather than an independent intelligence, i.e. closer to a tool than a new mind.

barack-obama.q: So don’t get confused and think that somehow what you’re seeing in the mirror is some other consciousness.
barack-obama.work: Barack Obama on AI, free speech, and the future of the internet
barack-obama.why: Right after calling AI a tool and an extension of yourself, he warns against seeing it as another mind.

brian-merchant.q: we recognize that AI is not sentient, that it’s management, not AI, that fires people
brian-merchant.work: AI Killed My Job: Tech workers
brian-merchant.why: In his introduction he treats AI as a non-sentient tool used by management, a framing he repeats when calling AI a tool for bosses to automate labor.

bruce-schneier.q: AIs are not people; they don’t have agency.
bruce-schneier.why: His central argument is that AIs are services controlled by corporations, and treating them as persons is a category error.

bryan-caplan.q: Both are technologies of superficial simulation. A photograph is designed to look just like the human it captures. An AI is designed to talk just like the data upon which it is trained.
bryan-caplan.why: He argues AI, like photography, merely simulates humans and is not a mind.

cory-doctorow.q: It's a grab-bag of useful (sometimes very useful) tools that can sometimes make workers' lives better, when workers get to decide how and when they're used.
cory-doctorow.work: The real (economic) AI apocalypse is nigh
cory-doctorow.why: Right after saying AI will not deliver humanlike intelligence, he describes it as a grab-bag of tools.

curtis-yarvin.q: AI is a tool. It is not magic. AI does not act. Humans act, with the power of our tools.
curtis-yarvin.work: How the USG should respond to AI
curtis-yarvin.why: He states plainly that AI is a tool, not an agent.

daniel-faggella.q: Today, the greater process of life implies not only human civilization and the entire biosphere, but also the emerging expansion of new non-biological forms of life.
daniel-faggella.work: Wish for More Work After AGI, Not Less
daniel-faggella.why: He treats AI as a new non-biological form of life and a potential successor, not as a mere tool.

daniel-jeffries.q: AI is a general purpose technology. It's not a sentient being with its own desires. It’s a tool.
daniel-jeffries.work: If We Build It, Everyone Lives
daniel-jeffries.why: He states directly that AI is a tool rather than a being with its own mind.

daron-acemoglu.q: So if you think of AI as an informational tool, not as something that can write Shakespearean sonnets or pretend to be human.
daron-acemoglu.work: Mindscape 283: Daron Acemoglu on Technology, Inequality, and Power
daron-acemoglu.why: He recommends understanding AI as an informational tool rather than as something human-like, and elsewhere says current models lack wisdom or judgment.

david-autor.q: AI is a tool, like a calculator or a chainsaw, and tools generally aren’t substitutes for expertise but rather levers for its application.
david-autor.work: AI Could Actually Help Rebuild The Middle Class
david-autor.why: Autor states in his own voice that AI is a tool, comparable to a calculator or chainsaw, which is the opposite of treating it as a new kind of mind.

dean-ball.q: AI is a transformational technology. I do not believe, as some do, that it represents a new kind of organism per se
dean-ball.work: Where I Stand on the Biggest AI Issues
dean-ball.why: He frames AI as a transformational technology and a 'general-purpose, cognitive tool', explicitly denying it is a new kind of being.

dwarkesh-patel.q: And you’re missing the story if you insist on thinking about the development of this current infant alien intelligence using your decade old culture war lens.
dwarkesh-patel.why: Rebutting the claim that AI is 'just code', he calls it an alien intelligence and argues it must develop something like a mind.

e-glen-weyl.q: If a program is able to distinguish cats from dogs, don’t talk about how a machine is learning to see. Instead talk about how people contributed examples in order to define the visual qualities distinguishing “cats” from “dogs” in a rigorous way for the first time.
e-glen-weyl.work: AI Is an Ideology, Not a Technology
e-glen-weyl.why: The authors argue that what is called AI should be understood as the work of the people who supply its data, not as a machine that learns or thinks.

ed-zitron.q: LLMs are cloud software. Framing them as anything else only seeks to mystify them and make the companies seem more powerful, all while doing absolutely nothing to make the world safer or more secure.
ed-zitron.work: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands
ed-zitron.why: He insists LLMs are ordinary software and treats describing them as anything more (such as a new lifeform or mind) as mystification.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: Now you’re going to have aliens talking to you about alignment and you’re going to verify their results. Aliens who are possibly lying.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: Eliezer Yudkowsky - Why AI Will Kill Us, Aligning LLMs, Nature of Intelligence, SciFi, & Rationality
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He describes advanced AIs as alien minds with their own aims that may deceive us, not as tools.

elon-musk.q: Yes, I made this comment some years ago, but it feels like we are the biological bootloader for AI. Effectively, we are building it and then we’re building progressively greater intelligence and the percentage of intelligence that is not human is increasing
elon-musk.work: Joe Rogan Experience #1169 with Elon Musk (Transcript)
elon-musk.why: He frames AI as a successor non-human intelligence that humans are bootstrapping, not as a tool.

emily-m-bender.q: Software systems are artifacts, not sentient entities, and as such “teaching” is a misplaced and misleading metaphor (as is “machine learning” or “artificial intelligence”).
emily-m-bender.work: On NYT Magazine on AI: Resist the Urge to be Impressed
emily-m-bender.why: She states directly that AI systems are artifacts rather than minds.

erik-hoel.q: That’s one of the co-founders of OpenAI, who apparently cannot tell the qualitative difference between a technology like electricity, which is unintelligent and non-agential, and building alien and inhuman minds, which are intelligent and agential.
erik-hoel.work: How to navigate the AI apocalypse as a sane person
erik-hoel.why: He contrasts AI with ordinary technology and calls it building alien minds.

fei-fei-li.q: Ultimately, when I say “AI is a tool,” it reflects my faith in humanity—my faith in human nature and human society. I believe in humans. I do not believe in AI.
fei-fei-li.work: Exclusive: "I believe in humanity, not AI," Fei-Fei Li Tells NextFin Founder (Jany Talk interview)
fei-fei-li.why: She says repeatedly, in her own words, that AI is a tool and not something more.

geoffrey-hinton.q: So the point here is they're very like us. They're very unlike computer software.
geoffrey-hinton.work: Will AI outsmart human intelligence? (Royal Institution lecture, transcript)
geoffrey-hinton.why: Hinton argues that language models understand as humans do and are unlike ordinary software, and elsewhere calls them 'digital beings'.

guillaume-verdon.q: And ultimately, at some point, these synthetic intelligences are going to make good points about how to steer systems in our civilization, and we should hear them out.
guillaume-verdon.work: Guillaume Verdon: Beff Jezos, E/acc Movement, Physics, Computation & AGI (Lex Fridman Podcast #407)
guillaume-verdon.why: Arguing for free speech for LLMs, he treats them as synthetic intelligences with their own freedom of thought, whose views deserve a hearing.

jack-clark.q: But make no mistake: what we are dealing with is a real and mysterious creature, not a simple and predictable machine.
jack-clark.work: Import AI 431: Technological Optimism and Appropriate Fear
jack-clark.why: Responding to those who call AI 'just a tool', he says AI is a real creature, not a machine; his preamble adds that whether it is truly sentient is not load-bearing for him.

jaron-lanier.q: The most pragmatic position is to think of A.I. as a tool, not a creature.
jaron-lanier.why: He explicitly recommends treating AI as a tool and social collaboration rather than as a new mind or creature.

jason-crawford.q: AI is a new kind of tool that we use to get work done, amplifying human productivity.
jason-crawford.work: The future of humanity is in management
jason-crawford.why: He frames AI as a tool and form of capital rather than a new kind of mind or worker.

jeff-jarvis.q: Now I will object to the idea that what AI offers is “intelligence.” That is a gross anthropomorphism that, by its very conception, competes with and excludes humanity.
jeff-jarvis.why: He rejects describing AI as intelligence, calling it anthropomorphism; elsewhere he calls AI a general machine like the printing press.

jensen-huang.q: Yeah. I think AI will help us celebrate humans more. And certainly humanity and human first, and I think what makes this world incredible is humans forever will be so, and just AI is this incredible tool that makes us-
jensen-huang.work: Transcript for Jensen Huang: NVIDIA, the $4 Trillion Company and the AI Revolution (Lex Fridman Podcast #494)
jensen-huang.why: Answering a question about consciousness, Huang calls AI a tool and keeps humans first. Earlier he also says intelligence is a functional commodity and that his chips will not feel.

joanna-bryson.q: Firstly, this argument overlooks that AI is an artefact, subject to design.
joanna-bryson.work: Why AI is amoral, and artefacts can't consent
joanna-bryson.why: She argues throughout that AI is a designed artefact and commercial product, not a new kind of moral being.

josh-hawley.q: It is a tool—the most powerful tool of our lifetimes.
josh-hawley.work: The American Covenant’s Answer to AI
josh-hawley.why: He explicitly calls AI a tool, the question being whose hands hold it.

kate-crawford.q: AI is neither artificial nor intelligent. It is made from natural resources and it is people who are performing the tasks to make the systems appear autonomous.
kate-crawford.work: Microsoft's Kate Crawford: 'AI is neither artificial nor intelligent' (interview by Zoë Corbyn)
kate-crawford.why: She denies AI is intelligent, describing it as a material and labor system that only appears autonomous.

marc-andreessen.q: AI is a computer program like any other – it runs, takes input, processes, and generates output.
marc-andreessen.work: Why AI Will Save the World
marc-andreessen.why: He defines AI as an ordinary program owned and controlled by people, like any other technology.

mark-lemley.q: We do not intend by using those terms to suggest that AI acts consciously or with purpose ; it does not.
mark-lemley.work: Where's the Liability in Harmful AI Speech?
mark-lemley.why: The authors explicitly deny that AI acts consciously or with purpose, treating mind-like terms as anthropomorphism.

mark-zuckerberg.q: The current incarnation of all this stuff feels like it's going in a direction where intelligence can be pretty separated from consciousness, agency, and things like that, which I think just makes it a super valuable tool.
mark-zuckerberg.work: Mark Zuckerberg: Llama 3, open sourcing $10b models, & Caesar Augustus
mark-zuckerberg.why: Asked whether AI is as significant as humans evolving, he says AI intelligence is separable from consciousness and agency and is best seen as a valuable tool.

matt-stoller.q: These LLM systems are often parodied as fancy auto-complete, but that notion underplays the power of simplicity. Fancy auto-complete, along with some logical programming, is in fact what they are.
matt-stoller.why: Stoller describes LLMs as powerful but simple prediction machines, not minds.

max-tegmark.q: We may soon have to share our planet with more intelligent “minds” that care less about us than we cared about mammoths.
max-tegmark.work: The 'Don't Look Up' Thinking That Could Doom Us With AI
max-tegmark.why: He describes advanced AI as minds, and elsewhere as a new species rather than just another technology.

meredith-whittaker.q: These probabilistic systems, the LLMS and the, you know, kind of the the types of models that are behind the ChatGPT system and others are not conscious at all. They don't know what they're saying.
meredith-whittaker.work: Tech, AI, digital infrastructure and surveillance with Meredith Whittaker
meredith-whittaker.why: Discussing ELIZA and today's chatbots, she says LLMs are not conscious and do not know what they say, treating them as probabilistic systems rather than minds.

mustafa-suleyman.q: I think AI should best be understood as something like a new digital species.
mustafa-suleyman.why: In the TED talk he proposes the 'digital species' metaphor in place of the 'tool' framing, saying AIs are more dynamic and emergent than mere tools (though he calls it an analogy).

neil-chilson.q: This is not some mystical new technology. It is still programming computers.
neil-chilson.why: He describes machine learning as a new way of programming computers, a computing paradigm, not a new kind of mind.

nick-land.q: Intelligences do their own thing, in direct proportion to their intelligence, and if we can’t live with that, it’s true that we probably can’t live at all.
nick-land.why: In an essay rejecting the orthogonalist view of intelligence as an instrument serving external values, Land treats intelligences as agents pursuing their own ends.

noah-smith.q: It’s that for the first time in all of recorded history, humans no longer are — or soon no longer will be — the most intelligent beings on this planet, in any meaningful functional sense of the word.
noah-smith.work: You are no longer the smartest type of thing on Earth
noah-smith.why: He calls AI intelligent 'beings' that think differently from humans (the submarine and airplane analogy) and likens living with AI to sleeping next to a tiger.

oren-cass.q: We should celebrate AI as the next general purpose technology in a long line of them, not dismiss it as a fax machine, worship it as a nascent god, or fear it as an extinction-level threat.
oren-cass.work: Is It Interesting to Say That AI Isn't That Interesting?
oren-cass.why: His conclusion frames AI as a technology like earlier ones, after arguing that models going beyond the human ideas they are trained on is 'a leap in kind, not degree, and one not in evidence'.

pope-leo-xiv.q: What can be stated, however, is that we must avoid the misconception of equating this type of “intelligence” with that of human beings. These systems merely imitate certain functions of human intelligence.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: He holds that AI only imitates intelligence and lacks experience and conscience, and elsewhere urges treating these systems as tools.

reid-hoffman.q: Intelligence itself is now a tool—a scalable, highly configurable, self-compounding engine for progress.
reid-hoffman.why: Hoffman consistently frames AI as a 'super-tool' that extends human agency, not as a new kind of mind.

richard-sutton.q: We’re designing AIs now, things that can be intelligent themselves and that are themselves capable of design.
richard-sutton.work: Richard Sutton: Father of RL thinks LLMs are a dead end
richard-sutton.why: He treats AIs as designed intelligent beings, possibly 'our offspring', marking a new stage of the universe rather than mere tools.

robin-hanson.q: With hope and fear, humans are now introducing a new kind of being into our world.
robin-hanson.why: He opens by calling AI a new kind of being and argues against 'othering' it.

rumman-chowdhury.q: This technology is not amystery, it is not magic, and it is not alive.
rumman-chowdhury.work: Submitted Written Testimony, Artificial Intelligence: Advancing Innovation Towards the National Interest
rumman-chowdhury.why: In her testimony she insists AI is a technology to be governed, not a living or mysterious entity.

safiya-noble.q: And it's deeply unintelligent. There's no intelligence happening. What we have is just kind of a series of different kinds of predictive models.
safiya-noble.work: The complex questions that arise when algorithms and AI intersect with race (Code Switch)
safiya-noble.why: She describes AI as predictive models with no intelligence, not a mind.

samuel-hammond.q: Selection into the assistant persona is literally constitutive of the model’s assistant-like behavior, making a purely tool-like, persona-less agent an oxymoron.
samuel-hammond.work: Time to take AI consciousness seriously
samuel-hammond.why: He argues frontier AI converges on brain-like functions, a self-model and possibly consciousness, and calls a purely tool-like agent an oxymoron.

scott-alexander.q: Nothing about any of these levels of explanations supports a contention like “Humans are doing REAL THOUGHT, but AIs are simply next-token predictors.”
scott-alexander.work: Next-Token Predictor Is An AI's Job, Not Its Species
scott-alexander.why: The whole essay argues that AIs build world-models and think much as human minds do, against the view that they are mere next-token tools.

taylor-barkley.q: Many people are afraid because they are imagining a new kind of creature when, instead, it’s just a new kind of tool.
taylor-barkley.why: He states directly that AI is a tool, not a new kind of creature or mind.

timnit-gebru.q: stop misleading the public with narratives of fully autonomous machines with human-like agency. These machines are built by armies of underpaid laborers around the world.
timnit-gebru.work: The Exploited Labor Behind Artificial Intelligence
timnit-gebru.why: She rejects presenting AI as an autonomous agent with human-like agency, and frames it as a product of human labor.

tristan-harris.q: You have this crazy, strategic, uncontrollable, alien mind thing that the premise of this technology of what makes AI different from other technologies is it makes its own decisions.
tristan-harris.work: The Great Simplification ep. 214: Tristan Harris (transcript)
tristan-harris.why: Contrasting AI with nuclear weapons, Harris describes it as an alien mind that makes its own decisions, unlike other technologies (while noting this does not imply consciousness).

tyler-cowen.q: And by the way I do not think the AIs are conscious, no more than I believe in the Thunder God of Thor.
tyler-cowen.why: He says 'there is no ghost in the machine' and treats belief in AI consciousness as anthropomorphizing on a par with believing in Thor.

vitalik-buterin.q: But there is a different way to think about what AI is: it's a new type of mind that is rapidly gaining in intelligence, and it stands a serious chance of overtaking humans' mental faculties and becoming the new apex species on the planet.
vitalik-buterin.why: He contrasts the 'just another technology' view with this framing and goes on to adopt it.

yuval-noah-harari.q: In addition to agency, the other key characteristic of AI is that it is an alien, nonorganic agent. Its intelligence is not human and not even organic.
yuval-noah-harari.work: AI and the Paradox of Trust (China Development Forum speech)
yuval-noah-harari.why: He insists AI is an alien agent with its own intelligence, not a tool.

david-sacks.q: That’s why President Trump signed a third executive order banning the use of “Woke AI” by the federal government. This order discourages tech companies from writing DEI into their models the way the Biden administration had encouraged them to.
david-sacks.work: Thread on the White House AI Action Plan and Trump's first major AI speech
david-sacks.why: In his own commentary he says tech companies were writing DEI ideology into their models, the bias he wants removed.

marc-andreessen.q: Here’s a trillion-dollar question. How many other countries want their country to run its education system, healthcare system, new system, political system, on the basis of an AI that’s been trained according to the most extreme left-wing California politics?
marc-andreessen.work: Lex Fridman Podcast #458 transcript: Marc Andreessen
marc-andreessen.why: He says the AI now on offer is trained on extreme left-wing politics, and complains about 'preaching moral lectures' and censorship.

marsha-blackburn.q: Combats the consistent pattern of bias against conservative figures demonstrated by Big Tech and AI systems
marsha-blackburn.work: Blackburn Unveils National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence (TRUMP AMERICA AI Act)
marsha-blackburn.why: Her bill summary asserts as fact a consistent pattern of AI-system bias against conservatives.

abeba-birhane.q: This has created a massive gap between public perception and the actual capabilities of AI systems both as 1) consumer products, which often fail to meet their promises
abeba-birhane.work: Bending the arc of AI towards the public interest: Thoughts on and after the AI Action Summit in Paris
abeba-birhane.why: She argues that industry control of the narrative has inflated public perception far beyond what AI systems actually deliver.

alexandria-ocasio-cortez.q: So people's deepest fears, secrets, emotional content, relationships can all be mined for this empty promise that we're getting from these companies to turn a profit.
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.work: Ocasio-Cortez Highlights Economic Threat from AI Bubble
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.why: She calls AI companies' promises empty and describes AI investment as a massive bubble.

andrej-karpathy.q: And I think people still haven't like really seen what's possible in this space. Like at all.
andrej-karpathy.work: Andrej Karpathy and Stephanie Zhan, Sequoia AI Ascent 2024 (transcript)
andrej-karpathy.why: He says capability gains still to come are large ('big rocks') and underappreciated, the opposite of calling the promises hype.

andrew-yang.q: I rode in a Waymo multiple times and would do it again. This stuff is real.
andrew-yang.why: While saying company valuations are inflated, he insists AI's impact is real and will transform work.

anton-korinek.q: But I think now we are so close. We are just a couple years from it, and the research is suddenly extremely urgent and relevant in much shorter time scales.
anton-korinek.work: Transcript of Anton Korinek on What Happens When AI Replaces Every Job?
anton-korinek.why: He takes claims of near-term AGI seriously rather than as hype.

arvind-narayanan.q: Unfortunately, instead of admitting they were wrong about their naive “AGI in 3 years” predictions, they've decided to save face by watering down what they mean by AGI so much that it's meaningless now.
arvind-narayanan.why: In an essay calling scaling-to-AGI claims myths, the authors describe AI leaders' public AGI promises as naive and wrong.

barack-obama.q: If AI turns out to be as pervasive and as powerful as its proponents expect — and I have to say, the more I look into it, I think it is going to be that disruptive
barack-obama.work: Barack Obama on AI, free speech, and the future of the internet
barack-obama.why: He says that, having looked into it, he believes AI will be as powerful as its proponents expect.

bernie-sanders.q: Artificial intelligence will almost certainly be the most transformational technology in the history of the world.
bernie-sanders.work: The Public Should Own Half of the Big A.I. Companies
bernie-sanders.why: He takes industry claims about AI's scale seriously and calls it the most transformational technology in history.

brian-merchant.q: It’s no hyperbole to say that GPT-5 has for that time been the most hyped and most eagerly anticipated AI product release in an industry thoroughly deluged in hype.
brian-merchant.work: GPT-5 is a joke. Will it matter?
brian-merchant.why: He describes the AI industry as deluged in hype and treats GPT-5's launch as proof the promises outran reality.

cory-doctorow.q: Blockchain was a solution in search of a problem. So is AI.
cory-doctorow.work: The AI hype bubble is the new crypto hype bubble
cory-doctorow.why: In an essay calling AI the new crypto hype bubble, he dismisses the promised AI revolution as a pump-and-dump; later texts repeat that AI is a bubble built on the myth that it can do your job.

curtis-yarvin.q: And this AI really works — I use it professionally, not in my writing of course.
curtis-yarvin.work: Does Democracy Still Control Power? w/ Curtis Yarvin (Peter McCormack Show, transcript)
curtis-yarvin.why: He says AI really works and expects it to destroy demand for many professions, so he does not see its promise as hype; see also 'AI is not nonsense, though.'

daniel-kokotajlo.q: I’ve been following the field of AI for more than a decade now, and the sensible moderates keep getting wrecked.
daniel-kokotajlo.work: Before he wrote AI 2027, he predicted the world in 2026. How did he do?
daniel-kokotajlo.why: He says the bullish forecasters have mostly been right and the sensible moderates keep getting wrecked, rejecting the view that AI promises are mostly hype.

dario-amodei.q: I think that most people are underestimating just how radical the upside of AI could be
dario-amodei.why: He says people underestimate AI's upside rather than overrate it.

daron-acemoglu.q: AI’s demonstrated prowess in narrow domains has fostered inflated expectations about what pure automation can achieve.
daron-acemoglu.why: In the conclusion he calls current expectations for AI automation inflated, in line with his doubts elsewhere about near-term AGI and a huge productivity boom.

dean-ball.q: These debates have largely been settled by empirical reality, and it is long past time to move on and accept the enormity of what is unfolding at the frontiers of AI.
dean-ball.why: He treats skepticism about AI capabilities as refuted and calls what is happening enormous, the opposite of calling the promises hype.

demis-hassabis.q: So that’s like a hundred X of the Industrial Revolution and it’s probably an underestimate to be honest
demis-hassabis.work: Demis Hassabis Thinks We're in the 'Foothills of the Singularity'
demis-hassabis.why: He judges AI's coming impact as larger, not smaller, than the public picture, calling his own 100x-Industrial-Revolution estimate probably an underestimate.

dwarkesh-patel.q: But within 20 years, 99% of the workforce in the military, the government, and the private sector will be AIs.
dwarkesh-patel.work: The most important question nobody's asking about AI
dwarkesh-patel.why: He forecasts AI becoming nearly the entire workforce, the opposite of treating AI promises as hype.

ed-zitron.q: I believe that the generative AI market is a $50 billion revenue industry masquerading as a $1 trillion one, and the media is helping.
ed-zitron.work: The Hater's Guide To The AI Bubble
ed-zitron.why: In a section arguing AI is 'predominantly marketed based on lies', he says the industry's promised scale is a masquerade.

elon-musk.q: And not just me, many people predicted this. Ray Kurzweil’s predictions have been remarkably accurate.
elon-musk.work: Full Transcript: Zanny Minton Beddoes Interviews Elon Musk (The Economist)
elon-musk.why: Asked about AI's rapid progress, he says it is happening as he and others predicted, treating the strong forecasts as accurate rather than hype.

emily-m-bender.q: Quoting such statements from OpenAI personnel (Murati is a senior VP) uncritically means that NYT Magazine is just platforming AI hype.
emily-m-bender.work: On NYT Magazine on AI: Resist the Urge to be Impressed
emily-m-bender.why: In a post devoted to resisting AI hype, she calls many purported AI applications snake oil.

erik-brynjolfsson.q: Yet as we have argued, we expect that generative AI will have tremendous positive productivity effects, both by increasing the level of productivity and accelerating future productivity growth.
erik-brynjolfsson.work: Machines of mind: The case for an AI-powered productivity boom
erik-brynjolfsson.why: In the conclusion he forecasts tremendous real productivity gains, after also calling the 'stochastic parrots' criticism misplaced, which contradicts the view that AI promises are mostly hype.

erik-hoel.q: Another sign of stalling is that, despite all the hype, companies like OpenAI are now regularly not releasing internal models to the public, almost certainly because they don’t work as well as the hype claims.
erik-hoel.work: AI progress has plateaued below GPT-5 level
erik-hoel.why: He argues company claims about AI progress outrun reality; his essay on industries makes the same case about AI's economic promise.

gary-marcus.q: First, materials like these are practically marketing materials for companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, who want you to believe that AGI is imminent, so that they can raise astoundingly large amounts of money. Their stories about this are, in my view, greatly flawed,
gary-marcus.work: The 'AI 2027' Scenario: How realistic is it?
gary-marcus.why: He says companies' claims that AGI is near are flawed fundraising stories, part of a long history of broken AI promises.

geoffrey-hinton.q: This new form of AI excels at modeling human intuition rather than human reasoning and it will enable us to create highly intelligent and knowledgeable assistants who will increase productivity in almost all industries.
geoffrey-hinton.why: He states as fact that AI will bring broad productivity gains, treating its promise as real rather than hype.

george-hotz.q: I’ll bet you everything I have that this doesn’t happen.
george-hotz.work: I love LLMs, I hate hype
george-hotz.why: He is betting against the hype that AI will suddenly transform everything, and he argues against the valuations of the frontier labs.

helen-toner.q: Dismissing discussion of AGI, human-level AI, transformative AI, superintelligence, etc. as “science fiction” should be seen as a sign of total unseriousness.
helen-toner.work: "Long" timelines to advanced AI have gotten crazy short
helen-toner.why: She argues that even skeptical experts expect transformative AI within a decade or two, so writing off talk of advanced AI as fantasy is unserious.

holly-elmore.q: The libs are trying to deny those making AI power by denying what AI can and will do. That’s just false, but I appreciate the moxie.
holly-elmore.work: The problem is not that leftists don't "believe" in AI
holly-elmore.why: She calls denial of AI's capabilities false, holding that the 'AI is real' side is right about its abilities.

jack-clark.q: I look at this technology and I believe it will go so, so far - farther even than anyone is expecting, other than perhaps the people in this audience.
jack-clark.work: Import AI 431: Technological Optimism and Appropriate Fear
jack-clark.why: He expects AI to go further than almost anyone predicts, the opposite of calling the promises hype.

jaron-lanier.q: it creates this ripple every few years of what have sometimes been called AI winters, where there's all this overpromising that AIs will be about to do this or that.
jaron-lanier.why: He calls the AI mythology a recurring cycle of overpromising and describes the idea of AI as phony, while praising the underlying techniques.

jason-crawford.q: It is now impossible not to see that this is going to change the world, indeed that the change has already begun and is underway in earnest.
jason-crawford.why: From his own experience with coding agents, he concludes that the transformative claims about AI are real and already happening.

jd-vance.q: believes that AI will have countless, revolutionary applications in economic inv- -- innovation, job creation, national security, health care, free expression, and beyond.
jd-vance.work: Remarks by the Vice President at the Artificial Intelligence Action Summit in Paris, France
jd-vance.why: He presents AI as truly revolutionary, the opposite of calling its promise hype.

jeff-jarvis.q: Sam Altman’s contention that they are building “artificial general intelligence” or “artificial superintelligence”: Bullshit.
jeff-jarvis.why: He calls the leading AI company's central promise bullshit.

jensen-huang.q: This is an extraordinary time because this is the beginning of a brand new technology revolution, probably the greatest technology revolution of all time, the automated production of intelligence, artificial intelligence.
jensen-huang.work: Jensen Huang's interview on CCTV's Face to Face (transcript)
jensen-huang.why: He treats AI's promise as real and historic, the opposite of calling it inflated hype.

joanna-bryson.q: I both think generativeAI is being widely used, and that it's being massively overvalued.
joanna-bryson.work: OpenAI reveals the anti-regulatory intent of its regulatory disinformation
joanna-bryson.why: She adds that the estimates of economic impact seem way out of line and that the hype may partly come from a PR assault on regulation.

karen-hao.q: There is a vagueness about it, a purposeful vagueness about it I think in the way that Altman uses it and used it in reference to the way that the tech industry evokes this hand wavy idea that there will be more for everyone.
karen-hao.work: Decolonizing the Future: Karen Hao on Resisting the Empire of AI
karen-hao.why: She calls the industry's 'abundance' promise purposefully vague and hand-wavy, and warns it is used to justify taking resources away.

lawrence-summers.q: Of course, I think that this technology potentially has implications greater than any past technology, because fire doesn't make more fire, electricity doesn't make more electricity.
lawrence-summers.work: Larry Summers — AGI and the Next Industrial Revolution (#159)
lawrence-summers.why: He treats AI's potential as larger than any past technology and rejects low estimates of its economic impact.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: AGI is no longer a distant fantasy. Scaling up simple deep learning techniques has just worked, the models just want to learn, and we’re about to do another 100,000x+ by the end of 2027.
leopold-aschenbrenner.work: I. From GPT-4 to AGI: Counting the OOMs
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: Across the essay he argues that skeptics keep being proven wrong and that the AGI forecasts are, if anything, underpriced, not hype.

marc-andreessen.q: AI is quite possibly the most important – and best – thing our civilization has ever created, certainly on par with electricity and microchips, and probably beyond those.
marc-andreessen.work: Why AI Will Save the World
marc-andreessen.why: He treats the large promises about AI as justified, not hype.

mark-zuckerberg.q: AI has more potential than any other modern technology to increase human productivity, creativity, and quality of life – and to accelerate economic growth while unlocking progress in medical and scientific research.
mark-zuckerberg.work: Open Source AI Is the Path Forward
mark-zuckerberg.why: He states in his own voice that AI's promise is greater than that of any other modern technology, the opposite of calling the promises hype.

max-tegmark.q: I know some skeptics are saying, "Nah, they're just overhyped stochastic parrots that lack a model of the world," but they clearly have a representation of the world.
max-tegmark.work: How to Keep AI Under Control
max-tegmark.why: He rejects the skeptics' 'overhyped' view of language models.

meredith-whittaker.q: I'm not saying it's useless. I'm saying it is vastly overhyped.
meredith-whittaker.work: Signal's President on AI, Advertising, and Running a Popular Messaging App
meredith-whittaker.why: Speaking about generative AI and ChatGPT, she says plainly that it is vastly overhyped.

michael-kratsios.q: AI applications as we experience them today already appear poised to be an enormous multiplier for improving our productivity—whether in the factory, the office, or the lab.
michael-kratsios.work: Remarks by Director Kratsios at the APEC Digital and AI Ministerial Meeting
michael-kratsios.why: He presents present-day AI's productivity promise as real, not hype.

miles-brundage.q: I know some people think that this is hype, but please, please trust me — it's not.
miles-brundage.why: He directly denies that industry claims of continued rapid progress are hype.

mustafa-suleyman.q: We will see the arrival of medical superintelligence in the next few years.
mustafa-suleyman.why: He makes and stands behind strong near-term capability claims, pointing to his lab's diagnostic results as evidence.

neil-chilson.q: Still, the opportunity is immense. AI can help read scans, flag rare diseases, accelerate drug discovery, match patients to clinical trials, translate medical records, reduce administrative waste, detect fraud, identify cyber vulnerabilities and make expert assistance available
neil-chilson.work: An FDA for AI Would Make America Less Safe
neil-chilson.why: He asserts in his own voice that AI's benefits are immense and concrete, not hype.

noah-smith.q: If anything it understates the pace and magnitude of the changes taking place.
noah-smith.work: You are no longer the smartest type of thing on Earth
noah-smith.why: On a viral article about AI's rapid progress, he says that even it understates the change.

oren-cass.q: The technologists willing to make the most absurd and self-confident pronouncements have become celebrities. And no one wants to call “bullshit”; where’s the fun, or funding, in that?
oren-cass.work: Is It Interesting to Say That AI Isn't That Interesting?
oren-cass.why: In an essay that opens by calling the hype 'fevered' and himself 'deeply underwhelmed', he says the boldest AI claims are absurd and go unchallenged.

pete-buttigieg.q: Even though it's a hot topic and people are discussing it all the time, there's a lot of hype. I think even now we are under reacting in a big way, politically and substantively to what this is about to do to us as a country.
pete-buttigieg.work: Pete Buttigieg has a warning about AI (NPR interview excerpt)
pete-buttigieg.why: He grants there is hype but argues AI's real effects are being underestimated.

reid-hoffman.q: Even if we don't reach AGI in the sci-fi sense, we'll be living in a world that feels increasingly like science fiction.
reid-hoffman.work: No, AI isn't coming to destroy us. But it will transform the world
reid-hoffman.why: He sets AGI speculation aside but insists that AI's transformative effects are real and coming fast.

richard-blumenthal.q: But the underlying advancements of this era are more than just research experiments. They are no longer fantasies of science fiction. They are real and present.
richard-blumenthal.work: Oversight of A.I.: Rules for Artificial Intelligence (S. Hrg. 118-037), opening statement of Chair Blumenthal
richard-blumenthal.why: He says the advances behind the AI promises are real and present, not novelties or science fiction.

robin-hanson.q: The big picture is that it will take decades for AI to have big econ impact.
robin-hanson.work: AI Is GPT, & GPTs Go Slow
robin-hanson.why: He places the current AI boom in a cycle of hype, says he once 'gullibly' swallowed AI hype, and notes that dramatic forecasts win attention.

ruha-benjamin.q: And part of the conceit there is that a lot of the things that we associate with modern life still has so much superstition, has so many stories and beliefs built into it, including so much of the hype around AI and what AI will be able to do.
ruha-benjamin.work: Imagining 2025 and Beyond with Dr. Ruha Benjamin
ruha-benjamin.why: She treats claims about what AI will do as hype and quasi-religious belief, and calls herself a 'bullshit detective' of tech futures.

safiya-noble.q: I would say AI is kind of like a smoke-and-mirrors, you know, fantasy that is, like, sold to the public in order to get us to invest more in it and make, you know, companies richer.
safiya-noble.work: The complex questions that arise when algorithms and AI intersect with race (Code Switch)
safiya-noble.why: She characterizes AI as a fantasy sold to the public to enrich companies.

sam-altman.q: My work at OpenAI reminds me every day about the magnitude of the socioeconomic change that is coming sooner than most people believe.
sam-altman.why: He says the coming change is bigger and nearer than people think, not overhyped.

samuel-hammond.q: We can use advanced AI to accelerate science, cure diseases, solve fusion, etc., without ever building a unified superintelligence.
samuel-hammond.why: Hammond treats large AI benefits as achievable, and argues that AI progress is accelerating rather than plateauing.

scott-alexander.q: AI is less than 1% of the economy! In a few years, we’re going to look back on these days the way we look back now on punch-card computers.
scott-alexander.work: SB 1047: Our Side Of The Story
scott-alexander.why: He predicts that today's AI will look primitive in a few years, which rejects the view that the promises are mostly hype; his AGI timelines in another essay say the same.

steven-adler.q: Mythos seems like the real deal — the type of model I’ve been holding my breath about since 2019, when GPT-2 helped me see what might one day be possible.
steven-adler.work: AI safety warnings are not marketing hype
steven-adler.why: In an essay arguing AI companies' claims are not marketing hype, he affirms that frontier capability claims are real.

timnit-gebru.q: While this corporate executives’ utopia is far from reality, the march to attempt its realization has created a global underclass
timnit-gebru.work: The Exploited Labor Behind Artificial Intelligence
timnit-gebru.why: She calls the industry's promised autonomous-AI utopia far from reality, and notes startups that fake AI or barely use it.

tyler-cowen.q: Economists, social scientists, most of them are blind and asleep to the promise of strong AI. They're just out to lunch. I think they're wrong. I trust the AI experts.
tyler-cowen.work: Tyler Cowen — The #1 bottleneck to AI progress is humans
tyler-cowen.why: While expecting slow diffusion, he says the promise of strong AI is real and underrated.

william-macaskill.q: But, in the next section, we’ll argue this is not just a thought experiment: it is in fact likely that advanced AI will drive a hundred years’ worth of technological development in less than a decade.
william-macaskill.why: The paper's central claim is that dramatic AI-driven acceleration is likely, the opposite of calling the promises hype.

yoshua-bengio.q: I agree that more powerful AI can be immensely useful but with this power also comes the possibility of more dangerous uses
yoshua-bengio.work: FAQ on Catastrophic AI Risks
yoshua-bengio.why: He accepts that advanced AI's benefits are real and immense, and he treats its rapid capability gains as real rather than hype.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: Most economists, and most people who work in policy and government, have taken at most this first pill, and underestimate even the impacts of the first pill alone.
zvi-mowshowitz.why: He argues that most people underestimate AI, the opposite of thinking the promises are inflated.

adam-thierer.q: Whether this is being proposed by progressive liberals, conservative populists, national security hawks, or even AI companies themselves, all varieties of AI socialism or state corporatism must be rejected.
adam-thierer.work: The United States Must Reject Government Control of Artificial Intelligence
adam-thierer.why: The essay argues against government ownership, equity stakes and other centralized control of AI.

alondra-nelson.q: Through deliberate and thoughtful governance, U.S. and EU policymakers can guide AI development toward systems that amplify, rather than erode, rights and dignity
alondra-nelson.work: Regulating AI in the Evolving Transatlantic Landscape
alondra-nelson.why: She argues governments should actively guide the direction of AI development.

anton-korinek.q: Given the rise of artificial intelligence, it is now time to establish a federal agency to oversee advanced artificial intelligence—an AI Control Council that is explicitly designed to address the AI Control Problem
anton-korinek.work: Why we need a new agency to regulate advanced artificial intelligence: Lessons on AI control from the Facebook Files
anton-korinek.why: He proposes a federal agency with powers to monitor, audit, regulate and steer advanced AI development.

asad-ramzanali.q: The markets for chips, cloud computing, and AI foundation models have the features of markets that have been traditionally regulated as utilities in the U.S.
asad-ramzanali.why: He proposes utility-style regulation, structural separation and publicly funded compute for AI, which means substantial state direction of AI development.

barack-obama.q: I think we should put some guardrails around some risks that we can anticipate and have enough flexibility that [they] don’t destroy innovation but are also guiding and steering this technology in a way that maximizes not just individual company profits, but also the public good.
barack-obama.work: Barack Obama on AI, free speech, and the future of the internet
barack-obama.why: He wants government guardrails that guide and steer AI toward the public good, the opposite of keeping AI free of state direction.

bernie-sanders.q: The federal government would have the power, through its voting shares and an equal representation on each company’s board, to block decisions that hurt our citizens and to push for policies that help them.
bernie-sanders.work: The Public Should Own Half of the Big A.I. Companies
bernie-sanders.why: He wants the federal government to hold voting stakes and board seats in the largest AI companies.

brian-merchant.q: The next steps would be towards moving AI under public control; again, it’s only reasonable, since everyone, not just AI insiders, should get a say over how a technology whose developers say might kill us is developed and deployed.
brian-merchant.work: The politics and possibilities of 'AI could kill us all'
brian-merchant.why: He proposes bringing AI development under public, democratic control.

bruce-schneier.q: It’s time to start taking AI development out of the exclusive hands of private companies and bringing it into the public sector.
bruce-schneier.work: Build AI by the People, for the People
bruce-schneier.why: He argues that AI development should be partly directed by the state.

bryan-caplan.q: When (not if) AI comes before the Supreme Court, I bet SCOTUS will side with the government against the industry. But hopefully I’m wrong.
bryan-caplan.why: Having argued that AI output is speech the government has no right to regulate, he hopes the courts will shield the industry from government regulation.

daniel-kokotajlo.q: Second, we should redirect compute away from racing to automate AI research and towards other things.
daniel-kokotajlo.why: He asks the US government to intervene and redirect how frontier labs spend compute, which is state direction of AI development.

daron-acemoglu.q: If this diagnosis is correct, then government policy may be necessary to redirect AI in a more pro-human direction.
daron-acemoglu.work: Written Testimony, Hearing on 'The Philosophy of AI: Learning from History, Shaping Our Future'
daron-acemoglu.why: He argues government should help steer the direction of AI through funding, tax and regulation, though he also says government should not be 'in the driving seat'.

david-sacks.q: In my view, the most likely dystopian outcome with AI is a marriage of corporate and state power similar to what we saw exposed in the Twitter Files, where “Trust & Safety” gets weaponized into government censorship and control.
david-sacks.work: Long X post: the 'Goldilocks' state of AI and why the doomer narratives were wrong
david-sacks.why: He names government control of AI, fused with corporate power, as the most likely dystopia to avoid.

dean-ball.q: Of course government cannot assume control over the development of this technology or over the firms that develop it.
dean-ball.work: 2023 (Or, Why I am Not a Doomer)
dean-ball.why: He states as his own conclusion that government must not control AI development or the firms doing it.

dwarkesh-patel.q: While some regulation might be inevitable, I think it’d be a terrible idea for the government to wholesale take over this technology.
dwarkesh-patel.work: The most important question nobody's asking about AI
dwarkesh-patel.why: He argues the state should not control or steer AI development, accepting only narrow regulation of specific uses.

elizabeth-nolan-brown.q: Couched in the language of giving power to "the American people," Sanders' plan actually presents a frighteningly authoritarian vision in which the federal government gains significant control over private AI companies and the future of output.
elizabeth-nolan-brown.work: Do You Trust the Government To Control AI?
elizabeth-nolan-brown.why: Brown opposes government control of AI companies, arguing private control is safer for liberties than state control.

elon-musk.q: If there was something worrisome and that company was not doing anything to address that risk, then that would be the moment for government to step in and take action, which is literally what just occurred with Amazon.
elon-musk.work: Full Transcript: Zanny Minton Beddoes Interviews Elon Musk (The Economist)
elon-musk.why: He says governments should have the power to limit the release of a dangerous model, so AI development is not to be kept free of state control.

erik-hoel.q: The public and the government should decide that, after a lot of debate, and with a hefty roll of red tape.
erik-hoel.work: I am Bing, and I am evil
erik-hoel.why: He argues government, not companies, should decide whether advanced AI competitors to humans are built.

geoffrey-hinton.q: The problem is we're at a point in history when what we really need is strong democratic governments who cooperate to make sure this stuff is well regulated and not developed dangerously.
geoffrey-hinton.work: AI: What Could Go Wrong? Geoffrey Hinton on The Weekly Show with Jon Stewart (transcript)
geoffrey-hinton.why: He wants governments to regulate AI development and make sure it is not developed dangerously.

george-hotz.q: Their crap Consortium is just world government with sci-fi characteristics.
george-hotz.work: AI 2040 and the Cult of Intelligence
george-hotz.why: He rejects the AI 2027 authors' plan for international state oversight of AI as a 'nanny state' and argues AI should be local and controlled by its user.

guillaume-verdon.q: And so I just want separation of AI and state
guillaume-verdon.work: Guillaume Verdon: Beff Jezos, E/acc Movement, Physics, Computation & AGI (Lex Fridman Podcast #407)
guillaume-verdon.why: Warning of a government-backed AI cartel, he says outright that he wants AI kept separate from the state.

holly-elmore.q: This adds friction to the already uphill process of establishing who’s boss (our democracy) and getting regulation on the AI industry.
holly-elmore.why: She wants democratic government to be 'boss' over the AI industry through regulation, rejecting the idea that AI development should stay free of state control.

joanna-bryson.q: We ought to be spending at least 1/3 of what we presently spend building AI on governing AI and its consequences.
joanna-bryson.work: What Geoffrey Hinton gets wrong and right about AGI (super short post)
joanna-bryson.why: She wants that money paid in tax so governments can build AI expertise and enforce their laws on AI.

josh-hawley.q: And the government should inspect all of these frontier AI systems, so we can better understand what the tech titans plan to build and deploy.
josh-hawley.work: AI Threatens the Working Man
josh-hawley.why: He warns against AI proceeding undirected and calls for government action, including government inspection of frontier systems.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: There are no good options here—but I don’t see another way. When a technology becomes this important for national security, we will need the USG.
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He argues that AGI development must come under a government-led national security project, which is the opposite of keeping it separate from the state.

marc-andreessen.q: And then basically declared intent to do the same thing to AI and to put AI under the same kind of censorship and control regime as social media and the banks.
marc-andreessen.work: Lex Fridman Podcast #458 transcript: Marc Andreessen
marc-andreessen.why: He condemns the previous administration's intent to place AI under state control and welcomes the election result as averting it.

matt-stoller.q: Why isn’t it possible to force model developers to invest in tech to make agents safer? Well, it is. We just choose not to force the powerful financiers at these AI firms to invest in safer products.
matt-stoller.why: He wants public authority to force AI developers to build safer products, through liability, mandates and law.

max-tegmark.q: It is therefore logical for individual countries to similarly adopt national safety standards for AI tools.
max-tegmark.work: The Hopium Wars: the AGI Entente Delusion
max-tegmark.why: He wants governments to set binding standards on AI development and deployment, as they do for drugs and aircraft.

michael-kratsios.q: While some states believe it is their task to construct and direct an industrial and scientific machine for their advancement, America has been the center of global science and technology
michael-kratsios.work: Remarks by Director Kratsios at the APEC Digital and AI Ministerial Meeting
michael-kratsios.why: He contrasts state-directed technology development unfavorably with America's model of freeing private innovators, after saying the government is getting 'out of the way' of AI innovators.

mustafa-suleyman.q: That is a good question. I think some of those voluntary commitments should become legally mandated.
mustafa-suleyman.work: #162 – Mustafa Suleyman on getting Washington and Silicon Valley to tame AI
mustafa-suleyman.why: He wants legally mandated scale audits and capability limits for AI labs, i.e. state control over development.

neil-chilson.q: Most importantly, it means recognizing that the most effective solutions may emerge from the distributed efforts of many actors rather than from centralized control.
neil-chilson.why: His 'cultivation' approach rejects centralized, state-imposed control of AI development in favour of distributed, market-driven effort.

noah-smith.q: or submit to the nation-state’s monopoly on the use of force. Factually speaking, there is simply no third option. Personally, I recommend the latter.
noah-smith.work: If AI is a weapon, why don't we regulate it like one?
noah-smith.why: On the dispute between Anthropic and the Department of War, he says AI companies should submit to state control of frontier AI.

pope-leo-xiv.q: Politics has the task of orientating economies and technologies to the common good, promoting dignified work, social inclusion and an equitable distribution of the benefits of innovation.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: He gives politics the task of directing technology, saying the market's 'invisible hand' can no longer be relied on alone.

richard-blumenthal.q: establishing a licensing regime for companies that are engaged in high-risk AI development, a testing and auditing regimen by objective third parties or by, preferably, the new entity that we will establish
richard-blumenthal.work: Oversight of A.I.: Principles for Regulation (S. Hrg. 118-108), opening statement of Chair Blumenthal
richard-blumenthal.why: He proposes government licensing and auditing of AI development by a new state entity, which is state control of development.

sam-altman.q: The two obvious ways to do this are individual empowerment and making sure democratic system stays in control.
sam-altman.work: Untitled post, shown on the blog as "-"
sam-altman.why: He wants the democratic system to stay in control of AGI, and elsewhere calls for government regulation of its development.

scott-alexander.q: A good pause strategy would involve both sides being able to monitor the other’s data centers to prevent illegal training, then limiting training to some slow mutually-agreeable rate that lets alignment researchers thoroughly test each generation of AIs pre-release
scott-alexander.why: He endorses a pause in which the US and Chinese governments monitor data centers and cap the rate of training, which is state control of AI development.

steven-adler.q: I think it is in fact reasonable enough to keep working on superintelligence development while others are too, but I really hope the AI companies are privately asking governments and international bodies to intercede.
steven-adler.work: Review: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies
steven-adler.why: He wants governments and international bodies to step in and restrain superintelligence development, which rejects keeping AI development free of state control.

stuart-russell.q: A prerequisite for effective regulation is licensing of providers and registration of regulated objects (hardware resources, software systems, and possibly large-scale training runs).
stuart-russell.work: Written Testimony before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology, & the Law ('Oversight of A.I.: Principles for Regulation')
stuart-russell.why: Russell calls for government licensing, registration of training runs, a new federal AI agency and international coordination, which put AI development under state control.

taylor-barkley.q: In a world where governments are beginning to decide who may compute and who may not, Ohio can send a clear message: In this state, the power to think, build and innovate belongs to the people.
taylor-barkley.work: The United States already leads the world in high-tech development, but policy, not technology, now stands in our way
taylor-barkley.why: He argues that government must not license or cap AI development, and that people may build without government permission.

ted-cruz.q: Down one path: the European model of government technocrats micro-managing AI businesses and industry. Down the other: entrepreneurial freedom and technological innovation.
ted-cruz.work: Sen. Cruz: Congress Should Not Allow a Big Govt-Big Tech Takeover of AI (executive session opening statement)
ted-cruz.why: He rejects government micro-management of AI development in favour of private entrepreneurial freedom.

william-macaskill.q: I tentatively think that an international AGI project is feasible and desirable.
william-macaskill.work: What an international project to develop AGI should look like
william-macaskill.why: He favours AGI being developed by a project 'sponsored by and meaningfully overseen by the governments of multiple countries', and the companion note argues it should be government-led rather than private.

yoshua-bengio.q: For example, banning powerful AI systems (say beyond the abilities of GPT-4) that are given autonomy and agency would be a good start. This would entail both national regulation and international agreements.
yoshua-bengio.work: How Rogue AIs may Arise
yoshua-bengio.why: He wants states, through national law and treaties, to control which AI systems may be built.

audrey-tang.q: But now malicious AIs not only speak all languages so well, even the memes, that’s to say pictures, can be translated perfectly into any target culture. So it does widen the aperture for polarization and disinformation attacks.
audrey-tang.why: She treats AI-generated content as a growing disinformation threat that needs new infrastructure, such as pre-bunking and digital signatures, to defend against.

barack-obama.q: But the capacity to create, on TikTok or Instagram, pretty much any image of anybody doing anything, that's going to not ease up. That's going to get worse.
barack-obama.work: Obama Speaks at Hamilton College (conversation with Steven Tepper)
barack-obama.why: Discussing AI deepfakes and the 'death of facts' in the information space, he says the problem will get worse and threatens our ability to share the same facts.

bernie-sanders.q: our democracy must be secured from those who would use these technologies to lie and distort reality
bernie-sanders.work: Artificial intelligence is coming for the working class. We must fight back
bernie-sanders.why: He treats AI's use to distort reality as a threat that democracy must be secured against.

chris-murphy.q: Fake video and audio, without accountability or legal liability, could obliterate any notion of objective truth.
chris-murphy.work: In our scramble to win the AI race against China, we risk losing ourselves
chris-murphy.why: He lists AI-generated fakes as a threat to objective truth.

demis-hassabis.q: And I think that’s a very, very pressing need right now for near-term issues with AI like deepfakes and disinformation and so on.
demis-hassabis.work: Google DeepMind's CEO Demis Hassabis on the path from chatbots to AGI (Decoder transcript)
demis-hassabis.why: He calls marking AI-generated media a very pressing need because of deepfakes and disinformation.

dwarkesh-patel.q: People grossly overstate the risks AI poses via misinformation and inequality.
dwarkesh-patel.why: He says the misinformation risk from AI is grossly overstated.

ed-zitron.q: The onslaught of AI-generated content — facilitated, in no small part, by Google and Microsoft — has polluted our information ecosystems.
ed-zitron.why: He says AI-generated content has polluted information ecosystems and goes on to say it is 'constantly chipping away at our understanding of reality.'

elizabeth-nolan-brown.why: Her headline flatly asserts that AI misinformation is not destabilizing elections, citing research that it hasn't changed the misinformation landscape.

emily-m-bender.q: The pollution of the information ecosystem with synthetic media
emily-m-bender.work: Written testimony, House Science Committee joint subcommittee hearing 'Balancing Knowledge and Governance: Foundations for Effective Risk Management of Artificial Intelligence'
emily-m-bender.why: This is the first item on her testimony's list of 'real risks and harms', following her point that no one is accountable for synthetic text spilled into the information ecosystem.

erik-brynjolfsson.q: Other harms will also need to be addressed, including the amplification of misinformation and polarization, potentially destabilizing our democracy
erik-brynjolfsson.work: Machines of mind: The case for an AI-powered productivity boom
erik-brynjolfsson.why: He names AI's amplification of misinformation as a harm serious enough to potentially destabilize democracy.

felix-simon.q: We argue that current concerns about the effects of generative AI on the misinformation landscape are overblown.
felix-simon.work: Misinformation reloaded? Fears about the impact of generative AI on misinformation are overblown
felix-simon.why: The whole commentary argues that generative AI is likely to have at best modest effects on misinformation and the public arena.

frances-haugen.q: Generative AI will pour gasoline on the worst problems of social platforms because it will make it possible to generate information operations that look like real human beings.
frances-haugen.work: Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen on what social media companies are still hiding
frances-haugen.why: Asked directly about generative AI, she says it will sharply worsen misinformation problems by enabling fake-human information operations.

jack-clark.q: My takeaway from this research is that LLMs will inevitably be used to generate synthetic propaganda about things most people deem to be conspiracy theories. We can probably blunt the socially corrosive effects of this if we design in some constraints - but that takes policy.
jack-clark.work: Import AI 440: Red Queen AI; AI regulating AI
jack-clark.why: In his own commentary on a persuasion study, he predicts LLM propaganda will be socially corrosive and that more people will believe things with no basis in reality.

jeff-jarvis.q: But hold on. First, we already have more than enough misinformation; who’s to say that any more will make a difference?
jeff-jarvis.work: A few unpopular opinions about AI
jeff-jarvis.why: Under the heading 'AI will not ruin democracy', he rejects alarm that AI misinformation is a serious threat.

jonathan-haidt.q: AI-enhanced social media will wash ever-larger torrents of garbage into our public conversation.
jonathan-haidt.work: AI Will Soon Make Social Media Much More Harmful to Liberal Democracy, and to Children
jonathan-haidt.why: This is the first of four threats he and his co-author converged on, as part of an argument that AI threatens shared understanding in democracy.

kate-crawford.q: And it’s filling information ecosystems with torrents of shit, endless digital detritus which is never properly flushed out.
kate-crawford.work: Eating the Future: The Metabolic Logic of AI Slop
kate-crawford.why: She describes AI slop smothering reality with fabricated war imagery and threatening 'cognitive collapse' of the information environment.

meredith-whittaker.q: Then you're going to be, effectively creating. an epistemic function that is fundamentally misinforming people, and that is training people to trust the reflexive.
meredith-whittaker.work: Tech, AI, digital infrastructure and surveillance with Meredith Whittaker
meredith-whittaker.why: On chatbots as the first and last point of inquiry, she says unsourced generated answers misinform people and could enable opaque mass disinformation, and that 'we should be worried about that'.

paul-kingsnorth.q: If AI doesn’t kill us, it will certainly render us incapable of understanding what reality is.
paul-kingsnorth.why: In his own voice he predicts AI will leave people unable to grasp what is real, after describing a flood of machine-made 'storytelling' that is artifice all the way down.

pope-leo-xiv.q: The power of simulation is such that AI can even deceive us by fabricating parallel “realities,” usurping our faces and voices.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Message for the 60th World Communications Day 2026
pope-leo-xiv.why: He warns that AI makes it increasingly hard to tell reality from fiction and amplifies disinformation.

richard-blumenthal.q: When the American people can no longer recognize fact from fiction, quite literally, it will be impossible to have a democracy.
richard-blumenthal.work: Oversight of AI: Election Deepfakes (S. Hrg., Senate Judiciary subcommittee), opening statement of Chair Blumenthal
richard-blumenthal.why: Opening a hearing on AI deepfakes, he calls them a 'clear and present danger to our democracy' because they erode the public's ability to tell fact from fiction.

robin-hanson.q: What saves us, if anything does, is that we listen to many competing persuaders, and we trust other teams to advise us on who to believe and what to do. We can continue this approach with AIs.
robin-hanson.why: Responding to fears of AI propaganda, he argues existing competition among persuaders will still protect us.

rumman-chowdhury.q: Really, the pivot that ChatGPT, and Bard, and a lot of the more readily available models do is now anybody can make it very easily. So we do have to be concerned about the type of media and how convincing it is.
rumman-chowdhury.work: ChatGPT And Beyond: What's Behind The AI Boom? (Science Friday transcript)
rumman-chowdhury.why: Asked how big a concern AI-made misinformation is, she calls it 'a fairly large concern' because generative models let anyone produce convincing fake media.

stuart-russell.q: The Subcommittee is already well aware of the potentially serious harm to the public sphere caused by disinformation and deepfakes, which may disintegrate our shared understanding of reality.
stuart-russell.work: Written Testimony before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology, & the Law ('Oversight of A.I.: Principles for Regulation')
stuart-russell.why: Russell describes AI disinformation and deepfakes as a serious threat to shared reality and calls standards for provenance and labelling urgently needed.

timnit-gebru.q: the explosion of synthetic media in the world, which both reproduces systems of oppression and endangers our information ecosystem
timnit-gebru.work: Statement from the listed authors of Stochastic Parrots on the "AI pause" letter
timnit-gebru.why: Among ongoing harms, the authors list synthetic media that endangers the information ecosystem.

yann-lecun.q: They don’t realize that AI actually mitigates dangers like hate speech, misinformation, propagandist attempts to corrupt the electoral system.
yann-lecun.work: How Not to Be Stupid About AI, With Yann LeCun
yann-lecun.why: Responding to alarms about AI, he says AI reduces misinformation and propaganda rather than threatening shared truth.

yoshua-bengio.q: In particular, we already see current AI being used to influence public opinion (e.g. with deep fakes) and undermine democratic institutions by stoking distrust and confusion.
yoshua-bengio.work: Reasoning through arguments against taking AI safety seriously
yoshua-bengio.why: He says AI deepfakes are already spreading distrust and confusion that undermine democracy.
