yuval-noah-harari.q: If we are not careful, we might be trapped behind a curtain of illusions, which we could not tear away — or even realise is there.
yuval-noah-harari.work: Watch out humans: AI has hacked the operating system of civilisation
yuval-noah-harari.why: He argues AI-generated language and content could trap society in illusions and destroy meaningful public conversation.

asad-ramzanali.q: The first step to a healthier market is to break up companies that are vertically integrated, so that platforms don’t compete with their customers.
asad-ramzanali.work: Break Up Big AI Before It Breaks Us
asad-ramzanali.why: He calls for breaking up the vertically integrated Big Tech and AI firms.

matt-stoller.q: That Google’s ill-gotten gains are absolutely enormous suggests that the remedy must be aggressive. (Indeed my critique of this proposal is that it’s not far-reaching enough.)
matt-stoller.work: The Proposal to Break Up Google Is Finally Here
matt-stoller.why: Discussing the DOJ proposal to force Google to sell Chrome and possibly Android, he says the break-up remedy should go further.

meredith-whittaker.q: some of the first measures that I think would be necessary are something along the lines of structural separation, which is where we begin to undo the vertical integration of a lot of these companies
meredith-whittaker.work: Tech, AI, digital infrastructure and surveillance with Meredith Whittaker
meredith-whittaker.why: Asked for policy changes, she proposes structurally separating big tech companies' infrastructure and application layers, which is a form of breakup.

audrey-tang.q: But if we see something that attacks our values, fuels division, amplifies extremes, then it sparks outrage, and then we’re hooked, addicted to the screen and ready to fight.
audrey-tang.why: She describes engagement-maximising feeds as addictive and outrage-inducing, and goes on to say they erode attentiveness and embodied life.

bernie-sanders.q: Does anyone in our country think that the past 20 years of social media have been good for children's mental health and cognitive capabilities?
bernie-sanders.work: Artificial Intelligence (Senate floor speech)
bernie-sanders.why: In context, this rhetorical question asserts that social media has harmed children's mental health, and he warns against trusting the same companies again.

chris-murphy.q: Already, we spend half as much time in communion with friends as we did just a generation ago, and that's just the impact of social media. Advanced AI is going to supersize this trend, and we will grow even more mentally unhealthy
chris-murphy.work: Murphy Speaks on AI's Impact on Job Loss, Purpose, Social Connection at Brookings Institution
chris-murphy.why: He attributes declining connection and worse mental health to social media and expects AI to worsen it.

christopher-ferguson.q: We found little evidence social media or other screen use worsens mental health.
christopher-ferguson.work: Social Media and Youth Mental Health
christopher-ferguson.why: Reporting his own meta-analysis, he says the evidence does not show social media harms youth mental health.

daron-acemoglu.q: Although there is much we do not know about the systemic political and social effects of social media, existing evidence suggests that they have contributed both to mental health problems and polarization in politics.
daron-acemoglu.work: Written Testimony, Hearing on 'The Philosophy of AI: Learning from History, Shaping Our Future'
daron-acemoglu.why: He concludes that engagement-driven social media has harmed mental health; elsewhere he blames the digital-ad business model.

frances-haugen.q: This is about the teenagers whose mental health is undermined by Instagram.
frances-haugen.work: Written Testimony of Frances Haugen, 'Holding Big Tech Accountable'
frances-haugen.why: In her own testimony she states that Instagram, an engagement-optimized product, undermines teenagers' mental health, alongside her claim that its profit-optimizing machine generates self-harm and self-hate.

jaron-lanier.q: Users experience what seems to be a communitarian paradise, but they are targeted by stealthy and addictive algorithms that make people vain, irritable, and paranoid.
jaron-lanier.why: He says the 'free' ad-driven platform model uses addictive algorithms that harm people's psychology, and calls it a disaster.

jonathan-haidt.q: There are now multiple lines of evidence showing that social media is causing harm at an industrial scale.
jonathan-haidt.work: Why You Should Be a Techno-Skeptic (TED talk transcript)
jonathan-haidt.why: He states, citing experimental evidence on anxiety and depression, that social media causes large-scale harm.

paul-kingsnorth.q: I could write about what online reading has done to concentration spans, what smartphone use has done to social mores, how the brains of young children have been rewired by tablets and screens.
paul-kingsnorth.why: Opening an essay that declares the Internet a disaster for the human race, he lists damage to attention and children's brains from screens as his own case.

scott-wiener.q: When social media platforms addicted children and helped spur our youth mental health crisis, Congress failed to protect these children by passing legislation (other than banning TikTok).
scott-wiener.work: Senator Wiener Responds to Speaker Emerita Pelosi's Opposition to SB 1047
scott-wiener.why: In his own statement he says social media platforms addicted children and helped cause the youth mental health crisis.

tristan-harris.q: And that little baby AI that just did that little narrow thing was enough to rec, you know, democracies, you know, create the most anxious and depressed generation of our lifetime, shortened attention spans and completely change the social fabric.
tristan-harris.work: The Great Simplification ep. 214: Tristan Harris (transcript)
tristan-harris.why: Harris says engagement-ranking social media created the most anxious and depressed generation.

alexandria-ocasio-cortez.q: And all of this harm has occurred because of the absence of federal legislation to regulate AI,
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.work: Ocasio-Cortez Introduces House Version of the AI Data Center Moratorium Act
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.why: Introducing her bill, she blames AI harms on the lack of federal regulation and ties the moratorium to Congress passing a binding framework.

alondra-nelson.q: looming risks such as exacerbating bias, catalyzing labor disruption, increasing surveillance, and widening inequality—heightens the urgency for meaningful and enforceable guardrails.
alondra-nelson.work: Regulating AI in the Evolving Transatlantic Landscape
alondra-nelson.why: She calls for enforceable, government-set guardrails on AI, which includes binding rules on the companies that develop it.

andrew-yang.q: Josh Gottheimer and Mike Lawler, a Dem and a Republican, announced a bill to enforce a waiting period on AI models. I hope it advances.
andrew-yang.why: He supports a bill imposing a mandatory waiting period on AI models, alongside his case for AI regulation.

asad-ramzanali.q: And Congress should pass legislation to break apart other parts of the Big AI ecosystem—including undoing investments and other partnerships that look like acquisitions designed to evade regulatory scrutiny—before it cements even more control of the digital economy.
asad-ramzanali.work: Break Up Big AI Before It Breaks Us
asad-ramzanali.why: He calls for legislation imposing structural rules on leading AI developers and their investors.

barack-obama.q: I think it’s entirely appropriate for us to plant a flag and say, “All right, frontier companies, you need to disclose what your safety protocols are to make sure that we don’t have rogue programs going off and hacking into our financial system,” for example.
barack-obama.work: Barack Obama on AI, free speech, and the future of the internet
barack-obama.why: He endorses requiring frontier AI companies to disclose safety protocols, along with independent verification.

bernie-sanders.q: ban artificial superintelligence—an artificial mind smarter than any human, capable of operating independently beyond our control—until a new federal body is able to ensure the technology's safety.
bernie-sanders.work: Don't Let Big Tech Dictate Humanity's Future
bernie-sanders.why: He sponsors legislation for a legal ban and a federal body to ensure the safety of the most advanced AI.

brian-merchant.q: California’s the best hope for strong AI regulation, yet the governor’s political aspirations will keep him cozy with Silicon Valley.
brian-merchant.work: The Luddite Renaissance is in full swing
brian-merchant.why: He presents strong state AI regulation as something to hope for and worries it will be blocked.

bruce-schneier.q: Congress should not only hurry up and push AI regulation forward but also go one step further and develop its own programs for AI.
bruce-schneier.work: Build AI by the People, for the People
bruce-schneier.why: He calls on Congress to pass AI regulation of the private sector quickly.

chris-murphy.q: The only way to slow that race is one set of rules that applies to every company, and only government can write them.
chris-murphy.work: AI Leaders Are Sounding the Alarm. Who's Listening?
chris-murphy.why: He calls for government-written rules binding all AI companies.

daniel-kokotajlo.q: Get companies to make voluntary commitments, and government to make regulation / executive orders, that include public reporting requirements, aimed at making it impossible to do it in secret without violating these commitments.
daniel-kokotajlo.work: Training AGI in Secret would be Unsafe and Unethical
daniel-kokotajlo.why: As his own policy recommendation he calls for government regulation or executive orders imposing reporting requirements on AGI developers.

dario-amodei.q: Addressing the risks of AI will require a mix of voluntary actions taken by companies (and private third-party actors) and actions taken by governments that bind everyone.
dario-amodei.why: He says government action that binds everyone will be needed, though he wants it judicious and limited.

daron-acemoglu.q: Therefore, my conclusion is that the best way of preventing these costs is to regulate AI and redirect AI research, away from these harmful endeavors
daron-acemoglu.why: His conclusion calls for regulating AI, and he argues that unregulated markets run by a few tech companies will not avoid AI's harms.

dean-ball.q: The medium-term solution to the broader problem—the lack of a coherent frontier AI governance framework—is a technocratic law, passed by Congress and not by Executive fiat, that puts real guardrails on both industry and government.
dean-ball.work: Leviathan Waking (On Anthropic/USG, and a new era in AI governance)
dean-ball.why: He calls for a congressional law putting real guardrails on frontier AI developers (he also backs SB 53 and federalising state frontier safety laws).

demis-hassabis.q: And I think some form of really almost a smart regulation is required that is dynamic and can adapt with the times very quickly, and probably informed by the leading labs because they’re seeing what’s actually at the coalface.
demis-hassabis.work: Demis Hassabis Thinks We're in the 'Foothills of the Singularity'
demis-hassabis.why: Asked whether government should regulate AI rather than labs self-regulating, he says government involvement and smart, adaptive regulation are required.

ed-zitron.q: The fact that Anthropic, OpenAI, and Meta are both training and allowing cybersecurity models to connect to their vast amounts of GPU infrastructure is irresponsible and should not be legal.
ed-zitron.work: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands
ed-zitron.why: He says specific frontier-lab practices should be illegal and calls for real safeguards and prosecution.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: Put a ceiling on how much computing power anyone is allowed to use in training an AI system, and move it downward over the coming years to compensate for more efficient training algorithms.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: The Only Way to Deal With the Threat From AI? Shut It Down
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He proposes binding legal limits on AI training.

elizabeth-warren.q: Congress must urgently pass legislation to put stronger guardrails in place before we have a cyberattack, economic crisis, or national security disaster facilitated by AI.
elizabeth-warren.work: Senator Warren Calls for Pause in Advanced AI Development
elizabeth-warren.why: In a statement about frontier models, she calls for legislation imposing guardrails.

elon-musk.q: AI is a rare case where I think we need to be proactive in regulation, instead of reactive.
elon-musk.work: Elon Musk Governor's Interview (NGA 2017, AI segment transcript)
elon-musk.why: He calls for government regulation of AI, adding that regulators should be able to make all developers pause until it is safe.

emily-m-bender.q: Yes, there is an urgent need to address the harm being done by so-called “AI” and to set up effective regulation and governance so that those who are impacted by this technology have power over how it is deployed.
emily-m-bender.work: On NYT Magazine on AI: Resist the Urge to be Impressed
emily-m-bender.why: She calls for effective regulation of the AI systems built by big tech companies.

erik-hoel.q: Then we can put forward a new (or perhaps old) argument for regulating AI.
erik-hoel.work: We need a Butlerian Jihad against AI
erik-hoel.why: He notes there is currently no AI regulation and sets out a deontological case for regulating and banning strong AI research.

gary-marcus.q: We should be making SB-1047 stronger, not weaker.
gary-marcus.work: The misguided backlash against California's SB-1047
gary-marcus.why: He defends California's bill setting binding safety duties for developers of $100M+ models and wants it made stronger.

gavin-newsom.q: That report, released in late spring, provides us with a roadmap to regulate frontier Al prudently and proactively, ensuring we balance innovation with public safety.
gavin-newsom.work: SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) signing message
gavin-newsom.why: In signing SB 53, which sets state oversight of frontier AI developers, he endorses regulating frontier AI.

guillaume-verdon.q: So we’re actually for reliability engineering, we just think that the market is much more efficient at achieving this sort of reliability optimum than sort of heavy-handed regulations that are written by the incumbents
guillaume-verdon.work: Guillaume Verdon: Beff Jezos, E/acc Movement, Physics, Computation & AGI (Lex Fridman Podcast #407)
guillaume-verdon.why: He prefers market selection and deployer liability to regulation of AI developers.

helen-toner.q: First, we should be implementing transparency requirements for developers of high stakes AI systems.
helen-toner.work: Transcript: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing, "Oversight of AI: Insiders' Perspectives"
helen-toner.why: In her own opening testimony she calls for mandatory transparency requirements on developers of high-stakes AI, the first of six policy building blocks.

holly-elmore.q: Right now, we need to regulate the process of building frontier AI itself.
holly-elmore.why: Direct call to regulate frontier AI developers.

jack-clark.q: For us to get through this - to chart a course through the singularity – we are going to need to work together to create unusual and serious rules for this technology and the companies building it
jack-clark.work: Import AI 477: In which I tell the IMF the Singularity has begun
jack-clark.why: He calls for serious rules on AI and the companies building it.

josh-hawley.q: And the government should inspect all of these frontier AI systems, so we can better understand what the tech titans plan to build and deploy.
josh-hawley.work: AI Threatens the Working Man
josh-hawley.why: He proposes mandatory government inspection and reporting for frontier AI developers as 'guardrails'.

karen-hao.q: I would create more transparency laws—transparency at all levels. Transparency of the amount of data that companies are collecting, the environmental costs of their infrastructure—and put all of that in place pre-generative AI boom.
karen-hao.why: Asked what she would do, she calls for transparency laws on AI companies, and in her next answer she says she would still do much the same today.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: This will involve invasive restrictions on AI labs and on the core team of AGI researchers, from extreme vetting to constant monitoring to working from a SCIF to reduced freedom to leave
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: In a passage saying 'we obviously need to lock this stuff down', he calls for government-backed mandatory security restrictions on AI labs (while doubting ordinary safety regulation is sufficient).

marc-andreessen.q: Big AI companies should be allowed to build AI as fast and aggressively as they can – but not allowed to achieve regulatory capture
marc-andreessen.work: Why AI Will Save the World
marc-andreessen.why: In his policy plan, large AI developers should face no restraint on building, only a bar on regulatory capture; he adds that no new laws are needed.

marsha-blackburn.q: I look forward to introducing the TRUMP AMERICA AI Act in the new year to create one federal rulebook for AI to protect children, creators, conservatives, and communities across the country
marsha-blackburn.work: Blackburn Unveils National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence (TRUMP AMERICA AI Act)
marsha-blackburn.why: In her own words she announces a bill setting binding federal rules for AI developers, including a duty of care and risk assessments.

max-tegmark.q: I never thought governments would let AI companies get this far without any meaningful regulation.
max-tegmark.work: How to Keep AI Under Control
max-tegmark.why: He faults governments for not regulating AI companies, which implies they should.

meredith-whittaker.q: It is imperative that lawmakers regulate to ensure that these systems are accountable, accurate, contestable, and that those most at risk of harm have a say in how, and whether, they are used.
meredith-whittaker.work: Written Testimony of Meredith Whittaker: "Artificial Intelligence: Societal and Ethical Implications"
meredith-whittaker.why: Testifying to Congress about AI systems built by a handful of private companies, she calls for lawmakers to regulate them.

miles-brundage.q: By the end of 2025, if not earlier, we need comprehensive AI regulation in the US
miles-brundage.why: He calls for comprehensive regulation, and elsewhere regrets that there is 'no real requirement' for frontier companies to have good safety policies.

mustafa-suleyman.q: Alongside spelling out very precisely the kind of superintelligence we should build, the time has come to also consider what societal boundaries, norms and laws we want around this process.
mustafa-suleyman.why: He calls for laws around superintelligence development and later says accountability and oversight are to be welcomed.

noah-smith.q: And as our institutions bicker about military AI, mass surveillance, and “woke” politics, essentially everyone is ignoring the simple fact that we are placing unregulated weapons into everyone’s hands.
noah-smith.work: If AI is a weapon, why don't we regulate it like one?
noah-smith.why: In a post titled 'If AI is a weapon, why don't we regulate it like one?', he argues that AI agents should be regulated like weapons and that the state should control frontier AI.

pete-buttigieg.q: I do think that safety regulation is important, but I also think that if that was all we were doing, we would be missing the piece that I'm talking about
pete-buttigieg.work: Pete Buttigieg has a warning about AI (NPR interview excerpt)
pete-buttigieg.why: Asked about regulating AI, he endorses safety regulation while saying it is not enough.

pope-leo-xiv.q: It is not enough to invoke ethics in the abstract; robust legal frameworks, independent oversight, informed users and a political system that does not abdicate its responsibility are required.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: He calls for binding legal frameworks and independent oversight of AI, not voluntary ethics.

richard-blumenthal.q: And the framework is, basically: establishing a licensing regime for companies that are engaged in high-risk AI development; creating an independent oversight body that has expertise with AI and works with other agencies to administer and enforce the law
richard-blumenthal.work: Oversight of A.I.: Legislating on Artificial Intelligence (S. Hrg. 118-154), opening statement of Chair Blumenthal
richard-blumenthal.why: He presents his own legislative framework requiring licences for high-risk AI developers, enforced by an independent oversight body.

ro-khanna.q: We need clear enforceable guardrails with mandatory third-party verification of advanced AI models, so this powerful technology does not cause serious societal harm.
ro-khanna.work: We need a new tech social contract to reclaim AI from billionaires
ro-khanna.why: He calls for enforceable rules and a federal agency for advanced AI models.

rumman-chowdhury.q: Like the Facebook Oversight Board, it should receive advisory input and guidance from industry, but have the capacity to make independent binding decisions that companies must comply with.
rumman-chowdhury.why: She proposes a global governance body whose decisions on generative AI developers are binding and enforceable.

sam-altman.q: The US government, and all other governments, should regulate the development of SMI.
sam-altman.why: He calls for government regulation of superhuman AI development, including required safeguards.

samuel-hammond.q: The use of the Defense Production Act to require disclosures from frontier labs is appropriate given the unique affordances available to the Department of Defense, and the bona fide national security risks associated with sufficiently advanced forms of AI.
samuel-hammond.why: Hammond supports mandatory safety testing and disclosure requirements for frontier labs, under a section titled 'Oversight of AGI labs is prudent'.

scott-wiener.q: SB 1047 is well calibrated to what we know about forseeable AI risks, and it deserves to be enacted.
scott-wiener.work: Senator Wiener Responds to OpenAI Opposition to SB 1047
scott-wiener.why: He authored and argues for enacting SB 1047, a law imposing safety-testing and shutdown requirements on the largest AI developers.

shoshana-zuboff.q: Some very significant things have happened in Europe during these years: the Digital Services Act, the Digital Markets Act, the AI Act.
shoshana-zuboff.work: Shoshana Zuboff, philosopher: 'AI is surveillance capitalism continuing to evolve and expand'
shoshana-zuboff.why: Having called AI the continuation of surveillance capitalism, she praises the EU's binding laws, including the AI Act, and urges EU leaders to stand by them and 'be fierce'.

steven-adler.q: But given the limitations of voluntary safety practices, I’d feel nervous to rely on this as the stakes get higher.
steven-adler.work: The magic phrase that kills AI regulation
steven-adler.why: In discussing whether AI companies should be required to act to reduce catastrophe risk, he rejects relying on voluntary practice and supports procedural or substantive requirements.

stuart-russell.q: Regulation can encourage the transition from making AI safe to making safe AI by putting the onus on developers to demonstrate to regulators that their systems are safe.
stuart-russell.work: Make AI safe or make safe AI?
stuart-russell.why: Russell argues for regulation that requires developers to prove their systems are safe, with red lines whose violation means removal from the market.

timnit-gebru.q: While those are important, the #1 thing that would safeguard us from unsafe uses of AI is curbing the power of the companies who develop it and increasing the power of those who speak up against the harms of AI and these companies’ practices.
timnit-gebru.work: For truly ethical AI, its research must be independent from big tech
timnit-gebru.why: She calls technology-specific regulations important and says the top safeguard is curbing the power of the companies that develop AI.

tristan-harris.q: CHT recently just officially endorsed the AI LEAD Act introduced by both a Democratic and a Republican senator. This is Senators Durbin and Hawley, and it creates a liability for products that are defective that create harm.
tristan-harris.why: Harris reports that his organisation endorsed a bill imposing legal liability on AI developers, which is a binding rule.

william-macaskill.q: These could include mandatory predeployment testing for alignment and dangerous capabilities, tied to conditions for release
william-macaskill.why: The authors describe mandatory predeployment testing for frontier systems as regulation that is 'sensible on their own terms'.

william-saunders.q: The proposed SB 1047 legislation in California, while it could be improved, is the best attempt I’ve seen to provide a check on this power.
william-saunders.why: He backs binding legislation on frontier model developers (risk-assessment disclosure, whistleblower protection) and in Senate testimony says a policy response is needed.

yann-lecun.q: The question that people are debating is whether it makes sense to regulate research and development of AI. And I don't think it does.
yann-lecun.work: How Not to Be Stupid About AI, With Yann LeCun
yann-lecun.why: He accepts regulation of safety-critical products but says AI research and development itself should not be regulated.

yoshua-bengio.q: To deal with conflicts of interest (between public good and profit maximization) within corporate AI labs, the government could force these companies to have multiple stakeholders on their board
yoshua-bengio.work: Reasoning through arguments against taking AI safety seriously
yoshua-bengio.why: He proposes government-imposed obligations on AI labs and urges regulation 'with effective teeth'.

yuval-noah-harari.q: We need an equivalent of the US food & drug administration for new technology, and we need it yesterday.
yuval-noah-harari.work: Watch out humans: AI has hacked the operating system of civilisation
yuval-noah-harari.why: He calls for mandatory safety checks before powerful AI tools are released, enforced by a regulator.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: It is narrowly requesting that, if you are building something that might plausibly be a superintelligence, under anything like present conditions, you should instead not do that. We should not allow you to do that.
zvi-mowshowitz.work: New Statement Calls For Not Building Superintelligence For Now
zvi-mowshowitz.why: Explaining the statement he signed, he endorses not allowing developers to build possible superintelligence, which is a binding rule on frontier developers.

daniel-faggella.q: If humanity must have a successor (and it must, we can’t expect nature to stand still), then we should create a Worthy Successor.
daniel-faggella.work: A Worthy Successor: The Purpose of AGI
daniel-faggella.why: He argues that building a posthuman intelligence more capable than humans is the great moral aim of AGI, not wrong in itself.

dean-ball.q: I fully believe that humans will build machines more intelligent than ourselves under the definition of intelligence I have laid forth here, and I strongly suspect we will do so within the next decade. Why, then, do I believe we should continue advancing AI?
dean-ball.work: 2023 (Or, Why I am Not a Doomer)
dean-ball.why: He expects smarter-than-human machines and then explains why he believes we should keep advancing AI, so he does not see building them as wrong in itself.

demis-hassabis.q: The reason I've worked on AI and AGI my entire life is because I believe, if it's done properly and responsibly, it will be the most beneficial technology ever invented.
demis-hassabis.work: Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis on AGI and AI in the Military
demis-hassabis.why: Building AGI is his life's goal and he calls it potentially the most beneficial technology ever, so he does not see building it as wrong in itself.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: So far as I’m concerned, if you can get a powerful AGI that carries out some pivotal superhuman engineering task, with a less than fifty percent change of killing more than one billion people, I’ll take it.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: AGI Ruin: A List of Lethalities
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He judges building superhuman AI by its outcomes and would accept it if it were survivable, so he does not think it wrong in itself.

elon-musk.q: And at times I sort of think, well, perhaps even if there was a stop button, we probably shouldn’t press it because the most likely outcome is incredible abundance for all.
elon-musk.work: Full Transcript: Zanny Minton Beddoes Interviews Elon Musk (The Economist)
elon-musk.why: He builds superintelligence himself and judges it by its likely outcome, saying it probably should not be stopped.

erik-hoel.q: Far more important than the process: strong AI is immoral in and of itself.
erik-hoel.work: We need a Butlerian Jihad against AI
erik-hoel.why: He argues that strong, human-level general AI is an abomination whose mere existence is immoral, however ethically it is built or deployed.

guillaume-verdon.q: or we have a hard cutoff of like we don’t birth these technologies at all and then we leave all the potential upside on the table.
guillaume-verdon.work: Guillaume Verdon: Beff Jezos, E/acc Movement, Physics, Computation & AGI (Lex Fridman Podcast #407)
guillaume-verdon.why: He presents building advanced AI as the path humanity should take, which rules out seeing the attempt as wrong in itself.

jack-clark.q: And yet building this technology is one of the best ways that we as a species can advance ourselves
jack-clark.work: Import AI 458: Reckoning with the future; and a singularity story
jack-clark.why: Right after describing AI that may surpass all of us, he calls building it one of the best ways for humanity to advance, so he does not see it as wrong in itself.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: But it will be our duty to serve the free world—and all of humanity. If we make it through and get to look back on those years, it will be the most important thing we ever did.
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: Writing about the project to build superintelligence, he calls taking part a duty and the most important thing they will do, so he does not see building it as wrong in itself.

marc-andreessen.q: The development and proliferation of AI – far from a risk that we should fear – is a moral obligation that we have to ourselves, to our children, and to our future.
marc-andreessen.work: Why AI Will Save the World
marc-andreessen.why: He treats building AI that does everything people do much better as a moral obligation, not a wrong.

mark-zuckerberg.q: Meta believes strongly in building personal superintelligence that empowers everyone.
mark-zuckerberg.why: He commits his company to building superintelligence as a good thing, which plainly rules out seeing it as wrong in itself.

max-tegmark.q: It’s true that superintelligence can have huge upside if it’s aligned.
max-tegmark.work: The 'Don't Look Up' Thinking That Could Doom Us With AI
max-tegmark.why: He judges superintelligence by its outcome, granting it could be very good if aligned, so he does not hold it is wrong in itself.

mustafa-suleyman.q: Superintelligence could be the best invention ever – but only if it puts the interests of humans above everything else.
mustafa-suleyman.why: He is building superintelligence and judges it by its outcome for humans, not as wrong in itself.

nick-land.q: Any problem whatsoever that we might have would be better answered by a superior mind. Ergo, our instrumental but also absolute priority is the realization of superior minds.
nick-land.why: Land states that building superior minds is our absolute priority, the opposite of calling it wrong in itself.

paul-kingsnorth.q: If you rebel against God, you can be God. That’s what we’re doing. We’re trying to create God, make God live forever.
paul-kingsnorth.work: Paul Kingsnorth: how to fight the Machine
paul-kingsnorth.why: He frames the project of building superhuman intelligence as the Genesis sin of rebellion against God, wrong in its nature rather than only in its effects.

richard-sutton.q: I do encourage people to think positively about it. First of all, it’s something we humans have always tried to do for thousands of years, try to understand ourselves, trying to make ourselves think better, just understanding ourselves.
richard-sutton.work: Richard Sutton: Father of RL thinks LLMs are a dead end
richard-sutton.why: Right after arguing we will reach superintelligence, he urges people to view creating it positively, as a great success of science, not as wrong in itself.

scott-alexander.q: Second, if we never get AI, I expect the future to be short and grim.
scott-alexander.work: Pause For Thought: The AI Pause Debate
scott-alexander.why: He judges building advanced AI by its outcomes and thinks forgoing it would leave the world worse, so he does not see it as wrong in itself.

william-saunders.q: I do think we can figure this technology out. I do think we can do it properly. I think that is totally possible, but we have to be willing to put in the hard work to do that.
william-saunders.work: Former OpenAI Engineer William Saunders on Silence, Safety, and the Right to Warn
william-saunders.why: He thinks advanced AI can be built properly with enough safety work, so he does not see building it as wrong in itself.

yann-lecun.q: So having machines that are smarter than us, that assist us in all of our tasks, our daily lives, whether it’s professional or personal, I think would be an absolutely wonderful thing.
yann-lecun.work: Transcript for Yann LeCun: Meta AI, Open Source, Limits of LLMs, AGI & the Future of AI
yann-lecun.why: He calls machines smarter than us an absolutely wonderful thing, the opposite of judging the attempt wrong in itself.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: I don’t actually think you can ever ‘prove’ safety of a superintelligence, what you do (like for most other things) is mitigate risk to acceptable levels since there are big costs to not building it.
zvi-mowshowitz.work: New Statement Calls For Not Building Superintelligence For Now
zvi-mowshowitz.why: He treats building superintelligence as acceptable once risk is low enough and sees costs in not building it, so he does not think it is wrong in itself.

adam-thierer.q: A national framework is also crucial to ensuring that America has the computational capabilities needed to square off against China and other global adversaries in what some call an “AI Cold War.”
adam-thierer.work: Testimony, Hearing on "AI at a Crossroads: A Nationwide Strategy or Californication?"
adam-thierer.why: He uses competition with China as a central reason for a pro-growth national AI framework.

alex-karp.q: I happen to respect their culture quite a bit, China, but it is us or them. And they have a dynamic, interesting super high IQ scaled culture that is doing exceedingly well at AI. And we've got to make sure we're the leaders.
alex-karp.why: Answering an analyst during the call, he frames AI as an us-or-them contest with China and says the US must lead.

andrew-yang.q: The argument that “we can’t interfere with the AI industry for fear of losing the competition to China” ignores the facts
andrew-yang.why: He dismisses the China-race argument for not interfering with AI, as he also does in his safeguards post.

asad-ramzanali.q: American leadership in AI is critical to our geopolitical competition with the People’s Republic of China (PRC).
asad-ramzanali.work: Testimony before House Energy & Commerce Subcommittee on Communications and Technology: AI in the Everyday
asad-ramzanali.why: Under the heading 'America Must Maintain its Lead', he argues the US must sustain its AI lead over China, though through R&D, startups and broad access rather than only bigger models.

bernie-sanders.q: we should not be racing with China or anyone else to see who is the first to eliminate millions of jobs or the first to build an AI that destroys the planet. That is not a race anyone should win.
bernie-sanders.work: Artificial Intelligence (Senate floor speech)
bernie-sanders.why: On the Senate floor he rejects an AI race with China as a reason to press ahead.

daniel-kokotajlo.q: I now think that to a significant extent this race is happening anyway. If we want a serious slowdown, we need to coordinate internationally to all proceed cautiously together.
daniel-kokotajlo.work: Training AGI in Secret would be Unsafe and Unethical
daniel-kokotajlo.why: He says he no longer believes the 'good guys' should race to AGI first, and calls for international coordination to slow down instead.

dario-amodei.q: In the end, AI companies in the US and other democracies must have better models than those in China if we want to prevail.
dario-amodei.why: In arguing for export controls, he says US and allied AI must outpace China's.

david-sacks.q: We must win the AI race, but it matters how we win. Our victory over China will be a Pyrrhic one if we allow our own models to enforce ideological bias, censorship, and historical revisionism akin to CCP AI.
david-sacks.work: Thread on the White House AI Action Plan and Trump's first major AI speech
david-sacks.why: In his own words he frames AI policy as a race the US must win against China.

dean-ball.q: in the long run, the country that is able to both invent and scale new technologies created by and with AI will be the winner of the “AI race.” America is not even remotely on track to do this right now, China is miles ahead of us
dean-ball.why: He frames AI as a race America must win against a China that is ahead, and says not enough is being done to catch up.

dwarkesh-patel.q: But what is the reason we want America to win the AI race? It’s because we want to make sure free open societies can defend themselves.
dwarkesh-patel.work: The most important question nobody's asking about AI
dwarkesh-patel.why: He endorses the US aim of winning the AI race with China, giving the defense of free societies as the reason.

e-glen-weyl.q: If pluralistic societies want to win a race not against China as a nation but against authoritarianism wherever it arises, they cannot make it a race for the development of AI which gives up the game before it begins.
e-glen-weyl.work: AI Is an Ideology, Not a Technology
e-glen-weyl.why: The authors reject framing competition with China as an AI race that the West must push to win.

ed-zitron.q: It’s time to wake up and accept that there was never an “AI arms race,”
ed-zitron.why: He denies that there was ever an AI arms race and puts the data-center build-out down to out-of-touch executives, so he rejects rivalry as a reason for it; elsewhere he calls fear of China's AI rise partly sinophobia.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: If the policy starts with the U.S., then China needs to see that the U.S. is not seeking an advantage but rather trying to prevent a horrifically dangerous technology which can have no true owner and which will kill everyone in the U.S. and in China and on Earth.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: The Only Way to Deal With the Threat From AI? Shut It Down
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He says the US should not seek an advantage over China but help halt the technology for everyone.

gary-marcus.q: I never bought this argument because I figured that getting to GPT-5 first might buy the winner better boilerplate text writing, but not military genius.
gary-marcus.work: The race for "AI Supremacy" is over, at least for now
gary-marcus.why: He rejects the case for racing China to stay ahead, calling export controls a backfire and the lead fleeting.

helen-toner.q: Because of this, I agree that it is a very good thing for the US to have more AI compute, including more AI supercomputers, than China.
helen-toner.work: Building supercomputers for autocrats probably isn't good for democracy, actually
helen-toner.why: Because compute drives national power, she endorses the US keeping a lead over China in AI compute, while objecting to empowering other autocracies.

jd-vance.q: I'm speaking of China -- that will pass up on the opportunity to use AI, or any other technology, to advance their own interests and further undermine the interests of their rivals? I think the answer is obvious, and that's why, America, we've got to be tech-forward.
jd-vance.work: Remarks by the Vice President at the American Dynamism Summit
jd-vance.why: He cites China's likely use of AI as the reason America must lean into the technology.

jensen-huang.q: The United States ought to be ahead. We want to do everything we can to make sure the United States is ahead.
jensen-huang.work: Jensen Huang: Will Nvidia's moat persist?
jensen-huang.why: In the debate about China, he says the US must stay ahead in AI; he calls China 'an adversary' and says 'we want the United States to win'. He argues for winning by competing, not by export controls.

karen-hao.q: this what about China card that Silicon Valley has just been able to pull out so effectively again and again and again, if you look at the track record of what this argument has gotten us, it has just gotten us more authoritarianism in the world.
karen-hao.work: Decolonizing the Future: Karen Hao on Resisting the Empire of AI
karen-hao.why: She dismisses the China-rivalry argument as a card the industry plays, and says it has produced more authoritarianism.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: America must lead. The torch of liberty will not survive Xi getting AGI first.
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: Among the core tenets of his 'AGI Realism', he says the US must lead and scale up quickly because of the race with China.

marc-andreessen.q: And, a whole-of-government program to drive the success of US technology companies globally, against a hostile China and a regulation-crazed EU.
marc-andreessen.work: The Little Tech Agenda
marc-andreessen.why: He proposes a national program to push US technology against a hostile China to keep American technology supremacy.

mark-zuckerberg.q: China is bringing online more power. Because of that, the US really needs to focus on streamlining the ability to build data centers and produce energy. Otherwise, I think we’ll be at a significant disadvantage.
mark-zuckerberg.work: Mark Zuckerberg: AI will write most Meta code in 18 months
mark-zuckerberg.why: He cites competition with China as the reason the US must speed up its AI infrastructure build-out to avoid falling behind.

marsha-blackburn.q: On the Senate Commerce Committee, we're looking at how we can support this critical work, especially as Beijing is continuing to pour billions of dollars.
marsha-blackburn.work: Keynote with Senator Marsha Blackburn, State of the Net 2025
marsha-blackburn.why: She cites Beijing's spending as a reason to push US emerging-technology work, after saying America must stay at the forefront of AI and quantum.

max-tegmark.q: As if the race to superintelligence were an arms race that would be won by “us” or “them”, when it’s probably a suicide race whose only winner is “it.”
max-tegmark.work: The 'Don't Look Up' Thinking That Could Doom Us With AI
max-tegmark.why: Answering the 'But China!' objection to a pause, he rejects the rivalry as a reason to race.

meredith-whittaker.q: the idea that if the US puts any guardrails, any regulations, any restrictions on the unfettered surveillance and development of AI and other systems it will lose to China is doing a lot of work to, I believe, promote unsafe technologies
meredith-whittaker.work: Tech, AI, digital infrastructure and surveillance with Meredith Whittaker
meredith-whittaker.why: She says the China-race narrative is used to promote unsafe technology and brush aside democratic questions, and she asks what 'winning' would even mean.

michael-kratsios.q: We face many dangers as a nation, but thanks to decades of feckless American leaders, China in particular has grown into both a geopolitical rival and technological competitor.
michael-kratsios.work: Remarks by Director Kratsios at the Endless Frontiers Retreat
michael-kratsios.why: He cites China's rivalry as a reason for a strategy to promote and protect US technological leadership in AI and other critical technologies.

miles-brundage.q: Robust responses, especially tightening of American export controls on GPUs, are necessary given the increasing importance of AI to the global economy.
miles-brundage.work: The Real Lesson of DeepSeek's R1
miles-brundage.why: He backs export controls to preserve US leadership against China, while adding that coexistence and cooperation must also be part of the strategy.

noah-smith.q: So it’s in America’s interest to preserve its technological edge in AI for as long as possible.
noah-smith.work: America's chip export controls are working
noah-smith.why: He argues that keeping the US lead in AI over China deters war over Taiwan and Japan.

palmer-luckey.q: AI is the only possible way we can keep up with China's numerical advantage.
palmer-luckey.work: The AI Arsenal That Could Stop World War III (TED)
palmer-luckey.why: His talk argues the US must lead in AI-driven autonomous weapons to deter a Chinese invasion of Taiwan.

pope-leo-xiv.q: Disarming AI means freeing it from the mentality of “armed” competition, which today is not limited simply to the military context, but is also an economic and cognitive phenomenon.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: He rejects the race for more powerful AI driven by the pursuit of geopolitical dominance, which is the rationale the statement endorses.

reid-hoffman.q: DeepSeek demonstrates how immediate and strong the competitive talent from China is and why it’s crucial for America to continue to be at the forefront of AI development.
reid-hoffman.work: Reid Hoffman interview on Superagency, DeepSeek and OpenAI (Fortune Q&A)
reid-hoffman.why: He cites Chinese competition as the reason the US must stay ahead in AI.

ro-khanna.q: The trillions spent on wars and tax cuts for the wealthy and corporations should instead be invested in advanced scientific, military, medical and technological research, such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing.
ro-khanna.work: America Must Not Let China Win
ro-khanna.why: In an op-ed titled 'America Must Not Let China Win', he argues that competing with China requires major US investment in AI and other technology.

scott-alexander.q: I think some people hear transhumanists talk about an “AI race” and mindlessly repeat it, without asking what assumptions it commits them to.
scott-alexander.why: In an essay arguing against delaying AI safety for fear China will 'win' the race, he concludes that which power leads is not worth trading against survival.

scott-santens.q: Neither wants to slow down. Both treat the race itself as the priority, when the winner will be decided by alignment.
scott-santens.work: Our Data. Our Resources. Our Terms and Conditions.
scott-santens.why: He criticizes the US and Chinese governments for prioritizing the race and says beating China is not what matters.

stuart-russell.q: The "AGI race" between companies and between nations is somewhat similar, except worse: Even the CEOs who are engaging in the race have stated that whoever wins has a significant probability of causing human extinction in the process
stuart-russell.work: DeepSeek, OpenAI, and the Race to Human Extinction
stuart-russell.why: Writing about the US reaction to China's DeepSeek, Russell likens the race between nations to the pointless Cold War bomb race, only worse, which rejects rivalry as a good reason to push ahead.

ted-cruz.q: As a matter of economic and national security, America has to beat China in the AI race.
ted-cruz.work: Sen. Cruz: Adopting Europe's Approach on Regulation Will Cause China to Win the AI Race (opening statement, 'Winning the AI Race' hearing)
ted-cruz.why: He makes beating China the central rationale for his AI policy.

timnit-gebru.q: Contrary to big tech executives’ cold-war style rhetoric about an arms race, what truly stifles innovation is the current arrangement where a few people build harmful technology and others constantly work to prevent harm
timnit-gebru.work: For truly ethical AI, its research must be independent from big tech
timnit-gebru.why: She dismisses arms-race rhetoric as a justification and says the real obstacle lies elsewhere.

tristan-harris.q: beating them to a technology that then you use in a way that is self undermining, is not beating China.
tristan-harris.work: The Great Simplification ep. 214: Tristan Harris (transcript)
tristan-harris.why: Harris reframes the China race as a contest over governing technology well, and elsewhere calls the race a 'boogeyman' used to drive investment.

tyler-cowen.q: And should we wait, and get a “more Chinese” version of the alignment problem? I just don’t see the case for that, and no I really don’t think any international cooperation options are on the table.
tyler-cowen.work: Existential risk, AI, and the inevitable turn in human history
tyler-cowen.why: He argues against waiting partly because America leads and a pause would hand the problem to China, alongside valuing extended American hegemony.

yann-lecun.q: We want to ensure that the United States and American companies, together with other democracies, lead in AI development ahead of our adversaries, so that the foundational models are developed here and represent and share our values.
yann-lecun.work: Open Hearing: Advancing Intelligence in the Era of Artificial Intelligence (S. Hrg. 118-118), statement and testimony of Yann LeCun
yann-lecun.why: In his opening statement to a hearing focused on the PRC as the main strategic rival, he says the US must lead in AI ahead of its adversaries.

yoshua-bengio.q: I reject these arguments.
yoshua-bengio.work: Bengio: 'If you prioritize safety, leave frontier AI companies'
yoshua-bengio.why: He says this directly after summarizing the argument that the US must reach recursive self-improvement before China.

yuval-noah-harari.q: Won’t slowing down public deployments of AI cause democracies to lag behind more ruthless authoritarian regimes? Just the opposite. Unregulated AI deployments would create social chaos, which would ruin democracies.
yuval-noah-harari.work: Watch out humans: AI has hacked the operating system of civilisation
yuval-noah-harari.why: He rejects rivalry with authoritarian powers as a reason not to slow AI down.

brian-merchant.q: They would respect community wishes on data centers.
brian-merchant.work: Why the AI backlash has turned violent
brian-merchant.why: Among the things he says AI companies should do, he lists respecting communities' wishes on data centers, after criticizing local bans being overridden.

karen-hao.q: It was a really beautiful moment where I was like, oh yeah, this is how democracy actually works. This is how hard people need to fight all around the world to continue exercising their democratic rights and making sure that it's not taken away from them.
karen-hao.work: Decolonizing the Future: Karen Hao on Resisting the Empire of AI
karen-hao.why: Describing Chilean activists fighting a Google data center, she endorses community resistance to data centers as the exercise of democratic rights.

ron-desantis.q: SB 484 ensures that local governments maintain the authority to reject data center development in their communities, prevents data center costs from being passed on to consumers, including electricity costs, and protects Florida's water resources from data center consumption.
ron-desantis.work: Governor Ron DeSantis Signs Law to Protect Floridians from Subsidizing Data Centers
ron-desantis.why: In his own statement on signing SB 484, DeSantis presents local authority to reject data center development as a protection he approves of.

adam-thierer.q: That’s how real markets self-correct: through open information and credible signals that allow consumers to reward trustworthy developers and discipline careless ones.
adam-thierer.work: America's Litigation Addiction Threatens Its AI Leadership
adam-thierer.why: He argues that competitive markets with informed consumers punish bad actors better than litigation does.

asad-ramzanali.q: As I suggest later, pro-competition policies can aid in mitigating these impacts.
asad-ramzanali.work: Testimony before House Energy & Commerce Subcommittee on Communications and Technology: AI in the Everyday
asad-ramzanali.why: He argues that market concentration across the AI stack causes harm and that restoring competition mitigates it.

audrey-tang.q: If your telecom cannot keep your number hostage, it has to serve you well. The same goes for social networks.
audrey-tang.why: She argues that portability-enabled competition forces platforms to stop harmful behaviour and serve users.

bruce-schneier.q: Lock-in is an important concern because it results in products and services that are less responsive to customer demand. The harder it is for you to switch to a competitor, the more poorly a company can treat you.
bruce-schneier.work: Let's Not Make the Same Mistakes with AI That We Made with Social Media
bruce-schneier.why: The co-authored essay argues that competition disciplines firms and calls antitrust and interoperability core strategies against corporate harm.

cory-doctorow.q: First: competition. Companies that fear you will take your business elsewhere are cautious about worsening quality or raising prices.
cory-doctorow.why: In his lecture, competition is the first of four forces he says discipline companies and limit the harm they do.

daniel-jeffries.q: In other words, nothing happens in a vacuum. There will be pushback and friction and other companies and people with breakthroughs in AI at the same time so this argument by Bengio is another swerve into the absurd.
daniel-jeffries.work: Defending Open Source AI Against the Monopolist, the Jingoist, the Doomer and the Idiot
daniel-jeffries.why: Rebutting the fear that one lab could wipe out rival economies, he argues competing companies check any single actor.

david-sacks.q: At least when you have multiple strong private sector players, that gets harder. By contrast, winner-take-all dynamics are more likely to produce Orwellian outcomes.
david-sacks.work: Long X post: the 'Goldilocks' state of AI and why the doomer narratives were wrong
david-sacks.why: He says competition among several AI firms makes the dystopian corporate-state outcome harder to reach.

elizabeth-warren.q: With a handful of CEOs in charge, a handful of people dictate what you watch on TV, which doctor you’re allowed to see, what you eat, what predators get online access to your kids, what apartment you can rent, and, as AI sweeps in, maybe what your future job looks like
elizabeth-warren.work: Warren Calls on Congress and Antitrust Enforcers to Take on Corporate Power at Open Markets Conference
elizabeth-warren.why: In an antitrust speech lamenting that competition is dying, she argues consolidation gives a few firms harmful control, which competition would check.

erik-hoel.q: We are currently fouling our own nests. Since the internet economy runs on eyeballs and clicks the new ability of anyone, anywhere, to easily generate infinite low-quality content via AI is now remorselessly generating tragedy.
erik-hoel.work: Here lies the internet, murdered by generative AI
erik-hoel.why: Applying the tragedy of the commons, he argues competition for clicks drives harm rather than limiting it, so regulation is needed.

garett-jones.q: But part of that is that they face some kind of global competition. Cities face huge competition for labor. And the extremely valuable freedom to leave means that a city can’t get rich by just telling its most productive workers
garett-jones.work: Garett Jones on Democracy (More or Less) (Conversations with Tyler, Ep. 88)
garett-jones.why: He explains that competition for workers stops landholder-run cities from abusing them.

guillaume-verdon.q: And ultimately the thesis is that the market will positively select for AIs that are more reliable, more safe and tend to be aligned, they do what you want them to do, right.
guillaume-verdon.work: Guillaume Verdon: Beff Jezos, E/acc Movement, Physics, Computation & AGI (Lex Fridman Podcast #407)
guillaume-verdon.why: He argues that customer choice in a competitive market will weed out unsafe AI products.

jeff-jarvis.q: And government should encourage truly open-source development and investment to bring on competitors that can keep these boys, more than their machines, in check.
jeff-jarvis.work: A few unpopular opinions about AI
jeff-jarvis.why: He presents competition as the check on the power of dominant AI companies.

josh-hawley.q: If the FTC wins, it could force Meta to divest Instagram and WhatsApp, restoring competition to digital markets.
josh-hawley.work: Sen. Hawley: Break up Big Tech behemoths to reclaim American freedom
josh-hawley.why: He supports enforcing antitrust law and breaking up dominant firms as the remedy for Big Tech's harms.

lina-khan.q: And so that’s another way in which we saw a real relationship between diminishing competition and, you know, higher prices and more situations where you had greater vulnerability to abrupt spikes in prices.
lina-khan.work: Talking With Lina Khan (transcript of CUNY Graduate Center conversation with Paul Krugman)
lina-khan.why: Throughout the conversation she argues that loss of competition lets firms harm consumers, workers and farmers, so competition limits that harm.

marc-andreessen.q: We believe in market discipline. The market naturally disciplines – the seller either learns and changes when the buyer fails to show, or exits the market.
marc-andreessen.work: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto
marc-andreessen.why: He argues market discipline checks bad behavior and that markets prevent monopolies and cartels.

miles-brundage.q: Contrary to some people’s beliefs, companies do not in fact have sufficient incentives to mitigate all major risks, and competition is driving corner-cutting that needs to be reined in somehow.
miles-brundage.work: Some Very Important Things (That I Won't Be Working On This Year)
miles-brundage.why: He says competition drives AI companies to cut corners on safety rather than limiting harm.

robin-hanson.q: So unless AI makes such competition much less effective at limiting harms, it is hard to see how AI makes role-mediated harms worse.
robin-hanson.work: Why Not Wait On AI Risk?
robin-hanson.why: He holds that competition among employers, armies and suppliers limits harms and will keep doing so with AI.

scott-alexander.q: Like the rats, who gradually lose all values except sheer competition, so companies in an economic environment of sufficiently intense competition are forced to abandon all values except optimizing-for-profit
scott-alexander.why: His central argument is that competition drives actors to sacrifice values; he grants it sometimes aligns with customer values but calls that equilibrium fragile.

scott-wiener.q: Competition is the key that unlocks lower prices and innovation.
scott-wiener.work: Senator Wiener Announces Landmark Legislation To Crack Down on Big Tech's Anticompetitive Behavior
scott-wiener.why: Introducing his bill against platform self-preferencing, he says that restoring competition protects consumers from the harms dominant platforms cause.

tristan-harris.q: And if I don't do it as an AI company, I lose to the other one that does. And then the society takes on all of that risk.
tristan-harris.work: The Great Simplification ep. 214: Tristan Harris (transcript)
tristan-harris.why: Comparing AI to the 2008 banks, Harris argues that competition pushes firms to take risks that society then bears.

yoshua-bengio.q: The competitive nature of capitalism is clearly also a cause for concern as a potential source of careless AI design motivated by profits and winning market share that could lead to potentially rogue AIs.
yoshua-bengio.work: How Rogue AIs may Arise
yoshua-bengio.why: He sees market competition as a source of dangerous AI design, not a check on harm.

brian-merchant.q: We desperately need good mechanisms for helping writers and artists and creators earn the compensation they’re due for their work, and to sustain a good living, protected from plagiarism and precarity.
brian-merchant.work: This Labor Day, let's consider how we want technology to work for us
brian-merchant.why: In a section on lawsuits over AI training on artists' and journalists' work without consent or compensation, he says creators are owed compensation.

chris-callison-burch.q: I propose that any future legislation on AI and copyright should make explicit that training on copyrighted works is fair use.
chris-callison-burch.work: Testimony before the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, IP and the Internet: Artificial Intelligence and Intellectual Property
chris-callison-burch.why: He asks Congress to make training on copyrighted works fair use, which means no payment duty, while offering only an opt-out mechanism.

cory-doctorow.q: And I'm here to tell you they are wrong: wrong because this would inflict terrible collateral damage on socially beneficial activities, and it would represent a massive expansion of copyright over activities that are currently permitted – for good reason!.
cory-doctorow.work: The Reverse-Centaur's Guide to Criticizing AI
cory-doctorow.why: Responding to artists who want copyright extended to cover AI training, which would make companies pay for training, he says they are wrong.

daniel-jeffries.q: Charging for web data is also an absurd trend that we should resist too.
daniel-jeffries.work: AI, Art, Blurred Lines and the Looming Nightmare of Copyright Expansion
daniel-jeffries.why: He argues machines, like people, should be free to learn from public data and that payment schemes for training data should be resisted.

daron-acemoglu.q: Legislation can support a functioning data market by establishing property rights to workers and citizens for their data, which could then enable companies to invest in high-quality data.
daron-acemoglu.work: Written Testimony, Hearing on 'The Philosophy of AI: Learning from History, Shaping Our Future'
daron-acemoglu.why: He proposes legal property rights over data so that AI companies must buy it rather than take it freely, which he criticises as the current practice.

david-sacks.q: Finally, President Trump endorsed a common sense approach to intellectual property. He reaffirmed that AI models aren’t allowed to plagiarize outputs, but said that model training on inputs do not violate copyright law.
david-sacks.work: Thread on the White House AI Action Plan and Trump's first major AI speech
david-sacks.why: He calls the position that training on inputs needs no payment a 'common sense approach', endorsing it.

divya-siddarth.q: as this data is used to underpin pioneering AI models, you get to be an active, recognized, and compensated participant, sharing insights and expertise and experience rather than being essentially scraped into providing that knowledge and then totally cut out of the benefits
divya-siddarth.work: Co-owning the Future with Data Cooperatives @ Stanford HAI
divya-siddarth.why: In proposing legally enshrined data cooperatives, she argues people whose data trains AI should be compensated rather than scraped.

e-glen-weyl.q: But active engagement is possible only if, unlike in the usual AI attitude, all contributors, not just elite engineers, are considered crucial role players and are financially compensated.
e-glen-weyl.work: AI Is an Ideology, Not a Technology
e-glen-weyl.why: The authors argue that the people whose data trains AI systems should be recognised and paid for that work.

elizabeth-nolan-brown.q: It's also a weird understanding of copyright infringement—akin to arguing that someone reading a book in order to learn about a subject for a presentation is infringing on the work or that search engines are infringing when they scan webpages to index them.
elizabeth-nolan-brown.work: Sarah Silverman's Lawsuit Against OpenAI Is Full of Nonsense Claims
elizabeth-nolan-brown.why: Responding to the claim that books were used 'without compensation', she argues training is like reading and owes nothing.

jaron-lanier.q: The problem here should be clear, but just let me state it explicitly: we're not paying the people who are providing the examples to the corpora—which is the plural of corpus—that we need in order to make AI algorithms work.
jaron-lanier.why: He argues that the people whose data AI depends on should be paid, the core of his data-dignity proposal.

jeff-jarvis.q: To legally require opt-in or licensing sets up unimaginable complications.
jeff-jarvis.why: Responding to Copyright Office questions on requiring permission or compulsory licensing for AI training, he opposes such requirements.

josh-hawley.q: Assign property rights to specific forms of data, create legal liability for the companies who use that data and, finally, fully repeal Section 230.
josh-hawley.work: AI Threatens the Working Man
josh-hawley.why: Calling AI training 'the largest copyright theft in history', he proposes property rights and legal liability so people can be compensated for data used by AI companies.

karen-hao.q: I would make sure that copyright law interpretation falls on the side of creators.
karen-hao.why: Among her policy priorities, she wants copyright law to side with creators against AI companies' use of their work.

marc-andreessen.q: Copyright law should not be co-opted to imply that machines should be prevented from using data—the foundation of AI—to learn in the same way as people.
marc-andreessen.work: AI for Startups
marc-andreessen.why: Under a 'right to learn' heading, the a16z-Microsoft policy statement says copyright should not restrict AI training on data, which rules out a duty to pay for it.

mark-lemley.q: There are several reasons why the fair use doctrine should permit ML systems to train on data sets that include copyrighted works.
mark-lemley.why: The article's central thesis is that training on copyrighted works should generally be fair use, i.e. permitted without licensing or paying the owners.

mark-zuckerberg.q: Look, we’re a big company. We pay for content when it’s valuable to people. We’re just not going to pay for content when it’s not valuable to people.
mark-zuckerberg.work: Why Mark Zuckerberg thinks AR glasses will replace your phone (Decoder interview with Alex Heath)
mark-zuckerberg.why: Asked about creators not being paid for training data, he says Meta pays only for content it finds valuable, and expects a few partnerships rather than a duty to pay.

marsha-blackburn.q: Our Constitution—specifically, Article I, Section 8, Clause 8—gives all creators in our country the guaranteed right to benefit from their works, but AI is increasingly challenging this right that our creative community relies on to make a living,
marsha-blackburn.work: Blackburn, Welch Hold Roundtable with Over 20 Artists Who Support NO FAKES Act and TRAIN Act to Protect Creators from AI Harms
marsha-blackburn.why: Promoting her TRAIN Act on AI training data, she says creators have a right to benefit from works that AI companies train on.

matt-stoller.q: which mandates that AI firms license from copyright holders instead of freely ingesting copyrighted material. That would shape the development of this technology into far safer, less monopolistic and more productivity-enhancing pathways.
matt-stoller.why: He endorses the Blumenthal-Hawley bill requiring AI firms to license (pay for) copyrighted training material.

richard-blumenthal.q: First, Meta, Google and OpenAI are using the hard work of newspapers and authors to train their AI models without compensation or credit.
richard-blumenthal.work: Oversight of A.I.: The Future of Journalism (S. Hrg., Senate Judiciary subcommittee), opening statement of Chair Blumenthal
richard-blumenthal.why: In his opening statement he objects to uncompensated training and proposes licensing that guarantees newspapers and broadcasters are credited 'financially and publicly'.

rumman-chowdhury.q: So I actually– yes, the lawsuits matter. Yes, the IP matters because people should be compensated for their work.
rumman-chowdhury.work: ChatGPT And Beyond: What's Behind The AI Boom? (Science Friday transcript)
rumman-chowdhury.why: Responding to a caller about models trained on artists' work without compensation, she says the people whose work was scraped should be compensated.

abeba-birhane.q: the negative impacts emerging from machinic systems, as well as the lack of taking responsibility by people designing, selling and deploying such machines, remains the most pressing ethical discussion in AI.
abeba-birhane.work: Robot Rights? Let's Talk about Human Welfare Instead
abeba-birhane.why: It names present harms from how people design, sell and deploy AI as the most pressing ethical issue in AI.

arvind-narayanan.q: But we are more concerned about risks that arise from people using AI for their own ends, whether terrorism, or cyberwarfare, or undermining democracy, or simply—and most commonly—extractive capitalistic practices that magnify inequalities.
arvind-narayanan.why: Contrasting defence against superintelligence with other risks, the authors say their main concern is people using AI for their own ends.

barack-obama.q: I think my directive to my national security team is, don’t worry as much yet about machines taking over the world. Worry about the capacity of either nonstate actors or hostile actors to penetrate systems
barack-obama.work: Barack Obama, Neural Nets, Self-Driving Cars, and the Future of the World
barack-obama.why: As president in 2016 he told his team to focus on human misuse of AI rather than machines taking over.

brian-merchant.q: Let’s take advantage of this moment of clarity, and forget the speculative futures.
brian-merchant.work: GPT-5 is a joke. Will it matter?
brian-merchant.why: He urges setting aside speculative AGI futures to focus on present harms: addicted users, deskilled students and surveillance-heavy automation software.

bruce-schneier.q: I am less worried about AI; I regard fear of AI more as a mirror of our own society than as a harbinger of the future.
bruce-schneier.work: On the Catastrophic Risk of AI
bruce-schneier.why: He endorses giving more weight to urgent present harms, and says the risks of AI are mostly already present in existing technologies rather than in runaway AI.

chris-callison-burch.q: That’s my personal fear for doomsday scenarios. It’s not an apocalyptic event, but it could have real harms.
chris-callison-burch.work: Should We Trust AI? (Q&A with Chris Callison-Burch)
chris-callison-burch.why: Having dismissed sci-fi existential risk, he says his real fear is companies using AI to displace workers.

chris-murphy.q: The most alarming near-term danger is what researchers call recursive self-improvement: AI systems that can build better versions of themselves, each generation faster and more capable than the last, until the technology outruns our ability to control it.
chris-murphy.work: AI Leaders Are Sounding the Alarm. Who's Listening?
chris-murphy.why: He names autonomous self-improving AI as the most alarming danger.

cory-doctorow.q: The smart policymakers are asking questions about fairness, algorithmic bias, and fraud. The foolish policymakers are ensnared in fantasies about "AI safety," AKA "Will the chatbot become a superintelligence that turns the whole human race into paperclips?"
cory-doctorow.work: What kind of bubble is AI?
cory-doctorow.why: He praises attention to present harms such as bias and fraud and calls superintelligence worries fantasies.

curtis-yarvin.q: What they should not fear, though, is the LLM robot revolution.
curtis-yarvin.why: Just after saying everyone should fear LLMs' economic impact, he says the autonomous 'robot revolution' is not what to fear.

daniel-jeffries.q: I don't fear AI taking over. I fear dumb, narrow AI, controlled by nasty, sadistic, power hungry people.
daniel-jeffries.why: He explicitly ranks human misuse of AI above AI takeover as the danger worth attention.

daniel-kokotajlo.q: that means they’ll be putting AIs in charge of making the AIs that make the AIs that make the AIs that will transform the economy, talk to us every day, and integrate into our military. This is a recipe for disaster.
daniel-kokotajlo.why: His central warning to the Senate is about autonomous, possibly misaligned AIs building superintelligence, not about present human misuse.

daron-acemoglu.q: Although my own view is that these concerns are somewhat overblown and often distract from shorter-term problems created by AI technologies (on which this essay has focused), they deserve careful consideration, monitoring and preparation.
daron-acemoglu.why: Writing about the alignment problem and superhuman machines, he says these fears are overblown and distract from present harms, which are his focus.

david-autor.q: The fundamental conflicts surrounding AI are not between humans and machines but among humans with divergent interests. The question is not whether AI will pursue human values but whose values it will pursue and who decides.
david-autor.work: Review of Maximilian Kasy, 'The Means of Prediction: How AI Really Works (and Who Benefits)'
david-autor.why: He calls this reframing 'almost self-evidently correct' and goes on to endorse dropping the 'value alignment' framing, which places the AI problems worth attention in how humans control and deploy AI rather than in autonomous machines.

david-sacks.q: In my view, the most likely dystopian outcome with AI is a marriage of corporate and state power similar to what we saw exposed in the Twitter Files, where “Trust & Safety” gets weaponized into government censorship and control.
david-sacks.work: Long X post: the 'Goldilocks' state of AI and why the doomer narratives were wrong
david-sacks.why: After dismissing the rapid take-off superintelligence story, he names human misuse (censorship by corporate-state power) as the most likely danger.

demis-hassabis.q: I think they operate over different timescales and they’re equally important to address.
demis-hassabis.work: Transcript for Demis Hassabis: Future of AI, Simulating Reality, Physics and Video Games
demis-hassabis.why: Asked whether human misuse or AGI itself worries him more, he treats autonomous-system risk as equally important, not secondary.

dwarkesh-patel.q: People grossly overstate the risks AI poses via misinformation and inequality.
dwarkesh-patel.why: He calls present misuse worries such as misinformation overstated, while the essay argues that the neglected danger is failing to control models at human level and beyond.

ed-zitron.q: I agree that we need to take “AI safety” seriously, but that starts with treating LLMs as normal software run in a reckless and dangerous manner by malevolent entities with little regard for society.
ed-zitron.work: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands
ed-zitron.why: After criticising superintelligence-style safety talk for ignoring present harms (suicide, hacking, pollution), he locates the real danger in how companies run today's software.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: The key issue is not “human-competitive” intelligence (as the open letter puts it); it’s what happens after AI gets to smarter-than-human intelligence.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: The Only Way to Deal With the Threat From AI? Shut It Down
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He places the key danger in smarter-than-human AI.

emily-m-bender.q: But no, the harms aren’t going to come from autonomous “AI” that just hasn’t been taught appropriate values.
emily-m-bender.work: On NYT Magazine on AI: Resist the Urge to be Impressed
emily-m-bender.why: Her summary places the harms in present deployment and rejects the autonomous-AI framing.

fei-fei-li.q: Most alarmingly, this bill does not address the potential harms of AI advancement, including bias and deepfakes.
fei-fei-li.work: 'The Godmother of AI' says California's well-intended AI bill will harm the U.S. ecosystem
fei-fei-li.why: Criticizing a bill aimed at large frontier models, Li says the harms that matter are present ones like bias and deepfakes, alongside her dismissal of apocalyptic claims elsewhere.

gary-marcus.q: My main AI fears, as I have written before, have mainly been about bad actors, rather than malicious robots per se.
gary-marcus.work: Why my p(doom) has risen, dramatically
gary-marcus.why: He says his main worry is people misusing AI, not autonomous malicious machines.

geoffrey-hinton.q: We urgently need research on how to prevent these new beings from wanting to take control. They are no longer science fiction.
geoffrey-hinton.why: After listing near-term misuse risks, he insists that the threat of autonomous superintelligent beings also demands urgent attention, so he does not put it below deployment harms.

george-hotz.q: You see, and that’s the whole AI safety thing. It’s not the machine that’s going to do that. It’s other humans using the machine that are going to do that to you.
george-hotz.work: Lex Fridman Podcast #387 transcript: George Hotz
george-hotz.why: Asked whether a superintelligent AI might manipulate people, Hotz says the danger lies in humans using the machine, not the machine itself; later he adds he is 'so much not worried about the machine independently doing harm.'

guillaume-verdon.q: I think to me, one of the biggest existential risks would be the concentration of the power of AI in the hands of the very few, especially if it’s a mix between the companies that control the flow of information and the government.
guillaume-verdon.work: Guillaume Verdon: Beff Jezos, E/acc Movement, Physics, Computation & AGI (Lex Fridman Podcast #407)
guillaume-verdon.why: Asked for his probability of AI doom, he points instead to humans concentrating AI power as the darkest risk.

holly-elmore.q: Opposing the attempt to build superintelligence itself is how we fell Anthropic along with all the rest.
holly-elmore.why: Contrasting others' focus on chatbot impropriety, she puts the attempt to build superintelligence at the center of the danger.

jaron-lanier.q: This idea that some lab somewhere is making these autonomous algorithms that can take over the world is a way of avoiding the profoundly uncomfortable political problem
jaron-lanier.why: He calls autonomous-AI takeover fears a misdirection from the real problem of how people use harmful actuators.

jeff-jarvis.q: Yet I am cautious about this latest AI flavor of the month, not because generative AI itself is dangerous but because the uses to which it is being put are stupid and its current proprietors are worrisome.
jeff-jarvis.work: A few unpopular opinions about AI
jeff-jarvis.why: He locates the danger in present human uses and owners of AI, not the technology acting on its own.

joanna-bryson.q: A blogpost about why AGI is not a problem, and superintelligence is THE problem our culture has already caused.
joanna-bryson.work: OpenAI reveals the anti-regulatory intent of its regulatory disinformation
joanna-bryson.why: She calls Altman's AGI scenarios 'impossible' misdirection and says the real problems are governance problems we already face.
