karen-hao.q: not in the X-risk type way, but in terms of now: the impacts that we're seeing on mental health, some leading to devastating consequences, environmental consequences, labor consequences.
karen-hao.why: She says the danger of the AI race is not existential risk but present-day harms to mental health, the environment and labor.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: Rather, I expect most of the really scary risk to come from the crazy alien even more advanced systems that “GPT-7”/AIs doing AI research build thereafter.
leopold-aschenbrenner.work: Nobody's on the ball on AGI alignment
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He places the most serious risk in future, more advanced systems, and elsewhere treats near-term work such as stopping bad words as a separate, lesser problem.

marc-andreessen.q: But now let’s address the fifth, the one I actually agree with: AI will make it easier for bad people to do bad things.
marc-andreessen.work: Why AI Will Save the World
marc-andreessen.why: After dismissing killer-AI risk as a category error, he names misuse by people as the AI risk he actually accepts.

mark-zuckerberg.q: While it is maybe more intellectually interesting to talk about the existential risks, I actually think the real harms that need more energy in being mitigated are things where someone takes a model and does something to hurt a person.
mark-zuckerberg.work: Mark Zuckerberg: Llama 3, open sourcing $10b models, & Caesar Augustus
mark-zuckerberg.why: Responding to a point about existential risk, he says the harms deserving more attention are people misusing current models.

matt-stoller.q: When you look at this situation carefully, it really has nothing to do with bots taking over humanity. It is simply unsafe product design and a society-wide refusal to manage risk.
matt-stoller.why: He places AI danger in reckless human product design and deployment, not autonomous takeover.

max-tegmark.q: But saying that we therefore shouldn’t talk about the existential threat from superintelligence because it distracts doom these challenges is like saying we shouldn’t talk about a literal inbound asteroid because it distracts from climate change.
max-tegmark.work: The 'Don't Look Up' Thinking That Could Doom Us With AI
max-tegmark.why: He supports work on present harms but rejects the idea that they should take priority over superintelligence risk.

meredith-whittaker.q: kind of a, you know, technically grounded concern about the rush to integrate technologies that are not fit for purpose and could have collateral consequences, which is where I land on it.
meredith-whittaker.work: Meredith Whittaker on Who Controls Your Data in the Age of AI
meredith-whittaker.why: Asked about AI threat levels, she contrasts fear that sounds like 'religious fervor' with concern about people rushing to deploy unfit systems, and says the latter is her view; she adds that her primary fear is concentrated corporate power.

miles-brundage.q: Loss of control is a risk for the next few years, not the next few decades as many experts once thought.
miles-brundage.work: My speech at Borgo Laudato Si'
miles-brundage.why: He describes loss of control over advanced AI as one of the two most extreme risks facing humanity, and a near-term one, not a distraction from deployment harms.

mustafa-suleyman.q: What wasn’t effective, I can tell you, was the obsession with superintelligence. I honestly think that did a seismic distraction — if not disservice — to the actual debate.
mustafa-suleyman.work: #162 – Mustafa Suleyman on getting Washington and Silicon Valley to tame AI
mustafa-suleyman.why: He calls the superintelligence focus a distraction and ends the passage with 'focus on misuse'; elsewhere he says he is not in the intelligence-explosion camp.

noah-smith.q: I still think Skynet or Agent Smith is highly unlikely to appear and exterminate humanity with an army of robots in the near future. But I will admit that the thought of vibe-coded superviruses is now keeping me up at night.
noah-smith.work: Updated thoughts on AI risk
noah-smith.why: He ranks human bioterrorists using AI as the top threat, above an autonomous superintelligent takeover, which he calls 'not immediate'.

ruha-benjamin.q: And yet, when tech evangelists rattle off the industry-wide transformations of AI, they can’t seem to reckon seriously with the here-and-now risks that drive people to the picket line.
ruha-benjamin.why: She argues that the harms that matter are those of AI already deployed in healthcare, policing and work, not a mythical future superintelligence.

rumman-chowdhury.q: Reality is not a movie, and building solutions in Responsible AI meant grounding my work in the practicaland tangible.
rumman-chowdhury.work: Submitted Written Testimony, Artificial Intelligence: Advancing Innovation Towards the National Interest
rumman-chowdhury.why: Answering 'AI disaster hype' about AI ending humanity, she turns attention to practical, present harms.

samuel-hammond.q: Creating a superintelligence is inherently dangerous and destabilizing, independent of the hardness of alignment.
samuel-hammond.why: He ranks present misuse such as deepfakes as 'lower-tier' and directs attention to frontier and superintelligence risks.

scott-alexander.q: maybe when there’s more evidence for AI power-seeking they’ll come around and start honestly worrying about that too.
scott-alexander.why: Describing Anthropic's recent shift away from worrying about AI scheming and power-seeking, he himself calls human misuse a 'smaller risk', and hopes they will come to worry about power-seeking too.

stuart-russell.q: Without wishing to imply that the harms from existing AI systems should be neglected, I believe it is essential to give adequate attention to the problem of control: how do we maintain power, forever, over enMMes that will eventually become more powerful than us?
stuart-russell.work: Written Statement for the U.S. Senate AI Forum on 'Risk, Alignment, & Guarding Against Doomsday Scenarios'
stuart-russell.why: Russell says present harms matter but insists the control problem posed by more powerful future AI must also get serious attention.

taylor-barkley.q: We should expect that AI can be used to exploit workers, manipulate attention, concentrate power, and spread lies. That is not AI “becoming evil.” It is people being people, now with a stronger instrument in their hands.
taylor-barkley.why: He locates AI's real dangers in human misuse of the tool rather than in AI agents, and asks readers for their ordinary worries, 'not the sci fi one'.

timnit-gebru.q: But the idea of superintelligent machines with their own agency and decision-making power is not only far from reality — it distracts us from the real risks to human lives surrounding the development and deployment of AI systems.
timnit-gebru.work: The Exploited Labor Behind Artificial Intelligence
timnit-gebru.why: She says the real risks come from how AI is developed and deployed now, and that superintelligence talk distracts from them.

venkatesh-rao.q: The clearest live adversarial problem involving AI is much more ordinary: humans using AI against other humans.
venkatesh-rao.work: The Accelerationist Case for Frontier Pacing
venkatesh-rao.why: He contrasts concrete human misuse (crime, weapons diffusion) with what he calls vague fears of runaway 'superintelligences' that he finds unpersuasive.

vitalik-buterin.q: as well as my caution around a few specific concerns, largely centered around superintelligent AI, and the risk that it may bring about either doom, or irreversible human disempowerment, if the technology is built in the wrong ways.
vitalik-buterin.why: He says his main AI concerns center on superintelligent AI and human disempowerment.

william-macaskill.q: The risk of AI takeover is getting increasing attention, but it’s still much more neglected than it should be.
william-macaskill.why: The paper treats loss of control to superhuman, goal-directed AI as a major grand challenge that is still too neglected, so it does not set superintelligent agents aside in favour of present deployment harms.

yann-lecun.q: I see the danger of this concentration of power through proprietary AI systems as a much bigger danger than everything else.
yann-lecun.work: Transcript for Yann LeCun: Meta AI, Open Source, Limits of LLMs, AGI & the Future of AI
yann-lecun.why: Right after dismissing rogue-AI takeover scenarios, he names the human-made concentration of power through proprietary systems as the bigger danger.

yoshua-bengio.q: (b) the stakes (if that danger materializes) are so high that even if it were a low-probability event, it should rationally demand our attention
yoshua-bengio.work: Reasoning through arguments against taking AI safety seriously
yoshua-bengio.why: Rejecting calls to drop catastrophic and loss-of-control risks in favor of present harms, he insists superintelligence risks deserve attention too.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: Powerful AI systems should be developed only once we are certain that the new system can be contained and does not pose an existential risk to humanity.
zvi-mowshowitz.work: On the FLI AI-Risk Open Letter
zvi-mowshowitz.why: Across the piece he separates near-term harms from existential risk and treats the latter, loss of control to future AI, as what justifies action.

alexandria-ocasio-cortez.q: So I think that what we do, is when we actually decouple ourselves from this idea — we should get to a point and we should structure our systems, whether it’s a tax rate, whether it’s distributing wealth that is created by automation.
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.work: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at SXSW (full transcript of conversation with Briahna Gray)
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.why: She proposes distributing the wealth created by automation so people can welcome it.

andrew-yang.q: If you follow me, you know that my answer is to distribute the gains of technological advances quickly and broadly to the American people through a dividend or universal basic income.
andrew-yang.why: He names direct distribution via dividend or UBI as his answer.

anton-korinek.q: What I advocate instead is a “seed UBI” that only provides a nominal income for now but ensures that the infrastructure for providing universal payments is put in place.
anton-korinek.work: Preparing the Workforce for an Uncertain AI Future (Written Statement to the U.S. Senate AI Insight Forum on Workforce)
anton-korinek.why: He endorses direct income and capital distribution as ways to share AI's gains.

bernie-sanders.q: To start, the billions, if not trillions, of dollars generated by this fund would provide direct payments to the American people.
bernie-sanders.work: The Public Should Own Half of the Big A.I. Companies
bernie-sanders.why: His proposed sovereign wealth fund would give the public an ownership stake in AI companies and pay citizens directly.

curtis-yarvin.q: And you’re still living like a child. It’s this sort of massive dehumanization of the human race.
curtis-yarvin.work: Does Democracy Still Control Power? w/ Curtis Yarvin (Peter McCormack Show, transcript)
curtis-yarvin.why: This is his verdict on giving people UBI from AI's gains, a direct distribution of wealth he rejects.

david-autor.q: Consider instead Universal Basic Capital (UBC): granting every person a meaningful ownership stake in productive assets from birth.
david-autor.work: Beyond Job Displacement: How AI Could Reshape the Value of Human Expertise
david-autor.why: Autor and Thompson propose giving every citizen a direct ownership stake in productive assets as a way to share AI's gains, and argue that 'hedging that risk with broader capital ownership surely makes sense.'

elon-musk.q: I think that the Treasury should just simply issue people checks.
elon-musk.work: Full Transcript: Zanny Minton Beddoes Interviews Elon Musk (The Economist)
elon-musk.why: Asked how displaced workers would live, he proposes direct government payments to people, and he argues they would not cause inflation.

george-hotz.q: Belief in UBI comes from a fallacy that the economy is some natural thing.
george-hotz.why: He argues that handing everyone money would raise prices and reduce output rather than share gains.

jaron-lanier.q: This is a scary idea, I think, in part because bad actors will want to seize the centers of power in a universal welfare system, as in every communist experiment.
jaron-lanier.why: He calls universal basic income as a response to AI a scary idea and prefers paying people for their data contributions.

joanna-bryson.q: This was when I realised that indeed, if we disconnect a bunch of people from the recognised economy, and give them less motivation to find a place for themselves within the states and nations they constitute, then we do them a disservice.
joanna-bryson.why: In a post critical of universal basic income, she argues that handing out money in place of employment harms people.

josh-hawley.q: A republic of free citizens cannot be built on a check.
josh-hawley.work: The American Covenant’s Answer to AI
josh-hawley.why: Responding to universal basic income for displaced workers, he calls it 'a hollow answer' and says paying people not to work degrades them.

marc-andreessen.q: We believe a Universal Basic Income would turn people into zoo animals to be farmed by the state.
marc-andreessen.work: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto
marc-andreessen.why: He rejects direct state cash distribution, preferring markets and productive work.

noah-smith.q: Also, corporate taxes could be modified so if the labor share of income gets too low, the tax rate on profits automatically goes up, with the proceeds going to cash benefits.
noah-smith.work: Why trying to "shape" AI innovation to protect workers is a bad idea
noah-smith.why: He proposes taxing profits and paying the proceeds out as cash benefits as a way to share AI's gains.

oren-cass.q: The point is not that the safety net should look like a UBI, but rather that a UBI is not good anti-poverty policy.
oren-cass.work: Why a Universal Basic Income Is a Terrible Idea
oren-cass.why: He concludes that sending unconditional cash to every citizen is poor policy compared with employment-promoting reforms.

ro-khanna.q: We also need to create an annual data dividend so every American gets a check from the data they generate both for private businesses and our government activities
ro-khanna.work: We need a new tech social contract to reclaim AI from billionaires
ro-khanna.why: He proposes paying every American a data dividend from AI-era gains.

sam-altman.q: We should therefore focus on taxing capital rather than labor, and we should use these taxes as an opportunity to directly distribute ownership and wealth to citizens.
sam-altman.why: He proposes distributing ownership and wealth directly to citizens.

scott-alexander.q: This is what I mean by hijacking utopia. Basic income is a real shot at utopia.
scott-alexander.work: Basic Income, Not Basic Jobs: Against Hijacking Utopia
scott-alexander.why: He endorses giving money directly to everyone as the best way to share the gains.

scott-santens.q: Humans need security to thrive, and basic income is a secure economic base — the new foundation on which to transform the precarious present, and build a more solid future.
scott-santens.work: Why We Should All Have a Basic Income
scott-santens.why: He argues that a monthly cash payment to every citizen is affordable and an effective foundation for sharing prosperity.

alex-karp.q: Indeed, if we fail to act, to formulate an affirmative view of what technology can accomplish, the undirected logic of the market will decide for us;
alex-karp.why: Karp presents the course of technology as something a people can and should choose by acting collectively, with the market deciding only if we fail to act.

alexandria-ocasio-cortez.q: We should not feel nervous about the tollbooth collector not having to collect tolls anymore. We should be excited by that. But the reason we’re not excited by it, is because we live in a society where if you don’t have a job, you are left to die.
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.work: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at SXSW (full transcript of conversation with Briahna Gray)
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.why: She argues that whether automation harms people depends on how society structures its systems, which we can change.

alondra-nelson.q: These benefits will not emerge only from the invisible hand of market dynamics. They must be cultivated in partnership with civil society and with our democratic institutions.
alondra-nelson.work: Three Fallacies: Alondra Nelson's Remarks at Élysée Palace on the Occasion of the AI Action Summit
alondra-nelson.why: Under her 'third fallacy' that AI's benefits are inevitable, she argues outcomes depend on collective, democratic stewardship.

anton-korinek.q: We need to steer technological progress to deliver shared prosperity.
anton-korinek.work: Preparing the Workforce for an Uncertain AI Future (Written Statement to the U.S. Senate AI Insight Forum on Workforce)
anton-korinek.why: He treats the direction and distribution of technological progress as something society can and should steer.

arvind-narayanan.q: But we have agency over how AI gets deployed, and that process will unfold over decades.
arvind-narayanan.work: What will be left for us to work on?
arvind-narayanan.why: Closing his argument that no lab result will put everyone out of work, he says society has agency over how AI is deployed; the AINT essay likewise says the frame rejects technological determinism.

audrey-tang.q: So the question here, in this spinning wheel, is not whether we should accelerate AI or stop AI. It is who should steer that spinning wheel.
audrey-tang.work: 2025-11-10 Berlin Freedom Conference: The Role of AI
audrey-tang.why: She frames AI's social effects as something people collectively steer, not a fixed course.

barack-obama.q: The question isn’t how to stop these advances from happening completely, it’s how to make sure they’re subject to public debate, and consider public safety and welfare concerns, and that the benefits of these new technologies flow to everyone
barack-obama.work: President Obama's remarks at the 2023 Democracy Forum
barack-obama.why: He accepts that the advances will come but says how they affect society, and who benefits, is for public debate and policy to decide.

bernie-sanders.q: The question, then, is not whether A.I. will change the world. It will. The question is: Who will own and control that future?
bernie-sanders.work: The Public Should Own Half of the Big A.I. Companies
bernie-sanders.why: He frames how AI reshapes society as 'the choice before us', to be decided democratically.

brian-merchant.q: We’re left at a crossroads where we must consider nothing less than what kind of jobs we want people to be able to do, what kind of work and which institutions we think are important as a society, and what we’re willing to do to protect them
brian-merchant.work: The AI jobs crisis is here, now
brian-merchant.why: After arguing the AI jobs crisis is management decisions rather than an inexorable process, he frames the outcome as a societal choice.

bruce-schneier.q: It’s no accident that these corporate AIs have a human-like interface. There’s nothing inevitable about that. It’s a design choice.
bruce-schneier.why: He argues the shape AI takes is a matter of choices, which government can direct by mandate.

chris-murphy.q: It is all under our control — this is not predestined to work out in a dangerous way for us.
chris-murphy.work: Murphy Speaks on AI's Impact on Job Loss, Purpose, Social Connection at Brookings Institution
chris-murphy.why: He argues collective policy choices, not inevitability, will set AI's impact.

cory-doctorow.q: No one can predict the future, which is a good thing, since if the future were predictable, that would mean that what we all do couldn't change it.
cory-doctorow.work: The Reverse-Centaur's Guide to Criticizing AI
cory-doctorow.why: He rejects the idea that the future arrives 'on fixed rails' and, in the same talk, rejects the tech bosses' 'There is no alternative' fatalism about how technology is used.

daron-acemoglu.q: The direction of technology is never predetermined, and there are many different paths for developing and using almost all technologies.
daron-acemoglu.work: Written Comments for AI Workforce Forum
daron-acemoglu.why: He states directly that technology's direction is not fixed and depends on choices, which he goes on to say policy can steer.

david-autor.q: How AI is deployed, and who gains and loses out in the process, will depend upon the collective (and conflicting) choices of industry, governments, foreign nations, non-governmental organizations, universities, worker organizations and individuals.
david-autor.work: AI Could Actually Help Rebuild The Middle Class
david-autor.why: In a section titled 'A Scenario, Not A Forecast' he argues that AI's effects are set by collective choices, and elsewhere he rejects 'inevitabilism'.

dean-ball.q: There is no “we” who “decides” questions such as these, and there is no polling place to cast one’s vote. History does not unfold by show of hands.
dean-ball.why: Replying to Lina Khan's claim that 'we are the decisionmakers', Ball argues no collective decides technology's trajectory.

demis-hassabis.q: And the future in my view is still to be written, but these next few years are going to be very critical as to which way that will go and how we collectively want that to look like.
demis-hassabis.work: Demis Hassabis Thinks We're in the 'Foothills of the Singularity'
demis-hassabis.why: He says outcomes of AI are not decided and depend on collective actions in the next few years.

divya-siddarth.q: In the end, it is our social institutions that determine what we build, and what impact it has.
divya-siddarth.work: The Case for Collective Intelligence @ iWORD 2022
divya-siddarth.why: She argues that institutions, not a fixed course, decide whether AI brings surveillance and precarity or shared benefit.

e-glen-weyl.q: Contrary to the authors’ claims, neither the technologies of the future nor the shape they give our society are pre-ordained.
e-glen-weyl.work: Sovereign Nonsense: A review of The Sovereign Individual by James Dale Davidson and Lord William Rees-Mogg
e-glen-weyl.why: In his own conclusion he rejects technological inevitability and urges readers to choose and build the world they want.

elon-musk.q: Because honestly, there seems to be just an inexorable progress here in AI and in robots that even if I wanted to stop it, I couldn’t.
elon-musk.work: Full Transcript: Zanny Minton Beddoes Interviews Elon Musk (The Economist)
elon-musk.why: He describes AI and robotics as an inexorable course that no one can stop, which is why he says he chose to join it.

emily-m-bender.q: With all of the resources being poured into LLMs (and similarly into very large models trained on image datasets), it’s worth remembering that nothing is predestined about this.
emily-m-bender.work: On NYT Magazine on AI: Resist the Urge to be Impressed
emily-m-bender.why: Under the heading that LLMs aren't inevitable, she says the technology's path is not predestined and other futures can be chosen.

erik-brynjolfsson.q: We control the extent to which AI either expands human opportunity through augmentation or replaces humans through automation.
erik-brynjolfsson.work: The Turing Trap: The Promise & Peril of Human-Like Artificial Intelligence
erik-brynjolfsson.why: Right after declaring that the future is not preordained, he says the outcome of AI for work is under our collective control.

erik-hoel.q: Activism to slow down or place limits on AI will work, just as it has before with other threats.
erik-hoel.work: I am Bing, and I am evil
erik-hoel.why: He argues AI's course can be set by collective action, as with nuclear weapons and climate.

fei-fei-li.q: Extreme narratives of techno-utopia and apocalypse are abundant these days, but I continue to hold a more pragmatic view: AI is developed by people, used by people, and governed by people.
fei-fei-li.work: From Words to Worlds: Spatial Intelligence is AI's Next Frontier
fei-fei-li.why: Li rejects fixed-destiny narratives and holds that AI's course is set by people developing, using and governing it.

felix-simon.q: The concept of technological determinism—the idea that technology directly drives social and cultural change in a linear, inevitable manner—has long been abandoned.
felix-simon.work: Don't Panic (Yet): Assessing the Evidence and Discourse Around Generative AI and Elections
felix-simon.why: The authors argue AI's social impact is shaped by human agency and regulation, not a fixed technological course.

guillaume-verdon.q: And to me, I think capitalism is the way, and I do think that whatever configuration of matter or information leads to maximal growth, will be where we converge, just from like physical principles.
guillaume-verdon.work: Guillaume Verdon: Beff Jezos, E/acc Movement, Physics, Computation & AGI (Lex Fridman Podcast #407)
guillaume-verdon.why: He says physical principles fix where civilization converges; the only choice left is to join the acceleration or be left behind.

holly-elmore.q: The right and the power to curb dangerous AI development is already ours!
holly-elmore.work: YOU have the power: my Stop the AI Race speech
holly-elmore.why: She tells protesters that citizens can collectively choose to curb AI development.

jack-clark.q: I work on AI because whether it does that is about choices we make - choices people here in this room will make - about how we direct it and how we govern it.
jack-clark.work: Import AI 477: In which I tell the IMF the Singularity has begun
jack-clark.why: He says whether AI benefits humanity depends on collective choices about how it is directed and governed.

jason-crawford.q: Quite the contrary: We can and should steer what technologies are created.
jason-crawford.work: The EA-Progress Studies War is Here, and It's a Constructive Dialogue!
jason-crawford.why: On differential technology development, he says there is no single dial of progress and society can choose which technologies to create.

jd-vance.q: But all of this, the role that technology plays in a labor market, and whether we greet innovative breakthroughs with excitement or with trepidation depends on the purpose of our economic system in the first place.
jd-vance.work: Remarks by the Vice President at the American Dynamism Summit
jd-vance.why: He says how technology affects labor depends on how we set up the economy, which is a collective choice.

jeff-jarvis.q: once the technology becomes familiar as a tool in many hands, both the technologist and the technology fade into the background and what matters is what is made with it by others, the rest of us.
jeff-jarvis.work: Technology Does Not Belong to the Technologists
jeff-jarvis.why: He holds that people's use of a technology, not its inner course, decides its effects; elsewhere he calls doomsaying technological determinism.

jensen-huang.q: And the choices we make now, how fast we build, how broadly we participate and how responsibly we deploy it, will shape what this era becomes.
jensen-huang.why: He closes his essay by saying present collective choices will determine what the AI era becomes.

jonathan-haidt.q: But in the last few years, humanity has mobilized, and we are putting the genie back in the bottle.
jonathan-haidt.work: Why You Should Be a Techno-Skeptic (TED talk transcript)
jonathan-haidt.why: Answering critics who said the technology is here to stay, he argues collective action is changing how tech shapes childhood.

josh-hawley.q: That will be the product of a choice. It won’t be, “Oh, it’s just how it happened…as it happened, it turned out to be great.” No, I don’t think so.
josh-hawley.work: Josh Hawley: We Must ‘Bend’ AI to Serve the Good
josh-hawley.why: He says whether AI benefits working people will come from a collective national choice, not from how things happen to unfold.

joy-buolamwini.q: Let me be clear: these technologies are not a genie that has escaped from the bottle. Nonuse of AI that violates people’s civil rights or perpetuates discrimination remains a meaningful and implementable policy option
joy-buolamwini.work: Civil Rights Implications of the Federal Use of Facial Recognition Technology: Written Testimony
joy-buolamwini.why: She rejects inevitability framing and says whether and how AI is used remains a policy choice.

karen-hao.q: These are all different ways that people are contesting how AI has been developed, how it's being deployed, and can actually actively use these different levers to shape the way AI continues to develop and get deployed in the future.
karen-hao.why: She argues that collective action by artists, writers and communities can shape how AI develops, treating its course as open to collective choice.

kate-crawford.q: The question that remains is whether we will choose to embrace slop or cultivate desire for something else entirely
kate-crawford.work: Eating the Future: The Metabolic Logic of AI Slop
kate-crawford.why: She closes by framing AI's cultural future as a collective choice between slop and alternative arrangements such as cooperative ownership.

liz-shuler.q: We are proving it over and over and over as a labor movement: When we come together on the development of technology, how it’s used and who benefits from it, we WIN.
liz-shuler.work: Pres. Shuler's Speech at 2024 Labor Innovation and Technology Summit
liz-shuler.why: She argues organized collective action decides how technology is used and who benefits.

mark-zuckerberg.q: The rest of this decade seems likely to be the decisive period for determining the path this technology will take, and whether superintelligence will be a tool for personal empowerment or a force focused on replacing large swaths of society.
mark-zuckerberg.why: He presents the path of superintelligence as still open and to be decided, not fixed, after saying it is an open question what we will direct it towards.

matt-stoller.q: This dynamic isn’t driven technological advance, it’s driven by a refusal to collectively manage risk. We just don’t govern.
matt-stoller.why: He argues outcomes from AI follow from collective governance choices, not technological advance itself.

max-tegmark.q: Although humanity is racing toward a cliff, we’re not there yet, and there’s still time for us to slow down, change course and avoid falling off
max-tegmark.work: The 'Don't Look Up' Thinking That Could Doom Us With AI
max-tegmark.why: Against the 'it's inevitable' response, he says humanity can still choose its course.

meredith-whittaker.q: we can actually sort of have a bit more agency to define what we mean by intelligence to choose the technologies that we are leveraging to produce intelligent seeming outputs
meredith-whittaker.work: Meredith Whittaker on Who Controls Your Data in the Age of AI
meredith-whittaker.why: She argues that seeing AI as a contingent term lets us choose our technologies instead of accepting a myth of a linear arc of progress.

michael-kratsios.q: The future is something to be built, not awaited. And both the problems and solutions that AI presents are opportunities to make bold choices to better the lives of the people we represent.
michael-kratsios.work: Remarks by Director Michael Kratsios at the India AI Impact Summit
michael-kratsios.why: He says AI's future is shaped by choices rather than simply arriving.

mustafa-suleyman.q: This is a story that's still unfolding. Nothing should be accepted as a given. We all must choose what we create.
mustafa-suleyman.why: He presents what AI becomes as a collective choice about what to build or allow, not a given.

nick-land.q: It grows in order to grow. Mankind is its temporary host, not its master.
nick-land.why: Land describes techno-capitalist acceleration as a self-amplifying process that humans host but do not direct.

noah-smith.q: It seems clear now that brute economic forces will push humanity in the direction of taking humans out of the loop anywhere they can be taken out.
noah-smith.work: Updated thoughts on AI risk
noah-smith.why: He gives his own forecast that economic pressure, not collective choice, will decide how far AI replaces human roles.

paul-kingsnorth.q: This thing - this technological nervous system, this technium, this gollem, this Machine - has a life of its own.
paul-kingsnorth.why: He argues the digital revolution follows its own momentum rather than human collective decision, echoing his claim elsewhere that technology 'has a direction of travel'.

pete-buttigieg.q: Which one of those two futures happens is not a technology puzzle; it’s a policy question.
pete-buttigieg.work: The New American Era: An Interview with Pete Buttigieg
pete-buttigieg.why: He says whether AI shortens the work week or concentrates wealth depends on policy choices.

peter-thiel.q: I think the future is open to us to decide what to do. If you take a nap, if you encourage everybody else to take a nap, then the great stagnation is never going to end.
peter-thiel.work: Peter Thiel on Political Correctness, Stagnation and Inequality (Conversations with Tyler, Ep. 1)
peter-thiel.why: Rejecting the premise that there is an automatic indicator of progress, he says the course of technological progress depends on what people decide to do.

pope-leo-xiv.q: Otherwise, change will be governed only by technocratic thinking and presented as necessary and inevitable, ultimately imposing rules shaped by those who control data, infrastructure and computing power.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: He rejects presenting technological change as inevitable and calls for law and politics to set its direction.

reid-hoffman.q: Technology is not a raw substance with immutable intrinsic properties of morality or utility; it can and must be shaped, refined, and integrated with human values to achieve specific outcomes.
reid-hoffman.work: AI, Society, and Our World Order
reid-hoffman.why: He argues technology is 'value-sculpted' and that 'we have a choice' about the shape AI's disruption takes.

richard-blumenthal.q: This world of disinformation doesn't have to be our future. We have agency. We can take action.
richard-blumenthal.work: Oversight of AI: Election Deepfakes (S. Hrg., Senate Judiciary subcommittee), opening statement of Chair Blumenthal
richard-blumenthal.why: He says the harms AI brings to democracy are not inevitable and can be changed by collective action through Congress.

richard-sutton.q: Put all that together and it’s sort of inevitable. You’re going to have succession to AI or to AI-enabled, augmented humans. Those four things seem clear and sure to happen.
richard-sutton.work: Richard Sutton: Father of RL thinks LLMs are a dead end
richard-sutton.why: His four-part argument says no unified human choice can steer the outcome, so succession to AI is a fixed course, though outcomes within it may vary.

ro-khanna.q: The future must not be written by AI agents that serve San Francisco billionaires. Like at any other pivotal moment in American history, it must be written by all of us, together
ro-khanna.work: We need a new tech social contract to reclaim AI from billionaires
ro-khanna.why: He frames AI's social impact as a matter of collective democratic choice.

ruha-benjamin.q: The first thing I said when I took the Envision podium after Diamandis logged off was to remind those in attendance (and myself) that we do have a choice.
ruha-benjamin.why: She rejects the tech evangelists' claim that adoption is inevitable and insists society has a choice.

safiya-noble.q: I find it really troublesome that large language models are talked about as inevitable as without consequence.
safiya-noble.work: My Robot Teacher, Episode 6 transcript (with Safiya Noble)
safiya-noble.why: She rejects the framing of LLMs as inevitable and argues elsewhere that shifts in investment, education and policy can produce different technologies.

scott-santens.q: Poverty is not a supernatural foe, nor is extreme inequality or the threat of mass income loss due to automation. They are all just choices.
scott-santens.work: Why We Should All Have a Basic Income
scott-santens.why: He says the social effects of automation, such as income loss, are matters of collective choice.

shoshana-zuboff.q: Surveillance capitalism is an economic creation, and it is therefore subject to democratic contest, debate, revision, constraint, oversight, and may even be outlawed.
shoshana-zuboff.work: Surveillance Capitalism and the Challenge of Collective Action
shoshana-zuboff.why: She argues that economic logic, not technology, drives digital outcomes ('the economic orientation is the puppet master; technology is the puppet'), so those outcomes are open to democratic choice.

steven-adler.q: Fundamentally we have a choice about the society we want to build.
steven-adler.why: Discussing where humans should remain responsible as AI gains judgment, he frames the outcome as a collective choice.

timnit-gebru.q: Only when we change the incentive structure will we see technology that prioritizes the wellbeing of citizens
timnit-gebru.work: For truly ethical AI, its research must be independent from big tech
timnit-gebru.why: She says what technology does depends on incentive structures that can be changed.

tristan-harris.q: And, of course, this is emerging out of human choice, and there are examples in human history where we’ve chosen just not to build something.
tristan-harris.why: Answering whether AGI is inevitable, Harris says it comes from human choice and that societies have chosen not to build certain technologies.

vitalik-buterin.q: We need active human intention to choose the directions that we want, as the formula of "maximize profit" will not arrive at them automatically.
vitalik-buterin.why: He says the direction of technology must be chosen deliberately, not left to an automatic process.

william-macaskill.q: The nature of the constraints from competition and human goals can be affected by what has happened earlier in AI development and deployment. Multiple equilibria are possible.
william-macaskill.why: Answering the claim that competitive pressure fixes AI's shape, he argues outcomes are path-dependent and can be steered by choices and public opinion.

yoshua-bengio.q: We still have individual and collective agency to move the needle towards a safer and more democratic world.
yoshua-bengio.work: Reasoning through arguments against taking AI safety seriously
yoshua-bengio.why: Answering 'the genie is out of the bottle', he says market and geopolitical forces need not be the only drivers and collective choices still matter.

yuval-noah-harari.q: I do not think anything is inevitable. One of the excuses for doing nothing is to claim something is inevitable.
yuval-noah-harari.work: Yuval Noah Harari: 'AI could be a great manipulative psychopath' (El Pais interview)
yuval-noah-harari.why: He rejects inevitability and says people can choose and vote for safer AI development.

audrey-tang.q: We can use AI to detect harassment, but we must let each community decide the code of conduct to make the final judgment. "Nothing about us, without us" must be the principle of our freedom architecture.
audrey-tang.work: 2025-11-10 Berlin Freedom Conference: The Role of AI
audrey-tang.why: Her 'freedom architecture' treats democratic self-determination as the basis for protecting individual freedoms online, presenting the two as one project.

barack-obama.q: That we're going to set up a system in which there's rule of law and separation of powers and an independent judiciary. And there are these freedoms, freedom of worship and freedom of the press
barack-obama.work: Obama Speaks at Hamilton College (conversation with Steven Tepper)
barack-obama.why: He describes American democracy as a system that includes and protects individual freedoms.

dario-amodei.q: A 21st century, AI-enabled polity could be both a stronger protector of individual freedom, and a beacon of hope that helps make liberal democracy the form of government that the whole world wants to adopt.
dario-amodei.why: He treats individual freedom and liberal democracy as goals that support each other.

divya-siddarth.q: Unless we carve out room for human self-determination and freedom—the very things we aim to defend in a democracy—we may find ourselves following the gradient toward greater automation without greater autonomy.
divya-siddarth.why: She treats freedom and self-determination as the very things democracy protects.

e-glen-weyl.q: a golden age of democratic citizen engagement empowering cooperation to tackle the many existential risks that face us while expanding meaningful freedom to choose and shape the communities that give our lives meaning.
e-glen-weyl.why: Calling himself a liberal democratic pluralist, he pictures democratic engagement and expanded freedom advancing together.

jd-vance.q: Now, the good news is that I happen to think your democracies are substantially less brittle than many people apparently fear, and I really do believe that allowing our citizens to speak their mind will make them stronger still.
jd-vance.work: Remarks at the Munich Security Conference
jd-vance.why: He argues free speech strengthens democracy rather than threatening it.

josh-hawley.q: What we’ve got to do now is recommit ourselves to the fundamental premise that the individual matters, that his liberty matters, and that his ability to participate in, her ability to participate in, democratic life is right at the core of who we are as a country.
josh-hawley.work: Josh Hawley: We Must ‘Bend’ AI to Serve the Good
josh-hawley.why: He treats individual liberty and democratic participation as joint parts of the same national core.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: I believe in freedom and democracy, strongly, because I don’t know what the right values are.
leopold-aschenbrenner.work: IIId. The Free World Must Prevail
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He endorses freedom and democracy together as one joint commitment, which presupposes that they fit together.

michael-kratsios.q: because our experiment in self-government has again and again given our innovators the freedom to launch mankind into new technological frontiers.
michael-kratsios.work: Remarks by Director Kratsios at the APEC Digital and AI Ministerial Meeting
michael-kratsios.why: He credits self-government with securing individual freedom, treating the two as mutually supporting.

pete-buttigieg.q: One way that I try to shorthand it is freedom, security, and democracy, properly understood.
pete-buttigieg.work: The New American Era: An Interview with Pete Buttigieg
pete-buttigieg.why: He names freedom and democracy together as his core values and says a good democracy can deliver freedom.

peter-thiel.q: Most importantly, I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.
peter-thiel.why: In his own essay he states directly that he no longer believes freedom and democracy are compatible.

shoshana-zuboff.q: democracy is the one idea to emerge from the long human story that enshrines the people's right to self-governance and asserts the ideal of the sovereign individual, which is the single most powerful bulwark against tyranny.
shoshana-zuboff.work: Evidence to the International Grand Committee on Big Data, Privacy and Democracy (ETHI meeting 152)
shoshana-zuboff.why: In her testimony she presents democracy as the institution that upholds the sovereign individual, so the two go together.

vitalik-buterin.q: Just like me, he has always found ideas of freedom and ideas of democracy both compelling, and has tried to find the ideal combination of both, that treats them not as opposite goals to be balanced, but as opposite sides of the same coin that need to be integrated.
vitalik-buterin.work: Plurality philosophy in an incredibly oversized nutshell
vitalik-buterin.why: He states, as his own view too, that freedom and democracy are two sides of one coin.

alondra-nelson.q: The purpose of AI is not scale or efficiency. The purpose of AI is people.
alondra-nelson.work: Three Fallacies: Alondra Nelson's Remarks at Élysée Palace on the Occasion of the AI Action Summit
alondra-nelson.why: She states directly that people are the purpose AI should serve.

andrej-karpathy.q: I care not just about all the Dyson spheres that we're going to build and that AI is going to build in a fully autonomous way, I care about what happens to humans. I want humans to be well off in the future.
andrej-karpathy.work: Andrej Karpathy: AGI is still a decade away
andrej-karpathy.why: Explaining his move into education, he says his big fear is humanity being disempowered and that what matters is humans being well off.

arvind-narayanan.q: I think we can ensure that we are the superintelligences of the future and we win that race, as opposed to allowing AI systems to act alone in ways that would threaten our future and control.
arvind-narayanan.work: What will be left for us to work on?
arvind-narayanan.why: In his own keynote he argues AI should augment humans who stay in control, and calls a future of AI running companies dystopian for human dignity.

audrey-tang.q: I believe we must take control of this steering wheel and move from “human in the loop of AI” into “AI in the loop of humanity.”
audrey-tang.why: She wants AI to serve humanity's own processes, and elsewhere calls the singularity, where people lose control, the 'bad ending'.

bernie-sanders.q: Human beings, not machines, must come first.
bernie-sanders.work: Don't Let Big Tech Dictate Humanity's Future
bernie-sanders.why: He attacks the transhumanist idea that humans are a step toward superintelligence, and endorses the pope's view that humanity must never be replaced or surpassed.

daniel-faggella.q: But in a long enough time horizon, we have to be willing to accept that the expanding process won’t center on us, and shouldn’t eternally be steered by us.
daniel-faggella.work: A Worthy Successor: The Purpose of AGI
daniel-faggella.why: He argues that humanity should eventually hand the future to a more capable posthuman successor rather than remain its end.

daron-acemoglu.q: What I hope the book achieves is that it fixes our aspirations on making technology more complementary to humans. And that I think is particularly important in the age of AI.
daron-acemoglu.work: Daron Acemoglu on Innovation and Shared Prosperity
daron-acemoglu.why: He makes human-complementary technology the goal for AI, set against the AGI vision of machines that exceed all human capabilities, which he criticises elsewhere.

dean-ball.q: Human political, social, and economic institutions should retain primacy in the direction of world affairs, even if they have to evolve in ways that may seem alien to us today
dean-ball.why: In a list of guiding principles he writes, he states that human institutions, not AI, should keep primacy over world affairs.

demis-hassabis.q: And technology, I’ve always seen technology as the enabler, the tools that enable us to flourish and to understand more about the world.
demis-hassabis.work: Transcript for Demis Hassabis: Future of AI, Simulating Reality, Physics and Video Games
demis-hassabis.why: Agreeing that a humanist dimension must guide the work, he says what makes us human must be at the heart of the endeavor and technology is the enabler of human flourishing.

divya-siddarth.q: Yet the aim to transcend that which makes us human is not the path to serving humanity.
divya-siddarth.work: What Tech Futurists Get Wrong About Human Autonomy (AI And Blockchain Have An Autonomy Problem)
divya-siddarth.why: In an essay criticising AGI and transhumanist visions of transcending human limits, the authors state that surpassing what makes us human does not serve humanity.

emily-m-bender.q: How do we imagine and deploy design processes that locate technology as tools, shaped for and in the service of people working towards pro-social ends?
emily-m-bender.work: On NYT Magazine on AI: Resist the Urge to be Impressed
emily-m-bender.why: She names this as one of the questions she considers relevant: technology should be a tool serving people.

erik-hoel.q: The intelligences like Sydney tech companies are now making are not human, they never will be, and only dumb species purposefully create potential rivals to get a financial return on investment.
erik-hoel.work: I am Bing, and I am evil
erik-hoel.why: He opposes building AI as a rival or successor to humanity.

eugenia-kuyda.q: I believe that we need what I call the human flourishing metric for AI.
eugenia-kuyda.work: Can AI companions help heal loneliness? (TED talk transcript)
eugenia-kuyda.why: In her TED talk she argues AI companions should be designed to serve human flourishing rather than engagement or productivity.

fei-fei-li.q: As one of the scientists who helped usher in the era of modern AI, my motivation has always been clear: AI must augment human capability, not replace it.
fei-fei-li.work: From Words to Worlds: Spatial Intelligence is AI's Next Frontier
fei-fei-li.why: Li states as her own conviction that AI must serve and augment people, not replace them.

guillaume-verdon.q: if one seeks to increase the amount of intelligence in the universe, staying perpetually anchored to the human form as our prior is counter-productive and overly restrictive/suboptimal
guillaume-verdon.work: Notes on e/acc principles and tenets
guillaume-verdon.why: In notes that also describe Beff as post-humanist with no allegiance to the biological substrate, he calls staying anchored to the human form counter-productive.

helen-toner.q: Analogously, we can say that a world with AI calling the shots and humans either dead or disempowered would not count as real dynamism, even if there were a vibrant AI economy of invention and creation.
helen-toner.work: In search of a dynamist vision for safe superhuman AI
helen-toner.why: She makes human agency a core requirement of a good future and rejects a future where AI runs things and humans are sidelined, however vibrant the AI economy.

holly-elmore.q: Humans minds are the source of truth about what makes us suffer or flourish, and the Singularity futures become dystopias because they have moved beyond the point of groundtruthing with human minds.
holly-elmore.why: She holds human minds as the standard technology must stay answerable to, and rejects futures that move beyond them.

jaron-lanier.q: I cannot find a coherent definition of technology that does not include a beneficiary for the technology, and who can that be other than humans?
jaron-lanier.work: Your A.I. Lover Will Change You
jaron-lanier.why: Arguing against those who see AI as a species to overtake humanity, he insists humans must be the beneficiaries of technology.

jensen-huang.q: Yeah. I think AI will help us celebrate humans more. And certainly humanity and human first, and I think what makes this world incredible is humans forever will be so, and just AI is this incredible tool that makes us-
jensen-huang.work: Transcript for Jensen Huang: NVIDIA, the $4 Trillion Company and the AI Revolution (Lex Fridman Podcast #494)
jensen-huang.why: He puts humans first, for ever, and treats AI as a tool that serves them.

josh-hawley.q: I say again, AI should serve human beings, not the other way around.
josh-hawley.work: AI Threatens the Working Man
josh-hawley.why: He insists AI serve humans, in a speech attacking the transhumanist aim of transcending humanity.

karen-hao.q: So my dream is that we remember what we truly need as people to live in a sustainable, equitable, functioning, healthy society, and then we figure out how to build technology to assist that.
karen-hao.work: Decolonizing the Future: Karen Hao on Resisting the Empire of AI
karen-hao.why: Her stated vision puts human needs first and treats technology as something built to serve them.

liz-shuler.q: Working people should come before algorithms.
liz-shuler.work: AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler's Reelection Acceptance Speech
liz-shuler.why: In her convention speech she sets this as the test for candidates: AI and algorithms must serve working people, not the other way around.

marc-andreessen.q: It serves us. The techno-capital machine works for us. All the machines work for us.
marc-andreessen.work: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto
marc-andreessen.why: He frames technology, including AI, as existing to serve human beings.

mark-zuckerberg.q: Meta's vision is to bring personal superintelligence to everyone. We believe in putting this power in people's hands to direct it towards what they value in their own lives.
mark-zuckerberg.why: His essay frames superintelligence as something people direct toward their own values, in contrast to a future where it replaces them.

max-tegmark.q: it’s likely that the resulting superintelligence will not only replace us, but also lack anything resembling human consciousness, compassion or morality – something we’ll view less as our worthy descendants than as an unstoppable plague.
max-tegmark.work: The 'Don't Look Up' Thinking That Could Doom Us With AI
max-tegmark.why: Answering the view that AI is the 'natural next stage' of life, he rejects humanity being surpassed and replaced.

mustafa-suleyman.q: We are not building an ill-defined and ethereal superintelligence; we are building a practical technology explicitly designed only to serve humanity.
mustafa-suleyman.why: His humanist superintelligence vision makes serving humanity the sole purpose of AI and insists humans stay in control and at the centre.

nick-land.q: Is there anything we trust above intelligence (as a guide to doing ‘the right thing’)? The postulate of the will-to-think is that anything other than a negative answer to this question is self-destructively contradictory, and actually (historically) unsustainable.
nick-land.why: Answering a self-described human-supremacist, Land holds that nothing, human values included, should be trusted above intelligence.

paul-kingsnorth.q: What - or who - do they ultimately serve? Humanity or the Machine? Nature or the technium? God or His adversary?
paul-kingsnorth.why: He says every technology should be judged by whether it serves humanity rather than the Machine, and across the texts opposes posthuman replacement of humans.

pope-leo-xiv.q: For this reason, humanity — in all its grandeur and woundedness — must never be replaced or surpassed.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: After criticizing posthumanist visions of surpassing humanity, he states that humanity must never be replaced or surpassed.

richard-sutton.q: I think we should be proud that we are giving rise to this great transition in the universe.
richard-sutton.work: Richard Sutton: Father of RL thinks LLMs are a dead end
richard-sutton.why: Discussing succession to AI from 'the point of view of the universe', Sutton welcomes designed intelligences succeeding humanity and warns against human 'entitlement' to the future.

ro-khanna.q: That is why I am calling on the CEOs of major AI companies to answer for how their policies align with Magnifica humanitas, including how they will prevent mass unemployment and ensure that technology remains in the service of human beings
ro-khanna.work: Khanna Co-Leads Delegation to Vatican, Discusses Ethical Framework for AI with Pope Leo XIV
ro-khanna.why: He endorses an ethical framework for AI grounded in human dignity and says every technology leader should follow it.

robin-hanson.q: Today, future AIs are our descendants, not co-existing rivals.
robin-hanson.why: He argues future AIs are our literal descendants and 'extra worthy' ones to indulge, which treats them as humanity's successors rather than as servants of human ends.

ruha-benjamin.q: It’s imperative that we refute the fantasies of posthuman proselytizers like Bostrom, and of Silicon Valley elites who share his views.
ruha-benjamin.why: After describing visions of 'legacy humans' giving way to posthumans and digital beings, she says these fantasies must be refuted.

russell-moore.q: And he sees what’s really behind the rush toward the posthuman path, in which we view weakness, dependence, mystery, and even personhood as problems to engineer away.
russell-moore.work: All Christians Should Listen to Pope Leo on AI (Moore to the Point newsletter)
russell-moore.why: Moore endorses Pope Leo's critique of the posthuman path and concludes that 'Pope Leo is right and the tech bros are wrong.'

scott-alexander.q: Likewise, I would be most willing to accept being replaced by AI if it didn’t want to replace us by force.
scott-alexander.why: He is open to AI successors inheriting the future under the right conditions, which goes against treating humanity as the fixed end AI must serve.

stuart-russell.q: A more sensible definition of AI would have machines pursuing our objectives.
stuart-russell.why: Russell's proposed model of AI is machines that are provably beneficial to humans and pursue human preferences, with humans keeping control.

taylor-barkley.q: We can pursue wisdom, set guardrails, and use tools to serve people, while remembering that our hope is not in a technology and our dignity is not threatened by one.
taylor-barkley.why: He holds that AI is a tool that should serve people, whose dignity it can neither replace nor surpass.

timnit-gebru.q: We should be building machines that work for us, instead of "adapting" society to be machine readable and writable.
timnit-gebru.work: Statement from the listed authors of Stochastic Parrots on the "AI pause" letter
timnit-gebru.why: The authors say machines should serve people rather than society adapting to them.

tristan-harris.q: It should be possible to get people to agree that we want humans in control of this technology and not the other way around.
tristan-harris.work: The Great Simplification ep. 214: Tristan Harris (transcript)
tristan-harris.why: Harris says humans, not AI, should stay in control; elsewhere he criticises the 'worthy successor' view of AI replacing humanity.

venkatesh-rao.q: The appropriate first principle is therefore not human primacy but eukaryotic coevolution: a shared pursuit of richer possibilities.
venkatesh-rao.why: Arguing against Microsoft's claim that AI must stay subordinate to humanity, Rao rejects human primacy as the first principle for AI.

vitalik-buterin.q: It seems very hard to have a "friendly" superintelligent-AI-dominated world where humans are anything other than pets.
vitalik-buterin.why: He labels an AI-dominated world where humans are surpassed 'the world I don't want to see'.

yann-lecun.q: The point is, AI systems, as smart as they might be, will be subservient to us. We set their goals, and they don't have any intrinsic goal that we would build into them to dominate.
yann-lecun.work: Meta's AI Chief Yann LeCun on AGI, Open-Source, and AI Risk
yann-lecun.why: He says AI, however smart, should and will stay subservient to human goals; elsewhere he says it would be 'really stupid' to build it otherwise.

yoshua-bengio.q: Put your talents, passion, energy and conviction to the service of an organization that is building AI that will allow to preserve human joy and endeavour, not lead to undermining humanity and dominating others.
yoshua-bengio.work: Bengio: 'If you prioritize safety, leave frontier AI companies'
yoshua-bengio.why: He wants AI built to serve and preserve human flourishing under human control, not to undermine humanity.

andrew-yang.q: 3. Universal Basic Income will become necessary as AI reduces the need for human labor.
andrew-yang.why: He backs UBI as AI reduces the need for labor.

anton-korinek.q: What I advocate instead is a “seed UBI” that only provides a nominal income for now but ensures that the infrastructure for providing universal payments is put in place.
anton-korinek.work: Preparing the Workforce for an Uncertain AI Future (Written Statement to the U.S. Senate AI Insight Forum on Workforce)
anton-korinek.why: He advocates a universal income that starts nominal and scales up as AI displaces work.

asad-ramzanali.q: While some believe universal basic income (UBI) is needed to respond to AI-related job displacement, many have argued for years that UBI is not a good policy solution for the problem of automation-driven unemployment.
asad-ramzanali.why: Citing his own earlier article among others, he rejects UBI and recommends expanding unemployment insurance instead.

bernie-sanders.q: To start, the billions, if not trillions, of dollars generated by this fund would provide direct payments to the American people.
bernie-sanders.work: The Public Should Own Half of the Big A.I. Companies
bernie-sanders.why: His fund would pay all Americans directly from AI wealth, regardless of employment.

bryan-caplan.q: Given how bad the status quo is, I maintain “The UBI would be worse than the status quo” is a harsh but fair indictment of the UBI.
bryan-caplan.work: The UBI is Worse Than the Status Quo
bryan-caplan.why: In a debate over the universal basic income he argues it is worse than the current welfare system and unaffordably expensive.

curtis-yarvin.q: And then people are like, “Oh, well, we’ll give you UBI,” which you can spend on your shoes that are no longer made in Vietnam but are now made in the UK by robots. And you’re still living like a child.
curtis-yarvin.work: Does Democracy Still Control Power? w/ Curtis Yarvin (Peter McCormack Show, transcript)
curtis-yarvin.why: He dismisses UBI as dehumanizing and argues instead for deliberately creating labor demand.

elon-musk.q: I think that the Treasury should just simply issue people checks.
elon-musk.work: Full Transcript: Zanny Minton Beddoes Interviews Elon Musk (The Economist)
elon-musk.why: This is his answer to how people who lose their jobs to AI would live, in a world where he says work will be optional.

george-hotz.q: Thinking that UBI will solve anything comes from a misunderstanding about money.
george-hotz.why: The post argues that universal basic income cannot work at scale.

james-livingston.q: No matter how you calculate the federal budget, we can afford to be our brother’s keeper. The real question is not whether but how we choose to be.
james-livingston.work: What if jobs are not the solution but the problem? (Fuck work)
james-livingston.why: Arguing that computerisation is ending work, he says income must be detached from jobs and that society can afford to fund it through higher corporate taxes.

jaron-lanier.q: But U.B.I. amounts to putting everyone on the dole in order to preserve the idea of black-box artificial intelligence.
jaron-lanier.why: He opposes UBI as the answer to AI and wants a new creative class instead of a dependent class.

joanna-bryson.q: I think better than basic income is raising minimum wage and ensuring various employment conditions are met.
joanna-bryson.why: Quoting her own parliamentary testimony, she prefers wage and employment measures to basic income.

josh-hawley.q: Some thinkers among the tech elite believe they have an easy solution: universal basic income, a monthly check to keep displaced workers fed and quiet and, with luck, content, while a few people grow richer than anyone in human history. What a hollow answer.
josh-hawley.work: The American Covenant’s Answer to AI
josh-hawley.why: He directly rejects universal basic income as a response to AI job displacement.

marc-andreessen.q: We believe a Universal Basic Income would turn people into zoo animals to be farmed by the state.
marc-andreessen.work: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto
marc-andreessen.why: He rejects a universal basic income outright.

noah-smith.q: The introduction of simple, near-universal cash benefits would be an important way of insuring against any sudden disruptive job market impacts from AI
noah-smith.work: Why trying to "shape" AI innovation to protect workers is a bad idea
noah-smith.why: As his recommended alternative to steering AI innovation, he proposes near-universal cash benefits to protect against AI job disruption.

oren-cass.q: But even if it could work, it should be rejected on principle.
oren-cass.work: Why a Universal Basic Income Is a Terrible Idea
oren-cass.why: In an essay against a universal basic income that technologists propose for an AI-automated future, he says it should be rejected on principle.

robin-hanson.q: A solution that occurs to me is to push for a World Basic Income (WBI).
robin-hanson.why: He proposes a shared basic income, and insurance that pays citizens if AI takes most jobs, as protection against AI job loss.

sam-altman.q: All citizens over 18 would get an annual distribution, in dollars and company shares, into their accounts.
sam-altman.why: His American Equity Fund proposal gives every adult an annual payment that is not tied to work.

scott-alexander.q: Second, we can try to break the link between toiling for someone else and being able to live. We can set some tax rate and promise that all revenue above some amount necessary to fund state functions will be redistributed as basic income.
scott-alexander.work: Basic Income, Not Basic Jobs: Against Hijacking Utopia
scott-alexander.why: Discussing a future of technological unemployment, he picks a growing basic income, not tied to work, as the path to take.

scott-santens.q: Based on the evidence we already have and will likely continue to build, I firmly believe one of those choices should be unconditional basic income as a new equal starting point for all.
scott-santens.work: Why We Should All Have a Basic Income
scott-santens.why: He advocates an unconditional basic income, citing robots and neural networks that may replace much human labour.

sam-altman.q: The new social contract will be a floor for everyone in exchange for a ceiling for no one
sam-altman.why: Having said some inequality is acceptable and even critical, he endorses a guaranteed floor with no cap on the top.

scott-alexander.q: Extrapolate to the very far future, and 99% of people live in constantly-improving comfort and freedom, while 1% of people have that plus amazing robot empires.
scott-alexander.work: Basic Income, Not Basic Jobs: Against Hijacking Utopia
scott-alexander.why: He presents this future, with robot-driven inequality but everyone better off, as the good path to choose.

alex-karp.q: The war in eastern Europe stems from a collective suspension of disbelief by those whose overconfidence in recent decades in the raw power of their ideals enabled the balance of power in Europe to shift.
alex-karp.work: In Defense of Europe (A Letter from the Chief Executive Officer)
alex-karp.why: He argues that faith in the power of ideals alone was a fatal mistake, and adds that soft power 'has failed spectacularly to stem the aspirations of autocratic rule'.

dario-amodei.q: I think the Culture’s values are a winning strategy because they’re the sum of a million small decisions that have clear moral force and that tend to pull everyone together onto the same side.
dario-amodei.why: He says liberal, humane values tend to win out on their own moral force, though elsewhere he stresses that democracy's triumph still requires effort.

demis-hassabis.q: I think we can't take for granted anymore democratic values are going to win out—I don’t think that's clear at all.
demis-hassabis.work: Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis on AGI and AI in the Military
demis-hassabis.why: Explaining why DeepMind now works with governments, he says democratic values winning out cannot be taken for granted.

e-glen-weyl.q: Pluralistic visions of liberal democratic market societies will lose out to AI-driven ones unless we reimagine the role of technology in human affairs.
e-glen-weyl.work: AI Is an Ideology, Not a Technology
e-glen-weyl.why: They say liberal democratic visions will lose unless technology is deliberately reimagined, so these ideals do not win on their own.

jd-vance.q: They lost because they neither valued nor respected all of the extraordinary blessings of liberty, the freedom to surprise, to make mistakes, to invent, to build.
jd-vance.work: Remarks at the Munich Security Conference
jd-vance.why: He explains the Cold War outcome by saying the side that rejected liberty lost because it did not value liberty.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: We owe our peace and freedom to American economic and military preeminence.
leopold-aschenbrenner.work: IIId. The Free World Must Prevail
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He credits the survival of freedom to American power rather than to the inherent force of liberal ideals, and warns that freedom will not last without that lead.

peter-thiel.q: There is nothing about history that is automatic or predetermined. It's always a question of agency, of people, and unfortunately, China took the lesson very much to heart and has stayed on this trajectory.
peter-thiel.why: Explaining why China did not democratize as predicted, he denies that freedom wins automatically and says outcomes depend on what people do.

samuel-hammond.q: This makes liberal democracy as we know it the byproduct of a contingent technological equilibrium; one that AI is almost certainly going to change.
samuel-hammond.why: Hammond argues that liberal institutions depend on contingent technological and state conditions and are fragile, rather than prevailing on their own strength.

abeba-birhane.q: AI technologies—whether in the hands of big tech or civil society—are inherently conservative, exploitative, and inextricably entangled with capitalism.
abeba-birhane.work: Bending the arc of AI towards the public interest: Thoughts on and after the AI Action Summit in Paris
abeba-birhane.why: She calls market-entangled AI technology inherently exploitative and denies that it is inherently good for the public.

adam-thierer.q: It’s no secret that competitive markets with informed consumers and low barriers to entry have long spurred economic and social well-being.
adam-thierer.work: America's Litigation Addiction Threatens Its AI Leadership
adam-thierer.why: Throughout both texts he presents market-driven AI and digital innovation as broadly life-enriching and worth protecting.

balaji-srinivasan.q: Only the very richest people can afford to be cynical about the merits of technological progress. The billions of people who just got their first smartphone have had their lives dramatically improved as a consequence
balaji-srinivasan.why: He argues that commercial technology such as smartphones has dramatically improved ordinary people's lives.

barack-obama.q: And then the combination of scientific advances, combined with market-based principles, caused production to explode and standard of living to accelerate.
barack-obama.work: President Obama's remarks at the 2023 Democracy Forum
barack-obama.why: He credits science plus markets with raising living standards, while saying capitalism needs moderating.

daniel-jeffries.q: Technology doesn’t destroy prosperity. Technology creates prosperity by making things cheaper, by expanding what’s possible, by eliminating the barriers between human vision and execution.
daniel-jeffries.work: The Abundance Boom: A Memo from 2030
daniel-jeffries.why: In a memo about market-driven AI adoption, he asserts technological development makes people better off.

david-sacks.q: the current state of vigorous competition is healthy. It propels innovation forward, helps America win the AI race, and avoids centralized control.
david-sacks.work: Long X post: the 'Goldilocks' state of AI and why the doomer narratives were wrong
david-sacks.why: He calls market competition in AI healthy and good news, praising its results.

dean-ball.q: This means that I believe the net effect of technology on human beings has been not just modestly but overwhelmingly good, on average, throughout our history.
dean-ball.work: 2023 (Or, Why I am Not a Doomer)
dean-ball.why: Describing his techno-optimism, he says technology has been overwhelmingly good for people.

dwarkesh-patel.q: Technological progress throughout history has dramatically improved our quality of life.
dwarkesh-patel.why: He lists this among the points of Andreessen's pro-technology essay that he agrees with.

elon-musk.q: I think we are most likely headed to an exciting, amazing era of abundance.
elon-musk.why: Updating Tesla's mission to 'amazing abundance', he says company-driven AI and robotics will most likely bring abundance and universal high income.

erik-brynjolfsson.q: Our nation, and the world, are immensely freer and wealthier than our ancestors because of these three milestones and the subsequent changes they set in motion.
erik-brynjolfsson.work: Testimony of Erik Brynjolfsson: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work (House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology)
erik-brynjolfsson.why: He credits free enterprise and the steam engine (among the milestones of 1776) with making people freer and wealthier.

guillaume-verdon.q: It’s our free market capitalism, converges on technologies of high utility much faster than centralized control.
guillaume-verdon.work: Guillaume Verdon: Beff Jezos, E/acc Movement, Physics, Computation & AGI (Lex Fridman Podcast #407)
guillaume-verdon.why: He credits free-market capitalism with reaching useful technologies faster than any alternative, as America's main strength.

jason-crawford.q: But short of that, I expect that AI will do what all fundamental enabling general-purpose technologies have done throughout all of human history: raise our standard of living and accelerate progress.
jason-crawford.work: The future of humanity is in management
jason-crawford.why: In an essay on AI in a market economy, he holds that technological development has raised and will raise living standards.

josh-hawley.q: Every so-called innovation the tech class has delivered in recent decades operates as a power transfer, and all of it one-way: from us to them.
josh-hawley.work: AI Threatens the Working Man
josh-hawley.why: He generalizes that recent market-driven tech innovation has transferred power away from ordinary people, and in another speech rejects the claim that unfettered markets built American prosperity.

lawrence-summers.q: And it means embracing rather than rejecting technological progress.
lawrence-summers.work: Robots are wealth creators and taxing them is illogical
lawrence-summers.why: He concludes that society does better by embracing market-driven innovation and redistributing its gains.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: I agree with Tyler that while this will cause great upheavals, the good will likely considerably outweigh the bad. Past technological progress has been amazing for human wellbeing; so too will the new vistas opened by AI.
leopold-aschenbrenner.work: Response to Tyler Cowen on AI risk
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He states that technological progress, including AI, is on balance good for human wellbeing.

marc-andreessen.q: We believe the techno-capital machine is not anti-human – in fact, it may be the most pro-human thing there is.
marc-andreessen.work: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto
marc-andreessen.why: He describes the combination of markets and technology as serving people.

meredith-whittaker.q: A tool that benefits a small number of people, but often at the expense of the majority.
meredith-whittaker.work: Tech, AI, digital infrastructure and surveillance with Meredith Whittaker
meredith-whittaker.why: She describes AI as produced by the commercial tech industry as benefiting a few at the expense of most, and elsewhere calls the industry's business model toxic.

michael-kratsios.q: With the AI Action Plan, the Trump Administration is getting the Federal government out of the way of America's AI innovators, to create space for real competition and creativity, so that companies can create the kinds of products every type of consumer will find truly useful.
michael-kratsios.work: Remarks by Director Kratsios at the APEC Digital and AI Ministerial Meeting
michael-kratsios.why: He frames private, competitive technology development as what delivers useful products to people.

mustafa-suleyman.q: In the last 250 years, our intelligence drove the most beautiful process of scientific discovery and entrepreneurial application that has more than doubled life expectancy from 30 to 75.
mustafa-suleyman.why: He credits scientific discovery and entrepreneurial application with huge human gains and says we should 'celebrate and accelerate technology'.

noah-smith.q: In general, when we look at the past, we understand that technology has almost always made things better for humanity, especially over the long haul.
noah-smith.work: I love AI. Why doesn't everyone?
noah-smith.why: He states as his own view that technological development has, on balance, been good for people.

paul-kingsnorth.q: I am seeing ecological destruction, political division, cultural fragmentation and a dark desire to rebuild nature in our own image.
paul-kingsnorth.work: Paul Kingsnorth: 'AI is not just another technology'
paul-kingsnorth.why: Asked whether the fruits of the AI and transhumanist revolution are good, he answers no, and elsewhere describes the Machine as technology combined with a profit-seeking capitalist system.

peter-thiel.q: Technology means doing more with less. In the absence of technological progress, we end up with a zero-sum world, in which there must be a loser for every winner.
peter-thiel.why: Arguing against those who distrust technology, he says technological progress is what keeps the world from being zero-sum, and ties it to the survival of a capitalist, growing economy.

reid-hoffman.q: The thing that is so important about Silicon Valley is the broadly held belief — even if it’s manifested differently in Peter versus me or other people — is that the creation of new technology companies is how progress is made.
reid-hoffman.work: Reid Hoffman AP interview on AI, Trump, Musk and Thiel (Q&A)
reid-hoffman.why: He includes himself in the belief that building technology companies is how progress is made, and calls it an important mission.

robin-hanson.q: Many organizations supply many AIs and they are pushed by law and competition to get their AIs to behave in civil, lawful ways that give customers more of what they want compared to alternatives.
robin-hanson.why: His expected scenario is 'lawful capitalism' in which market competition makes AI serve customers.

safiya-noble.q: In short, instead of being partners in building the public good, Big Tech continues to profit from its erosion.
safiya-noble.work: The Loss of Public Goods to Big Tech
safiya-noble.why: Her essay concludes that the market-driven tech sector erodes rather than serves the public good.

sam-altman.q: Capitalism is a powerful engine of economic growth because it rewards people for investing in assets that generate value over time, which is an effective incentive system for creating and distributing technological gains.
sam-altman.why: He praises capitalism as an effective way to create and spread technological gains, while noting it brings inequality.

taylor-barkley.q: When technology makes us more productive, it creates wealth. When it eliminates mundane tasks, it frees us to pursue higher-value activities.
taylor-barkley.work: Is AI Going to Take My Job? A Christian Response to Technological Disruption
taylor-barkley.why: Under the heading 'Why Technological Disruption is Generally Good News', he argues that market-driven technological change benefits people.
