ted-cruz.q: The other path, as reflected in the SANDBOX Act, embraces small-business innovation and entrepreneurial freedom—a proven approach that with the Internet has already revolutionized our economy, improved our quality of life, and made America the global leader in the digital age.
ted-cruz.why: He credits entrepreneur-led technology with improving quality of life.

tyler-cowen.q: In my view the good will considerably outweigh the bad (at least from losing #2, not #1), but I do understand that the absolute quantity of the bad disruptions will be high.
tyler-cowen.work: Existential risk, AI, and the inevitable turn in human history
tyler-cowen.why: On the coming radical technological change in a decentralized society, he judges the benefits to considerably exceed the harms, as with the printing press.

venkatesh-rao.q: The result was not a world full of useless mouths. It was a world in which vastly more people could do things other than farm, while enjoying access to vastly more food.
venkatesh-rao.why: Rao presents productivity gains under capitalism as having left people far better off, and argues AI is likely to do the same.

vitalik-buterin.q: First, on balance technology and economic growth have been massively good for humanity, and any delay to it imposes costs that are hard to overstate.
vitalik-buterin.why: He states as his own view that technology and economic growth have been massively good on balance.

daron-acemoglu.q: One thing I tell my students is don't listen to comments too much. Because if you listen to every comment that you receive from every economist in every seminar, then you're just going to be at the very average of everybody's opinion, which is not an original place to be.
daron-acemoglu.why: He advises against defaulting to the average of informed opinion and, later in the interview, tells researchers to follow their own gut instinct; the advice is about research, not every hard question.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: But I predict that many of this book’s readers have high-level beliefs similar to those I outlined in Chapter 2, while employing a reasoning style that is really a special case of modest epistemology; and I think that this reasoning style is causing them substantial harm.
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He says modest epistemology, which weighs individual competence against group-level competence, is a harmful reasoning style.

elon-musk.q: The typical approach that people would take to how much rocket should cost is they would look historically at what the cost of rockets are and assume that any new rocket must be somewhat similar to the prior cost of rockets.
elon-musk.work: Transcript of Elon Musk: Digital Superintelligence, Multiplanetary Life, How to Be Useful (YC AI Startup School)
elon-musk.why: He presents this historical base-rate approach as the one to replace with first-principles reasoning from material costs.

tyler-cowen.q: on the tech per se I have an optimism that corresponds to the weighted average of what I hear.
tyler-cowen.work: Why I think AI take-off is relatively slow
tyler-cowen.why: He explicitly sets his own view on AI capabilities to the weighted average of informed opinion, and elsewhere says he always sides with the experts.

william-macaskill.q: So, if a chain of reasoning leads us to the conclusion that we’re living in the most important century ever, we should think it more likely that our reasoning has gone wrong than that the conclusion really is true.
william-macaskill.work: Are we living at the most influential time in history?
william-macaskill.why: He argues that a very low base rate should outweigh informal inside-view arguments, defending an 'outside-view' default over one's own reasoning.

dario-amodei.q: To the extent that such surveillance is currently legal, this is only because the law has not yet caught up with the rapidly growing capabilities of AI.
dario-amodei.work: Statement from Dario Amodei on our discussions with the Department of War
dario-amodei.why: He calls AI mass domestic surveillance incompatible with democratic values and says the law should catch up to bar it.

dean-ball.q: We really do want to ensure that mass surveillance and autonomous weapons/systems of control cannot be used to curtail our liberties—at least we want to try.
dean-ball.work: Clawed: On Anthropic and the Department of War
dean-ball.why: Right after saying that legal limits on the government's use of AI will be of paramount importance, he backs barring government AI mass surveillance and applauds the labs' red lines.

hoan-ton-that.q: Any ban on facial recognition will be devastating for victims of child rape and human trafficking.
hoan-ton-that.work: Statement of Hoan Ton-That before the Massachusetts Special Commission on Facial Recognition
hoan-ton-that.why: Testifying as Clearview AI's CEO, he opposes banning police use of facial recognition searches across billions of public images.

joy-buolamwini.q: Congress should enact a moratorium that halts law enforcement adoption of this technology unless and until appropriate regulatory mechanisms are put in place.
joy-buolamwini.work: Written Testimony, Hearing on Facial Recognition Technology (Part 1): Its Impact on our Civil Rights and Liberties
joy-buolamwini.why: She asks Congress to bar police use of face surveillance (crime-fighting included) and elsewhere says even flawless facial recognition would strengthen the surveillance state.

safiya-noble.q: Calls by Black Lives Matter and others to defund the police must include dismantling and outlawing the technologies of governments and law enforcement that exacerbate the conditions of racial and economic injustice.
safiya-noble.work: The Loss of Public Goods to Big Tech
safiya-noble.why: In a passage on AI and surveillance sold to police, she calls for outlawing such government and law-enforcement technologies.

dario-amodei.q: Even fully autonomous weapons (those that take humans out of the loop entirely and automate selecting and engaging targets) may prove critical for our national defense.
dario-amodei.work: Statement from Dario Amodei on our discussions with the Department of War
dario-amodei.why: He objects to fully autonomous weapons only because today's systems are unreliable, and says they may prove critical, so he does not hold 'never'.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: only deploying the specific technologies they invent (e.g., more limited autonomous weapons systems that we’re more confident we can trust)
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He recommends deploying autonomous weapons systems we are confident we can trust, rather than banning AI from deciding on lethal force.

max-tegmark.q: One is that we should avoid an arms race and lethal autonomous weapons.
max-tegmark.work: How to get empowered, not overpowered, by AI
max-tegmark.why: He endorses the Asilomar principle against lethal autonomous weapons and likens it to the bans on biological and chemical weapons.

palmer-luckey.q: I think that the ethics of warfare are so fraught, and the decisions so difficult, that to artificially box yourself in and refuse to use sets of technology that could lead to better results, is an abdication of responsibility.
palmer-luckey.work: The AI Arsenal That Could Stop World War III (TED)
palmer-luckey.why: Answering a question on killer robots and the view that AI should never decide who lives and dies, he rejects a blanket ban.

pope-leo-xiv.q: Therefore, it is not permissible to entrust lethal or otherwise irreversible decisions to artificial systems.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: He states as a moral rule that lethal decisions must never be entrusted to AI.

stuart-russell.q: In the view of many AI researchers, there should be a ban on algorithms that can decide to kill human beings.
stuart-russell.work: Written Testimony before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology, & the Law ('Oversight of A.I.: Principles for Regulation')
stuart-russell.why: In his list of urgent regulations, Russell puts forward a ban on algorithms that decide to kill, suggesting as the simplest rule that no device designed for physical harm be computer-controlled.

yoshua-bengio.q: It goes without saying that lethal autonomous weapons (also known as killer robots) are absolutely[ to be banned (since from day 1 the AI system has autonomy and the ability to kill).
yoshua-bengio.work: How Rogue AIs may Arise
yoshua-bengio.why: He says lethal autonomous weapons must be banned outright.

arvind-narayanan.q: interventions such as increasing resilience by fostering open-source AI will help to govern normal technology, but risk unleashing out-of-control superintelligence.
arvind-narayanan.why: The authors back making powerful AI widely available, including open model releases, and elsewhere oppose bans on open-weight models as nonproliferation that worsens risk.

daniel-jeffries.q: That's because, other than Meta, American companies have abandoned open source. This is a looming disaster and it's one that some people not only don't want to avoid, they want to make it much, much worse.
daniel-jeffries.work: Defending Open Source AI Against the Monopolist, the Jingoist, the Doomer and the Idiot
daniel-jeffries.why: In an essay defending open-weight AI against restriction, he calls the retreat from open release by leading American labs a disaster.

daniel-kokotajlo.q: the scientific community is able to do alignment research on the latest models and critique the safety case, and yet terrorists don’t have access to the weights.
daniel-kokotajlo.work: Training AGI in Secret would be Unsafe and Unethical
daniel-kokotajlo.why: The openness compromise he advocates explicitly keeps the weights of the latest systems from bad actors, so he does not favour open release.

demis-hassabis.q: I don’t know what the answer is to that, but I haven’t heard a compelling, clear answer to that from proponents of just open sourcing everything. So I think there has to be some balance there.
demis-hassabis.work: Demis Hassabis: Scaling, superhuman AIs, AlphaZero atop LLMs, AlphaFold
demis-hassabis.why: While backing open science, he says general-purpose foundation models should not simply be open-sourced because of bad-actor misuse.

elon-musk.q: I think I’m generally in favor of open sourcing, biased towards open sourcing.
elon-musk.work: Elon Musk: War, AI, Aliens, Politics, Physics, Video Games, and Humanity (Lex Fridman Podcast #400)
elon-musk.why: Discussing AI models, he favors open-sourcing them, perhaps after a delay of about six months, and criticizes OpenAI for becoming closed source.

eugenia-kuyda.q: I’m with [Zuckerberg] on this. I think this matter with releasing all these models took us so much closer to achieving great breakthroughs in this technology.
eugenia-kuyda.work: Replika CEO Eugenia Kuyda says it's okay if we end up marrying AI chatbots (Decoder interview)
eugenia-kuyda.why: Responding to Zuckerberg's open-source release of the biggest Llama model, which she says caught up with frontier closed models, she endorses releasing such models openly.

geoffrey-hinton.q: So I think it’s just crazy releasing weights.
geoffrey-hinton.work: Brook Silva-Braga interviews Geoffrey Hinton on CBS Mornings (transcript)
geoffrey-hinton.why: He compares model weights to fissile material and says a few companies controlling the technology is better than everyone having it.

george-hotz.q: Open source AI isn’t anti-safety. It’s anti-feudal.
george-hotz.why: He argues that powerful AI is either too dangerous for anyone or safe enough for everyone to have, and rejects closed labs keeping it.

helen-toner.q: The current status quo—where new models that push the frontier are kept private, and openly available equivalents are only released after a lag of months or years—is valuable.
helen-toner.work: Nonproliferation is the wrong approach to AI misuse
helen-toner.why: She favours keeping frontier models private and delaying open release, which is the opposite of releasing the most capable models openly.

jeff-jarvis.q: A good number of people in the room — I include myself among them — believe AI models must be open to provide competition to the big companies like OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google, which now control the technology
jeff-jarvis.why: He states he believes AI models must be open, and elsewhere champions open-weight models.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: The issue with simply open sourcing everything is that it’s not a happy world of a thousand flowers blooming in the US, but a world in which the CCP has free access to US-developed superintelligence
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He argues against openly releasing frontier models and supports open-sourcing only models that lag a couple of years behind.

mark-zuckerberg.q: I believe that open source is necessary for a positive AI future.
mark-zuckerberg.work: Open Source AI Is the Path Forward
mark-zuckerberg.why: In the essay announcing what he calls the first frontier-level open source model, he argues openly releasing leading models is necessary for a good AI future.

mustafa-suleyman.q: So what that means is if we just continue to open source absolutely everything for every new generation of frontier models, then it’s quite likely that we’re going to see a rapid proliferation of power.
mustafa-suleyman.work: #162 – Mustafa Suleyman on getting Washington and Silicon Valley to tame AI
mustafa-suleyman.why: He stands by his warning against 'naive open source' for future frontier models because it would spread state-like powers to small groups.

samuel-hammond.q: Within the next two years, frontier models will cross capability thresholds that even many open source advocates will agree are dangerous to open source ex ante.
samuel-hammond.why: Hammond supports open-sourcing models that are widely available, but says frontier models will soon be too dangerous to release openly.

stuart-russell.q: These risks are all dramatically increased by the availability of open-source LLMs,
stuart-russell.work: Written Statement for the U.S. Senate AI Forum on 'Risk, Alignment, & Guarding Against Doomsday Scenarios'
stuart-russell.why: Russell argues that open-source models make misuse worse and their guardrails easy to strip, and he wants every copy to carry regulator-activated termination code.

william-saunders.q: Anything that enables competitors to replicate technology and catch up: Keep Secure
william-saunders.why: His policy is to keep anything that would let others replicate frontier systems secure, relaxing security only once a model is shown not to be dangerous.

yann-lecun.q: So the future has to be open source, if nothing else, for reasons of cultural diversity, democracy, diversity.
yann-lecun.work: Meta's AI Chief Yann LeCun on AGI, Open-Source, and AI Risk
yann-lecun.why: Asked whether Meta should keep open-sourcing its most powerful models as they approach human-level intelligence, he answers 'yes' and concludes the future has to be open source.

yoshua-bengio.q: If we had the DNA sequence of an extremely dangerous virus, would it be best to share it publicly or not? If the answer is obvious to you in this case, think twice about the case for AGI algorithms and parameters.
yoshua-bengio.work: Reasoning through arguments against taking AI safety seriously
yoshua-bengio.why: He argues against openly releasing the weights of the most capable (near-AGI) systems, though he grants open-sourcing of today's weaker systems may currently help.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: I won’t belabor why I think this would likely get us killed and is categorically insane.
zvi-mowshowitz.work: DeepSeek Panic at the App Store
zvi-mowshowitz.why: After describing the plan to build AGI and make it freely available as open source, he calls that plan likely fatal and categorically insane.

adam-thierer.q: Every major technological revolution—but especially information and communications technology (ICT) revolutions—eventually feature calls for far-reaching political controls.
adam-thierer.work: The United States Must Reject Government Control of Artificial Intelligence
adam-thierer.why: He treats AI as the latest case of a recurring pattern and draws on the history of earlier communications technologies throughout.

alex-tabarrok.q: Nor is this argument purely theoretical. Between 1870 and today, hours of work in the United States fell by about 40% — from nearly 3,000 hours per year to about 1,800. Hours fells but unemployment did not increase.
alex-tabarrok.why: He uses the history of past productivity growth as evidence for how AI will affect work.

andrej-karpathy.q: With AI we're going to see the exact same thing. It's just more automation.
andrej-karpathy.work: Andrej Karpathy: AGI is still a decade away
andrej-karpathy.why: After noting that computers and mobile phones never showed up as a GDP jump, he predicts AI will follow the same pattern as earlier technologies (his diffusion essay does treat LLMs' bottom-up spread as unprecedented).

arvind-narayanan.q: For example, we assume that, despite the obvious differences between AI and past technologies, they are sufficiently similar that we should expect well-established patterns, such as diffusion theory to apply to AI, in the absence of specific evidence to the contrary.
arvind-narayanan.why: The authors state as their own working assumption that patterns from past technologies apply to AI.

asad-ramzanali.q: One instructive parallel for thinking about AI is looking back at the Second Industrial Revolution of the late 19th and early 20th Century.
asad-ramzanali.work: Testimony before House Energy & Commerce Subcommittee on Communications and Technology: AI in the Everyday
asad-ramzanali.why: He draws on railroads and the Second Industrial Revolution as a guide to AI and endorses 'normal technology' as a prediction of its development.

audrey-tang.q: Now we are seeing the same movement in AI. We are having a Linux moment for generative AI
audrey-tang.why: She reads AI's course through the PC and free-software revolution, and elsewhere through the mistakes of social media, as a guide.

brian-merchant.q: If we are to truly understand the impacts of mass automation technologies like AI, and why there’s a vociferous and fast-growing backlash to it, then it’s crucial that we rethink our dismissal of the Luddites.
brian-merchant.work: Understanding the Luddites in the age of AI
brian-merchant.why: His whole talk uses the first Industrial Revolution as a guide to how AI will be used and how the public will react.

bruce-schneier.q: There is a lot we can learn about social media’s unregulated evolution over the past decade that directly applies to AI companies and technologies.
bruce-schneier.work: Let's Not Make the Same Mistakes with AI That We Made with Social Media
bruce-schneier.why: The whole essay uses the history of an earlier internet technology as a direct guide to how AI will develop.

bryan-caplan.q: Agriculture was humanity’s dominant industry for millennia; yet when technology virtually wiped out agricultural jobs, we still found plenty of new work to do instead.
bryan-caplan.why: He uses the history of agriculture, the telephone and e-commerce as the guide to how AI will affect jobs.

chris-murphy.q: I don't believe that this technology, as some would say, is akin to the printing press or the train or a telephone, just another disruptive new technology that we will figure out how to live with.
chris-murphy.work: Murphy Speaks on AI's Impact on Job Loss, Purpose, Social Connection at Brookings Institution
chris-murphy.why: He denies AI is like past disruptive technologies.

christopher-ferguson.q: We’ve been through this cycle before, with concerns that violent video games make people violent (they don’t) and that social media leads to poor mental health in youths (it doesn’t) both turning into moral panics.
christopher-ferguson.work: A tragedy, a lawsuit, and the birth of an AI moral panic
christopher-ferguson.why: He uses earlier media-technology panics as the guide to how AI is being received.

daniel-jeffries.q: We've always adapted to new technology. Always.
daniel-jeffries.work: AI, Art, Blurred Lines and the Looming Nightmare of Copyright Expansion
daniel-jeffries.why: He uses the histories of coffee, recorded music and whale oil as guides to how AI will be opposed, adopted and adapted to.

daron-acemoglu.q: AI is a new technology. But there have been other transformative technologies, and history offers important clues about how to manage them.
daron-acemoglu.work: Written Testimony, Hearing on 'The Philosophy of AI: Learning from History, Shaping Our Future'
daron-acemoglu.why: His testimony argues that the history of past transformative technologies, especially the Industrial Revolution, guides how AI will play out.

david-autor.q: While one may worry that AI will simply render expertise redundant and experts superfluous, history and economic logic suggest otherwise.
david-autor.work: AI Could Actually Help Rebuild The Middle Class
david-autor.why: He uses the history of earlier technologies (the Industrial Revolution, computerization) as his guide to how AI will affect work, and says here that history argues against the fearful view.

dean-ball.q: AI is a general-purpose technology that, like electricity, will become so embedded into the world within a couple of decades that it will be nearly impossible to imagine life without it.
dean-ball.work: Where I Stand on the Biggest AI Issues
dean-ball.why: He reasons about AI's diffusion and regulation by analogy to electricity and other general-purpose technologies.

elon-musk.q: So the future is going to be very, very different from the past. There’s no analogy or metaphor that I think illustrates the magnitude of change that we’re going to experience here.
elon-musk.work: Full Transcript: Zanny Minton Beddoes Interviews Elon Musk (The Economist)
elon-musk.why: He says no past analogy captures the AI-and-robots change; elsewhere he says the usual slow regulatory timeline 'is not relevant to AI'.

erik-brynjolfsson.q: For instance, when American factories first electrified, there was negligible productivity growth for the first 30 years.
erik-brynjolfsson.work: Testimony of Erik Brynjolfsson: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work (House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology)
erik-brynjolfsson.why: He treats AI as a general purpose technology and uses electrification's history to explain why AI's productivity gains are delayed.

erik-hoel.q: This isn’t like any technology ever made before. Ever. There is no analogy.
erik-hoel.work: How to navigate the AI apocalypse as a sane person
erik-hoel.why: He rejects comparing AI to earlier general-purpose technologies like electricity.

felix-simon.q: These institutions have already evolved to accommodate new media, such as film and photography (Habgood-Cote, 2023; Jurgenson, 2019), even though it has always been possible to manipulate these media.
felix-simon.work: Misinformation reloaded? Fears about the impact of generative AI on misinformation are overblown
felix-simon.why: He uses the history of earlier media such as photography, film and Photoshop, and past 'moral panics', as a guide to how generative AI will be absorbed.

jack-clark.q: In Part 1, I outline what the past few years of AI progress have looked like and discuss why, if the technology advances as much as I think, that AI cannot be treated as a normal technology.
jack-clark.work: Import AI 458: Reckoning with the future; and a singularity story
jack-clark.why: He argues that, on his expected trajectory, AI cannot be treated like earlier technologies.

james-livingston.q: Haven’t the doomsayers, those damn Malthusians, always been proved wrong by rising productivity, new fields of enterprise, new economic opportunities? Well, yeah – until now, these times.
james-livingston.work: What if jobs are not the solution but the problem? (Fuck work)
james-livingston.why: He grants that past technological change created new work but says that pattern no longer holds in the age of computerisation.

jason-crawford.q: But short of that, I expect that AI will do what all fundamental enabling general-purpose technologies have done throughout all of human history: raise our standard of living and accelerate progress.
jason-crawford.work: The future of humanity is in management
jason-crawford.why: He explicitly uses earlier general-purpose technologies as the guide to what AI will do.

jd-vance.q: But the history of American innovation is that we tend to make people more productive, and then we increase their wages in the process.
jd-vance.work: Remarks by the Vice President at the American Dynamism Summit
jd-vance.why: Right after the ATM example, he uses the history of past innovations to argue AI will augment rather than replace workers.

jeff-jarvis.q: AI is, like the printing press, a general machine. Gutenberg could not design movable type to prevent its use in promoting propaganda or witch hunts.
jeff-jarvis.why: He repeatedly uses print and earlier media as the guide to AI's reception and effects.

jensen-huang.q: There’ll be more people working at the end of this industrial revolution than at the beginning of it, just like at the end of the last one, the beginning of this one.
jensen-huang.work: U.S. Leadership in AI w/ Jensen Huang and Congressman Ro Khanna (Stanford GSB, transcript)
jensen-huang.why: He bases his forecast for AI's labor effects directly on the precedent of the previous industrial revolution.

joanna-bryson.q: In my opinion, the only thing really novel here is reach.
joanna-bryson.work: Are AI companies and digital platforms etc new utilities? (Why, yes!)
joanna-bryson.why: She draws lessons for AI companies from earlier utilities like railroads and telecoms, and finds the analogy breaks down only on reach.

liz-shuler.q: If you know your labor history, you see this story play out in every big technological revolution we’ve ever had.
liz-shuler.work: Shuler's Speech at AFL-CIO and Microsoft's New Tech-Labor Partnership Event
liz-shuler.why: She uses electrification and earlier industrial revolutions as the guide to how AI will unfold for workers.

marc-andreessen.q: Historically, every new technology that matters, from electric lighting to automobiles to radio to the Internet, has sparked a moral panic – a social contagion that convinces people the new technology is going to destroy the world, or society, or both.
marc-andreessen.work: Why AI Will Save the World
marc-andreessen.why: He interprets the public reaction to AI through the history of earlier technologies.

max-tegmark.q: And if you think of AI, if you think of superintelligence in particular, as just another technology, like electricity, you're probably not very worried. But you see, Turing thinks of superintelligence more like a new species.
max-tegmark.work: How to Keep AI Under Control
max-tegmark.why: He argues superintelligence should not be compared to past technologies like electricity.

neil-chilson.q: AI is a newly popular paradigm for computing, and is set to follow a familiar pattern.
neil-chilson.why: He predicts AI's adoption from the history of databases, personal computers and automobiles.

noah-smith.q: In general, when we look at the past, we understand that technology has almost always made things better for humanity, especially over the long haul. But when we think about the technologies now being invented, we often forget this lesson — or at least, many of us do.
noah-smith.work: I love AI. Why doesn't everyone?
noah-smith.why: He applies the lesson of past technologies to AI, and in his labour-market posts he uses the history of automation (power looms, travel agents) to judge AI's effect on jobs.

oren-cass.q: The present technological revolution shows no signs of following a different course.
oren-cass.work: Why a Universal Basic Income Is a Terrible Idea
oren-cass.why: After noting that workers displaced by farm and factory mechanization found new vocations, he says the current revolution, including AI, will follow the same pattern.

reid-hoffman.q: To understand how we might adapt to and benefit from AI, look no further than the smartphone revolution.
reid-hoffman.why: He repeatedly uses smartphones, the power loom, the printing press and GPS as guides to how AI will be adopted.

robin-hanson.q: You might think that folks would take a lesson from our history of prior bursts of anxiety and concern about automation, bursts which have appeared roughly every three decades since at least the 1930s.
robin-hanson.why: He repeatedly treats AI like prior broad technologies and uses past automation scares as a guide.

sam-altman.q: If history is any guide, we will figure out new things to do and new things to want, and assimilate new tools quickly (job change after the industrial revolution is a good recent example).
sam-altman.why: He uses the industrial revolution as a guide to how people will adapt to AI, and elsewhere compares AI to the transistor.

samuel-hammond.q: Indeed, the rule from all past such transitions is for irreversible second order effects to displace previous modes of social organization and, ultimately, create a new kind of human. Why would the AI revolution be any different?
samuel-hammond.why: He reasons about AI from past technological revolutions; in another essay he treats AI as a general-purpose technology like electricity.

taylor-barkley.q: History keeps teaching the same lesson: new tools automate tasks, but they also enlarge the economic pie and open fresh avenues for human ingenuity.
taylor-barkley.work: Is AI Going to Take My Job? A Christian Response to Technological Disruption
taylor-barkley.why: He uses ATMs, tractors, spreadsheets and scanners as the guide to what AI will do.

ted-cruz.q: I would suggest Congress draw on the lessons we can learn from the dawn of the internet.
ted-cruz.work: Sen. Cruz: Adopting Europe's Approach on Regulation Will Cause China to Win the AI Race (opening statement, 'Winning the AI Race' hearing)
ted-cruz.why: He models AI policy on the history of the internet.

tristan-harris.q: And that is just an unprecedented kind of technology development that our labor markets have never faced before.
tristan-harris.work: The Great Simplification ep. 214: Tristan Harris (transcript)
tristan-harris.why: Rejecting the argument that farmers found other work after the tractor, Harris says AI is unlike earlier technologies because it automates all cognitive labour at once.

tyler-cowen.q: It's going to be a tough slog, like the printing press, like electricity. The people who study diffusion of new technologies never think there will be rapid takeoff.
tyler-cowen.work: Tyler Cowen — The #1 bottleneck to AI progress is humans
tyler-cowen.why: He forecasts AI's diffusion by direct analogy to the printing press and electricity and the diffusion literature.

venkatesh-rao.q: Something should strike you about this story: this is what is already happening. This is how non-AI-software eating the world has unfolded for decades, and it is how AI-eating-the-world is already unfolding in its early years.
venkatesh-rao.why: Rao argues AI is unfolding the same way earlier software did, using the history of software and of Christianization as his guide.

vitalik-buterin.q: But there is a different way to think about what AI is: it's a new type of mind that is rapidly gaining in intelligence, and it stands a serious chance of overtaking humans' mental faculties and becoming the new apex species on the planet.
vitalik-buterin.why: He calls this reference class dismissive and argues AI belongs with far rarer events like new apex species, 'much less well-trodden ground'.

william-macaskill.q: This will not merely be one more invention. The magnitude of the transformation will be beyond that of the printing press, or the steam engine, or electricity; more on a par with the evolution of Homo sapiens, or of life itself.
william-macaskill.why: He says superintelligence will exceed past general-purpose technologies such as electricity, so they are not the right comparison.

yann-lecun.q: And you see this along history, any technological revolution or cultural phenomenon was always accompanied by groups or reaction in the media that basically attributed all the current problems of society to that particular change.
yann-lecun.work: Transcript for Yann LeCun: Meta AI, Open Source, Limits of LLMs, AGI & the Future of AI
yann-lecun.why: He explains reactions to AI by the pattern seen with earlier technologies (electricity, trains, the printing press), treating that history as a guide.

yoshua-bengio.q: Secondly, AI has attributes that make it particularly risky amongst technological innovations.
yoshua-bengio.work: FAQ on Catastrophic AI Risks
yoshua-bengio.why: Answering 'humanity survived other dangerous technologies', he argues that superhuman AI is a special category unlike earlier technologies.

yuval-noah-harari.q: AI is an unprecedented threat to humanity because it is the first technology in history that can make decisions and create new ideas by itself.
yuval-noah-harari.work: 'Never summon a power you can't control': Yuval Noah Harari on how AI could threaten democracy and divide the world
yuval-noah-harari.why: He argues AI breaks from all previous inventions, which left decisions in human hands, so they are not a guide to it.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: I would strongly respond to #1 with a Big No
zvi-mowshowitz.work: On the FLI AI-Risk Open Letter
zvi-mowshowitz.why: Answering Aaronson's question whether the pause rationale would apply to the printing press, radio, airplanes or the Internet, he says a strong no: AI is not like those earlier technologies.

bernie-sanders.q: If AI and robotics become smarter than humans, there is a real possibility they will function independently of human control, with possible catastrophic outcomes. That obviously must not be allowed to happen.
bernie-sanders.work: Artificial intelligence is coming for the working class. We must fight back
bernie-sanders.why: He calls for acting now, including internationally, to prevent loss of control over future smarter-than-human AI.

chris-murphy.q: But part of America’s genius, especially in the last one hundred years, is our ability to see new emerging transformational technologies, and decide early to regulate and control them
chris-murphy.work: In our scramble to win the AI race against China, we risk losing ourselves
chris-murphy.why: He argues for regulating and controlling transformative technologies early, before harms arrive.

daniel-kokotajlo.q: This could be the day advanced unaligned AI builds swarms of nanobots, but probably it’ll be much earlier, e.g. the day it is deployed, or the day it finishes training, or even years before then when things go off the rails due to less advanced AI systems.
daniel-kokotajlo.work: Against GDP as a metric for timelines and takeoff speeds
daniel-kokotajlo.why: He argues the point after which we lose the ability to reduce AI risk probably comes well before advanced AI is deployed, so the work has to happen early.

dario-amodei.q: But in this current essay, I want to confront the rite of passage itself: to map out the risks that we are about to face and try to begin making a battle plan to defeat them.
dario-amodei.why: Before the 'powerful AI' he expects within a few years exists, he sets out to plan how to defeat its risks.

daron-acemoglu.q: they deserve careful consideration, monitoring and preparation.
daron-acemoglu.why: Of alignment concerns about future super-human machines, he says that although somewhat overblown they deserve preparation now; this is a mild hold.

demis-hassabis.q: I think what we’ve got to do in the next few years, in the time before those systems start arriving, is come up with the right evaluations and metrics.
demis-hassabis.work: Demis Hassabis: Scaling, superhuman AIs, AlphaZero atop LLMs, AlphaFold
demis-hassabis.why: Discussing models capable of an intelligence explosion, he says the evaluation and control work must be done before such systems arrive.

dwarkesh-patel.q: Which means that work to prepare for misaligned 2028 ASI still makes a lot of sense - I think this is a totally plausible outcome.
dwarkesh-patel.work: Why I don't think AGI is right around the corner
dwarkesh-patel.why: Although his median timelines are longer, he endorses preparing now for misaligned superintelligence.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: Solving safety of superhuman intelligence—not perfect safety, safety in the sense of “not killing literally everyone”—could very reasonably take at least half that long.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: The Only Way to Deal With the Threat From AI? Shut It Down
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He argues safety must be solved before superhuman AI is built, since failure on the first try is fatal and the work takes decades.

elon-musk.q: This time frame is not relevant to AI. You can’t take 10 years from the point at which it’s dangerous. It’s too late.
elon-musk.work: Joe Rogan Experience #1169 with Elon Musk (Transcript)
elon-musk.why: Contrasting AI with seat-belt regulation, he says oversight has to come before AI becomes dangerous, not after.

gary-marcus.q: We certainly aren’t prepared now, and if we don’t get moving, we won’t be prepared in 10, either.
gary-marcus.work: The 'AI 2027' Scenario: How realistic is it?
gary-marcus.why: Although he doubts AGI is near, he says preparation has to start now.

geoffrey-hinton.q: We urgently need research on how to prevent these new beings from wanting to take control.
geoffrey-hinton.why: He calls for urgent control research now, for beings he describes as not yet more intelligent than us.

helen-toner.q: We need to leap into action on many of the same things that could help if it does turn out that we only have a few years. These will likely take years and years to bear fruit in any case, so if we have a decade or two then we need to make use of that time.
helen-toner.work: "Long" timelines to advanced AI have gotten crazy short
helen-toner.why: The work she lists as urgent includes advancing the science of aligning, steering and controlling AI systems before human-level AI arrives.

holly-elmore.q: PauseAI’s most basic stance is that the default should be to pause frontier AI capabilities development to keep us from wading any further into a minefield, to give time for technical safety work to be done, and for proper governance to be established.
holly-elmore.work: The myth of AI 'warning shots' as cavalry
holly-elmore.why: She wants safety and governance work done before more capable systems are built.

jack-clark.q: We have to get alignment right: Alignment techniques that work today may break under recursive self-improvement as the AI systems become much smarter than the people or systems that supervise them.
jack-clark.work: Import AI 455: AI systems are about to start building themselves.
jack-clark.why: Writing before automated AI R&D exists, which he forecasts for around 2028, the author lists getting alignment right for those future systems as a top implication to work on now.

jan-leike.q: Even if our models never end up scheming on their own accord, we still need to be ready to detect and act upon scheming behavior for our models.
jan-leike.why: In a section titled 'Don't anchor on today's models', he argues for preparing for dangerous behavior that current models are not yet capable of.

jason-crawford.q: I see the trend towards greater safety, including safety work before new technologies are introduced, as something fundamentally good.
jason-crawford.work: A plea for solutionism on AI safety
jason-crawford.why: In an essay on AI safety he endorses doing safety work before new technologies are introduced.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: More generally, the more we can develop good science now, the more we’ll be in a position to verify that things aren’t going off the rails during the intelligence explosion.
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He argues that alignment research for superhuman systems must be done now, ahead of the systems that will need it.

max-tegmark.q: It's much better to be proactive rather than reactive; plan ahead and get things right the first time because that might be the only time we'll get.
max-tegmark.work: How to get empowered, not overpowered, by AI
max-tegmark.why: Speaking of AGI, he argues safety work must come before the technology arrives, not after mistakes.

miles-brundage.q: not about the steps right in front of us like getting solid security in place before those capabilities exist.
miles-brundage.why: He insists that security and governance for superhuman AI be in place before those capabilities arrive.

mustafa-suleyman.q: I think it's still a good five to 10 years before we have to really confront that. But it's time to start talking about it now.
mustafa-suleyman.why: On autonomy and recursive self-improvement, he says the danger is years away but preparation should start now, with safety designed in 'very early on'.

noah-smith.q: I’m not saying these won’t happen, but at least we have some time to think about how to prevent the “rise of the robots” scenario. I do think we should have some people (and AI) thinking about how to harden our society against that sort of attack.
noah-smith.work: Updated thoughts on AI risk
noah-smith.why: He argues for working on defences against autonomous-AI takeover now, before such AI exists.

richard-blumenthal.q: actually investing proactively in research so that we develop countermeasures against the kind of autonomous, out-of-control scenarios that are potential dangers
richard-blumenthal.work: Oversight of A.I.: Principles for Regulation (S. Hrg. 118-108), opening statement of Chair Blumenthal
richard-blumenthal.why: He calls for a regulatory agency that invests ahead of time in countermeasures against autonomous, out-of-control AI.

robin-hanson.q: Furthermore, I don’t see why its worth putting much effort into planning how to control AIs far in advance of seeing much detail about how AIs actually do concrete tasks where loss of control matters.
robin-hanson.work: Why Not Wait On AI Risk?
robin-hanson.why: He argues control work should wait until concrete systems exist.

sam-altman.q: But we will face this threat at some point, and we have a lot of work to do before it gets here.
sam-altman.why: He argues safety research and regulation should start long before superhuman AI arrives.

scott-alexander.q: If it turns out that superintelligence is centuries away and such research is premature, little will have been lost. But if our projections were too optimistic, and superintelligence is imminent, then doing such research now rather than later becomes vital.
scott-alexander.why: He argues that alignment research should be done now, before superintelligence arrives, because waiting risks being too late.

stuart-russell.q: It is far better to prepare now and then find we have plenty of time to spare, than to prepare too late and find our species at a dead end.
stuart-russell.work: Written Statement for the U.S. Senate AI Forum on 'Risk, Alignment, & Guarding Against Doomsday Scenarios'
stuart-russell.why: While saying AGI is not yet here, Russell argues for working on control now rather than waiting.

tristan-harris.q: So at the very least, what we should be looking at is changing this crazy ratio of 2001 going into. AI's power versus going into the steering, controllability and brakes on ai.
tristan-harris.work: The Great Simplification ep. 214: Tristan Harris (transcript)
tristan-harris.why: Harris calls for far more investment in controlling AI now, before capabilities race further ahead.

william-macaskill.q: The risk of AI takeover is getting increasing attention, but it’s still much more neglected than it should be.
william-macaskill.why: Writing before superintelligence exists, the authors say work on AI takeover risk deserves far more attention now, and they list takeover among the challenges that arise before superintelligence can help.

william-saunders.q: I think there's a really important but subtle distinction between putting in the effort to prevent problems versus putting in the effort after the problems happen.
william-saunders.work: Former OpenAI Engineer William Saunders on Silence, Safety, and the Right to Warn
william-saunders.why: He argues for preventive work before human-level systems arrive, saying we must not wait for the first AI 'plane crash'.

yoshua-bengio.q: However, sufficient investment in safety is necessary to ensure the safety answers are figured out before reaching AGI, whatever its timeline, and it is not currently what is happening.
yoshua-bengio.work: Reasoning through arguments against taking AI safety seriously
yoshua-bengio.why: He insists safety solutions be found before AGI arrives, since rules and treaties take years to put in place.

yuval-noah-harari.q: But when you learn to drive a car, the first thing they teach you is how to use the breaks. Only then you learn how to press the accelerator. With AI, we are pressing the accelerator before we have learned to use the breaks.
yuval-noah-harari.work: Artificial Intelligence: A Guest Post by Yuval Noah Harari
yuval-noah-harari.why: He argues the means of control should come before AI's capabilities are pushed forward.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: I think it was always valuable to get to thinking about such problems early, as much of this has long lead times and cannot be done in parallel, but I agree that we need to go heavily into real RSI-alignment now.
zvi-mowshowitz.why: On alignment for self-improving AI, he says the work was always worth doing early because of long lead times.

audrey-tang.q: So instead of making technology that disempowers communities, we should make technology that connects communities despite or because of their differences, and see the conflict that arises from these differences as energy.
audrey-tang.work: 2026-01-20 Doom Debate (Doom Debates, with Liron Shapira)
audrey-tang.why: In her pitch for plurality she says technology should connect diverse communities, and calls the singularity view the bad ending.

divya-siddarth.q: Really, this also means we get to move from a vision of the future that aims for large-scale autonomous AI, to one that acknowledges and takes strength and innovation from the contributions of people to existing AI systems.
divya-siddarth.work: Co-owning the Future with Data Cooperatives @ Stanford HAI
divya-siddarth.why: She favors collective, cooperative intelligence built from many people's contributions over aiming at autonomous AI.

e-glen-weyl.q: In such a future, dystopias of social collapse or subjugation to centralized artificial superintelligences could give way to an embrace of the power of diverse cooperation.
e-glen-weyl.why: The essay sets out Plurality, technology for cooperation across diverse groups, as his preferred direction against AI's aim of a singular general intelligence.

guillaume-verdon.q: e/acc is about having faith in the dynamical adaptation process and aiming to accelerate the advent of its asymptotic limit; often reffered to as the technocapital singularity
guillaume-verdon.work: Notes on e/acc principles and tenets
guillaume-verdon.why: He names accelerating the technocapital singularity as the aim of e/acc.

holly-elmore.q: They are trying to find ways for different, even unknown, utility functions to peacefully coexist and cooperate, and they do not think they can skip the process of mediation.
holly-elmore.why: She describes the Star Trek future she identifies with, preferred over Singularity futures, as one of cooperation among different minds.

pope-leo-xiv.q: it is not enough for artificial intelligence to make us more efficient or connected; it must also serve to build a universal human family, with shared rights and duties, where digital proximity becomes a real opportunity for encounter and mutual care.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: He sets fraternity and encounter across peoples as AI's aim, while criticizing posthumanist hopes of a new evolutionary stage.

alex-karp.q: The engineering elite of Silicon Valley may know more than most about building software. But they do not know more about how society should be organized or what justice requires.
alex-karp.work: Letter from the Chief Executive Officer (Palantir S-1)
alex-karp.why: Asking where authority over technology's use should reside, he argues that it should not be handed to an unelected technical elite, and ties his company's work to 'the strength and survival of democratic forms of government'.

alexandria-ocasio-cortez.q: this is why I say we need to be really zeroing in on the malpractice of governance, and how special interests have captured the only tool that we have to govern ourselves fairly, and not at a profit.
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.work: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at SXSW (full transcript of conversation with Briahna Gray)
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.why: She treats government as the people's tool of self-government and objects to its capture by special interests and money.

alondra-nelson.q: the best-case scenario is I think a public that's awakened to these issues and that really refuses a narrative that says that if you don't have a PhD in AI from MIT or in computer science that you can't have a say about how these technologies are going to be built and used.
alondra-nelson.work: A Conversation with Dr. Alondra Nelson on AI and Democracy
alondra-nelson.why: She rejects leaving decisions about AI to technical experts and wants the public to have a say.

audrey-tang.q: We must design for participation and democratic legitimacy. If AI makes all the decisions for us—even good ones—our civic muscle atrophies.
audrey-tang.why: She rejects handing decisions to AI even when they would be good ones, and insists authority come from democratic participation.

barack-obama.q: democracies in which everyone’s dignity is recognized, where the rule of law and human rights are respected by everybody, where people have a voice in how they’re governed
barack-obama.work: President Obama's remarks at the 2023 Democracy Forum
barack-obama.why: He says a better future is most likely under democratic government in which people have a voice in how they are governed.

bernie-sanders.q: It must be decided by workers, parents, teachers, artists, scientists, communities and the American people. It's our future. We must decide it.
bernie-sanders.work: The Public Should Own Half of the Big A.I. Companies
bernie-sanders.why: He argues that the American people, not unelected tech billionaires, must decide AI's future.

brian-merchant.q: This is the common fuel animating the rather disparate furies of militant doomers, anti-AI activists, data center protestors, and labor organizers alike: The profound antidemocratic tendency inherent in the modern AI project.
brian-merchant.work: Why the AI backlash has turned violent
brian-merchant.why: He condemns AI executives as an unaccountable new aristocracy and calls for subjecting them to a democratic process.

chris-murphy.q: Our nation will be better off if citizens and their government – not just the technology class – create the guardrails to assure we get as much of AI’s upside, and as little of the downside, as possible.
chris-murphy.work: The Tyranny of the Technology Class
chris-murphy.why: He argues that citizens and their elected government, not the tech elite, should set the rules for AI, and that Americans must not be 'sidelined by the technology class.'

curtis-yarvin.q: One conclusion of formalism is that democracy is—as most writers before the 19th century agreed—an ineffective and destructive system of government.
curtis-yarvin.why: Yarvin calls democracy ineffective and destructive and prefers owner-run government on the model of Dubai.

daron-acemoglu.q: The most critical lesson is that democratic governance, both in the context of how to best develop and use new technologies and how to confront the social changes that they are unleashing, is critical.
daron-acemoglu.work: Written Testimony, Hearing on 'The Philosophy of AI: Learning from History, Shaping Our Future'
daron-acemoglu.why: He makes democratic governance the central lesson for steering technology; elsewhere he warns against handing political decisions to technocracy without citizen input.

david-autor.q: You don’t need to be an automotive engineer to vote on who should have the right of way in crosswalks. Similarly, you don’t need a PhD in computer science to decide whether AI should abide by copyright laws.
david-autor.work: Review of Maximilian Kasy, 'The Means of Prediction: How AI Really Works (and Who Benefits)'
david-autor.why: Agreeing with Kasy, he rejects the 'myth' that AI is too complex for democratic deliberation, and argues that ordinary citizens rather than technical experts can and should decide AI governance questions.

divya-siddarth.q: We are told that transformative technologies like AI are too complicated, or too risky or too important to be governed democratically. But this is precisely why they must be.
divya-siddarth.work: How AI and Democracy Can Fix Each Other (transcript)
divya-siddarth.why: She insists democratic governance, not rule by a few, must decide even the most complex technical questions.

e-glen-weyl.q: Technocracy divorced from the need for public communication and accountability is thus a dangerous ideology that distracts technical experts from the valuable role they can play by tempting them to assume undue, independent power and influence.
e-glen-weyl.work: Why I Am Not A Technocrat
e-glen-weyl.why: The essay argues against leaving governance to experts and for expertise placed inside a broader democratic conversation.

elizabeth-warren.q: The future of artificial intelligence must be decided by the American people through their democratically elected representatives in government—not by a handful of CEOs and billionaire corporations.
elizabeth-warren.work: Senator Warren Calls for Pause in Advanced AI Development
elizabeth-warren.why: She places authority over AI with elected representatives rather than corporate executives.

garett-jones.q: No. The power of independent committees should be increased. More Congress should be like the Fed.
garett-jones.work: Garett Jones: Immigration, national IQ, & less democracy (Dwarkesh Podcast)
garett-jones.why: Asked whether presidential power should grow, Jones instead calls for shifting authority to insulated, appointed expert bodies, in line with his '10% less democracy' program for rich democracies.

holly-elmore.q: We AREN’T marching to beg the AI companies to be merciful and spare our lives— we are marching to show the world that we don’t have to lay down and accept our unelected overlords.
holly-elmore.work: YOU have the power: my Stop the AI Race speech
holly-elmore.why: She insists democratic citizens, not unelected AI companies, should hold power over AI.

james-livingston.q: But as Americans we’re accustomed to it because we believe in the sovereignty of the people, not the state or the cabinet or the Parliament or the party.
james-livingston.work: What I Told the Hedge Fund Managers in Miami
james-livingston.why: He grounds his call for 'more democracy' in the sovereignty of the people rather than state institutions.

jd-vance.q: It is the business of democracy to adjudicate these big questions at the ballot box.
jd-vance.work: Remarks at the Munich Security Conference
jd-vance.why: He argues big political questions belong to voters, and criticizes leaders who override or ignore them.

jeff-jarvis.q: He speaks of democratization. That occurs through the institutions of government and the vote, not companies.
jeff-jarvis.work: Technology Does Not Belong to the Technologists
jeff-jarvis.why: Answering Altman, he locates democratic authority in voting and government rather than in tech executives.

josh-hawley.q: A country governed by experts is not self-governing. A country governed by oligarchs is not a republic.
josh-hawley.work: The American Covenant’s Answer to AI
josh-hawley.why: He rejects leaving AI governance to experts or Silicon Valley oligarchs in favor of self-government by citizens.

karen-hao.q: Empires are antithetical to democracy, and allowing these companies to just do whatever they want, have access to embedded resources, over time will lead to the erosion of our foundation of democracy.
karen-hao.why: She argues that unaccountable corporate power erodes democracy, and she defends democratic self-rule against it.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: The European Parliament elections that do occur are mostly irrelevant to the political outcomes, which are dictated primarily by the backroom negotiations of European prime ministers and the machinations of technocracy.
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He criticises European rule by technocrats and backroom deals and calls for a real democratic politics in which citizens decide.

liz-shuler.q: What we’ve never seen is those same CEOs and billionaires being handed full control of our government; our democracy; our lives.
liz-shuler.work: Shuler: The State of Our Unions Is Under Attack and Fighting Back
liz-shuler.why: She condemns rule by CEOs and billionaires as oligarchy and calls for working people to build their own democratic power.

matt-stoller.q: it’s an argument about the inevitable weakness of democracy, and how self-government is a ruse that will lead to our collective annihilation, while an all-powerful caste by contrast can protect and enrich our lives. It’s very Divine Right of Kings, actually.
matt-stoller.why: He criticises the view that an elite caste rather than democratic self-government should manage AI, likening it to divine right of kings.

max-tegmark.q: I believe that all of humanity should have a say in humanity’s destiny, rather than a handful of tech bros and venture capitalists sealing its fate.
max-tegmark.work: The Hopium Wars: the AGI Entente Delusion
max-tegmark.why: He says humanity's future with AI should be decided by everyone rather than by a small unelected group.

meredith-whittaker.q: meaning that the people who are getting elected to federal office in particular, have to appeal to those who have billions of dollars if they want the resources they need to compete. That's an anti-democratic step.
meredith-whittaker.work: Tech, AI, digital infrastructure and surveillance with Meredith Whittaker
meredith-whittaker.why: Discussing threats to democracy, she condemns letting billionaires and multinational corporations override popular and elected power as anti-democratic.

michael-kratsios.q: We believe the way of progress is found in human judgment and friendly cooperation, in political freedom and civic responsibility, in sovereignty and independence, not global governance and technocratic control.
michael-kratsios.work: Remarks by Director Kratsios at the APEC Digital and AI Ministerial Meeting
michael-kratsios.why: He sets self-government and civic responsibility against technocratic control as the right basis, consistent with his praise of America's 'experiment in self-government'.

nick-land.q: Democracy, which both in theory and evident historical fact accentuates time-preference to the point of convulsive feeding-frenzy, is thus as close to a precise negation of civilization as anything could be
nick-land.why: In his own narrating voice, Land calls democracy close to the negation of civilization.

safiya-noble.q: But there are still troubling ideological world views from leaders in Silicon Valley. They believe technocrats can design a better society and that democracy is too messy.
safiya-noble.work: How AI discriminates and what that means for your Google habit
safiya-noble.why: She criticises the technocratic view that democracy is too messy and argues for 'pluralistic and pro-democratic priorities'.

sam-altman.q: It is important that the democratic process remains more powerful than companies.
sam-altman.work: Untitled post, shown on the blog as "-"
sam-altman.why: He says democratic processes, not companies or AI labs, should hold control over the future.

shoshana-zuboff.q: Surveillance capitalists now hold the answers to each question, though we never elected them to govern. This is the essence of the epistemic coup.
shoshana-zuboff.work: The Coup We Are Not Talking About
shoshana-zuboff.why: She condemns rule by unelected private powers as a coup and calls for democratic government to be the protagonist.

timnit-gebru.q: While we agree that "such decisions must not be delegated to unelected tech leaders," we also note that such decisions should not be up to the academics experiencing an "AI summer," who are largely financially beholden to Silicon Valley.
timnit-gebru.work: Statement from the listed authors of Stochastic Parrots on the "AI pause" letter
timnit-gebru.why: They reject handing AI decisions to unelected tech leaders or experts and say those affected should have a say.

william-macaskill.q: In contrast, democratic governance is the best approach to political power that has actually been tried. Governments also have far more legitimacy than companies to exercise political power (though more on this below).
william-macaskill.why: Arguing against control of AGI by a CEO or a company's shareholders, he holds that democratic governance has the most legitimacy.

william-saunders.q: While representative democracy is imperfect, it is the best tool we have for providing a check on individuals willing to impose risks on the rest of society.
william-saunders.why: He urges the public to demand a voice in high-risk decisions rather than leaving them to company executives, calling democracy the best check available.

yoshua-bengio.q: But in the future, who should decide where to draw the line and how to weigh the pros and cons? CEOs of companies or democratically chosen governments? The answer should be obvious if you believe in democracy.
yoshua-bengio.work: Reasoning through arguments against taking AI safety seriously
yoshua-bengio.why: He holds that elected governments, not company executives, should make the key decisions about powerful AI.

adam-thierer.q: They have no idea what the future holds, but their worst-case thinking will inspire costly, counter-productive proposals that will result in ineffective, poorly targeted interventions that will likely only prevent the transition to a better future for workers and the public.
adam-thierer.work: AI and the jobs apocalypse that wasn't
adam-thierer.why: He argues that technology will make workers better off and that new policy plans for labour markets would do more harm than good.

alexandria-ocasio-cortez.q: And when we talk about increased worker productivity, that's because millions of people stand to lose their jobs.
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.work: Ocasio-Cortez: "If Anyone Wants to Live Right Next to One of These Data Centers Here on this Committee, Please Raise Your Hand"
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.why: She says AI productivity gains come through layoffs and demands a policy plan for affected workers.

andrew-yang.q: Universal Basic Income will become necessary as AI reduces the need for human labor.
andrew-yang.why: He holds that market-driven productivity gains will not serve workers without intervention.

anton-korinek.q: Even if progress makes it possible, shared prosperity does not automatically materialize without thoughtful policy guidance
anton-korinek.work: Preparing the Workforce for an Uncertain AI Future (Written Statement to the U.S. Senate AI Insight Forum on Workforce)
anton-korinek.why: Korinek tells the Senate that productivity gains do not reach workers broadly without policy action.

barack-obama.q: Low-wage, low-skill individuals become more and more redundant, and their jobs may not be replaced, but wages are suppressed.
barack-obama.work: Barack Obama, Neural Nets, Self-Driving Cars, and the Future of the World
barack-obama.why: He predicts AI will suppress low-wage workers' pay and goes on to say the social compact must change to handle it.

bernie-sanders.q: The result? The wealthiest people in the world will get even richer, while working people lose their jobs and their income.
bernie-sanders.work: AI must benefit everyone, not just a handful of billionaires
bernie-sanders.why: He says that 'unless we act', AI-driven productivity will enrich the wealthy while workers lose income.

brian-merchant.q: We do know that it will be used to surveil workers, speed-up work, and be used as leverage against them.
brian-merchant.work: Understanding the Luddites in the age of AI
brian-merchant.why: He holds that, absent democratic checks and labor protections, AI will be used against workers, as industrial machinery was used to depress wages.

chris-murphy.q: If we do not use government policy and intervention to control for the job loss and to protect consumers, it won’t matter that we get to AGI before China.
chris-murphy.work: In our scramble to win the AI race against China, we risk losing ourselves
chris-murphy.why: He argues that without policy intervention AI's gains will come with devastating job loss.

cory-doctorow.q: Markets value automation primarily because automation allows capitalists to pay workers less.
cory-doctorow.work: The AI hype bubble is the new crypto hype bubble
cory-doctorow.why: He argues that market-driven automation is aimed at cutting workers' pay, not at making them better off.

curtis-yarvin.q: Probably mostly for the worse, since tech is the resource curse, the curse of an economy with inadequate labor demand.
curtis-yarvin.why: He expects LLM-driven productivity to leave most workers 'useless', like the non-oil workforce of a petrostate.

daron-acemoglu.q: So that's why I don't think we can say, oh, just let the market reap and after a while things are gonna get better.
daron-acemoglu.work: Mindscape 283: Daron Acemoglu on Technology, Inequality, and Power
daron-acemoglu.why: Arguing from the Industrial Revolution, he denies that productivity gains reach workers automatically and calls for institutions and policy to make it happen.

david-autor.q: But absent complementary institutional investments, technological innovation alone will not generate broadly shared gains.
david-autor.work: The Labor Market Impacts of Technological Change: From Unbridled Enthusiasm to Qualified Optimism to Vast Uncertainty
david-autor.why: In his policy conclusion he says innovation without institutional change will not spread gains broadly, which negates the claim that productivity growth helps most workers with policy left as it is.

elizabeth-warren.q: Taxing AI is one way we make sure the winnings from AI benefit all Americans, rather than channeling them only to the wealthy few.
elizabeth-warren.work: Why We Need to Tax AI
elizabeth-warren.why: She argues that without tax policy changes AI's gains will go only to the wealthy few.

erik-brynjolfsson.q: A bigger pie does not automatically mean everyone benefits evenly, or at all.
erik-brynjolfsson.work: Machines of mind: The case for an AI-powered productivity boom
erik-brynjolfsson.why: In the section on income distribution he denies that productivity gains automatically reach workers and goes on to call for updated social programs and tax policy.

geoffrey-hinton.q: But we know it’s not going to be like that. We know what’s going to happen is the extremely rich are going to get even more extremely rich and the not very well off are going to have to work three jobs.
geoffrey-hinton.work: Brook Silva-Braga interviews Geoffrey Hinton on CBS Mornings (transcript)
geoffrey-hinton.why: He says productivity gains ought to benefit everyone but, under current arrangements, will go to the very rich.

holly-elmore.q: If you think the benefits of AI company success are going to trickle down to you, think again.
holly-elmore.why: She denies that the gains from AI will reach ordinary workers.

james-livingston.q: Wages and median family income have stagnated, even though labor productivity has steadily risen, as Alan Greenspan reminds us, in keeping with the cybernation of work.
james-livingston.work: What I Told the Hedge Fund Managers in Miami
james-livingston.why: He points to stagnant wages despite rising productivity and argues income must be redistributed toward wages.

jaron-lanier.q: I don't buy that argument, because you need formal economic benefit to have a civilization, not just informal economic benefit.
jaron-lanier.why: He rejects the claim that data contributors are compensated by cheaper free services, arguing that without new arrangements their prospects decline.

jason-crawford.q: If capital increases instead of labor, then wages rise—that’s what has been happening throughout the entire industrial era.
jason-crawford.work: The future of humanity is in management
jason-crawford.why: He argues that AI productivity gains raise wages through normal economic mechanisms, without relying on policy change.

jensen-huang.q: The workers work for companies. And so companies, when they become more productive, earnings increase. I’ve never seen one company that had earnings increase and not hire more people.
jensen-huang.work: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 60 Minutes Interview (transcript)
jensen-huang.why: Asked about workers displaced by AI and robots, he says productivity gains turn into more hiring, and mentions no policy.

josh-hawley.q: Productivity like we’ve never seen. But here’s the flip side: millions of Americans out of work.
josh-hawley.work: AI Threatens the Working Man
josh-hawley.why: He argues that AI productivity left undirected brings mass unemployment, and calls for action to protect livelihoods.

lawrence-summers.q: Governments will, however, have to concern themselves with problems of structural joblessness.
lawrence-summers.work: Robots are wealth creators and taxing them is illogical
lawrence-summers.why: While opposing robot taxes, he says governments will need new policies such as retraining, wage subsidies and public employment to protect displaced workers.

liz-shuler.q: And so I can’t think of a more fitting day to talk about A.I. — the single biggest threat to working people of our lifetime, if we don’t harness it properly.
liz-shuler.work: AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler's Speech to the National Press Club
liz-shuler.why: She says AI threatens workers unless guardrails and policy change how it is used.

marc-andreessen.q: We believe a market sets wages as a function of the marginal productivity of the worker. Therefore technology – which raises productivity – drives wages up, not down.
marc-andreessen.work: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto
marc-andreessen.why: He holds that markets alone translate technology-driven productivity into higher wages.

mustafa-suleyman.q: I think that a large portion of the population are going to struggle to compete in the workplace with AI and we’re going to have to decide whether to shorten the working week or whether to increase taxes on some portion of capital.
mustafa-suleyman.work: Mustafa Suleyman on Silicon Valley Girl Podcast (Transcript): The Next 10 Years Will Change Humanity Forever
mustafa-suleyman.why: He expects structural disemployment from labor-replacing AI and says policy (shorter work weeks or taxing capital) will have to change in response.

noah-smith.q: And in that future, I think it’s possible — perhaps even likely — that the vast majority of humans will have good-paying jobs, and that many of those jobs will look pretty similar to the jobs of 2024.
noah-smith.work: Plentiful, high-paying jobs in the age of AI
noah-smith.why: Through comparative advantage alone, with no policy change mentioned, he expects most workers to keep well-paid jobs even if AI surpasses them at every task.

pete-buttigieg.q: The result of this could theoretically be a shorter workweek for all of us and more money in our pocket. But we've been promised that before, and often the opposite has happened.
pete-buttigieg.work: Pete Buttigieg has a warning about AI (NPR interview excerpt)
pete-buttigieg.why: He doubts gains will reach workers without the right policy choices, which he says politics must supply.

pope-leo-xiv.q: To think that new technologies will automatically benefit everyone is to ignore the evidence.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: He denies that technological progress benefits people automatically and calls for policy to share its gains.

ro-khanna.q: Like many chief executives, workers should receive compensation based on profits and the company’s performance, not solely hours worked. It’s the only way workers can fully thrive as A.I. increases America’s productive capacity.
ro-khanna.work: Democrats Must Not Repeat the Mistakes of Globalization
ro-khanna.why: Drawing on the globalization lesson, he argues AI productivity gains will not reach workers without new policy.

robert-shiller.q: In other words, there are externalities to robotization that justify some government intervention.
robert-shiller.why: He argues that job losses from automation harm workers and communities in ways that call for policy responses.

sam-altman.q: If public policy doesn’t adapt accordingly, most people will end up worse off than they are today.
sam-altman.why: He says that without a change in policy, AI-driven change will leave most people worse off.

scott-alexander.q: They have no value to contribute as workers – and since in the absence of a spectacular social safety net it’s unclear how they would have much money – they have no value as customers either.
scott-alexander.why: He argues that automation will push most humans out of work and that, absent a large safety net, they will not share the gains.

scott-santens.q: Then policy choices — the erosion of the minimum wage, the dismantling of unions, tax cuts for the rich, deregulation — broke the link between what the economy produced and what most people received.
scott-santens.work: Universal Basic Income Is Your Productivity Dividend. It's the Only Way to All Share What We All Built.
scott-santens.why: He argues productivity growth has not reached most workers for fifty years and that new policy (a UBI) is needed.

stuart-russell.q: Absent significant policy action (that is beyond the purview of this Subcommittee), substantial dislocation is likely in the medium term.
stuart-russell.work: Written Testimony before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology, & the Law ('Oversight of A.I.: Principles for Regulation')
stuart-russell.why: Russell says that without significant policy action, AI-driven change will bring substantial job dislocation for workers.

taylor-barkley.q: This pattern isn’t accidental. It reflects how markets work and how humans adapt. When technology makes us more productive, it creates wealth.
taylor-barkley.work: Is AI Going to Take My Job? A Christian Response to Technological Disruption
taylor-barkley.why: He attributes workers' gains from technology to how markets work, with no policy change required.

tristan-harris.q: But this is, that 15% is going to a few AI companies. It's not coming from the GDP of the human work and labor and paychecks going to regular people.
tristan-harris.work: The Great Simplification ep. 214: Tristan Harris (transcript)
tristan-harris.why: Harris argues that AI-driven growth would flow to a few companies rather than to workers' paychecks.

alexandria-ocasio-cortez.q: And that pressure is reflected on the extreme lengths that these companies are going to to allow unethical human interactions with these chat bots.
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.work: Ocasio-Cortez Highlights Economic Threat from AI Bubble
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.why: In her hearing remarks she says profit pressure drives companies to allow harmful chatbot behaviour, alongside her call for federal rules.

bernie-sanders.q: The future of humanity cannot be left in the hands of a few Big Tech oligarchs who are obsessed with money and power.
bernie-sanders.work: Don't Let Big Tech Dictate Humanity's Future
bernie-sanders.why: He argues profit-driven AI leaders cannot be trusted with safety and calls for a federal body to ensure it.

chris-murphy.q: AI companies have no incentive to protect us. They answer to investors, not the public
chris-murphy.work: AI Leaders Are Sounding the Alarm. Who's Listening?
chris-murphy.why: He argues market pressure prevents companies from making AI safe on their own.

daniel-kokotajlo.q: Amodei, Altman, and Musk have all agreed on the need to “pace the frontier.” But they haven’t meaningfully paced the frontier yet. I think that the US government should intervene.
daniel-kokotajlo.why: He says the companies have not acted on their own safety commitments and that government intervention is therefore needed.

daron-acemoglu.q: it would be naïve to expect that unregulated markets would make the right trade-o⁄ s about these outcomes
daron-acemoglu.why: He argues that unregulated markets will not avoid AI's harms by themselves, so outside regulation is needed.

demis-hassabis.q: So a defector has some advantage and this is the classic problem with the race to the bottom dynamic. And we’ve got to change that somehow and I think urgently. And I think part of that is some form of government involvement.
demis-hassabis.work: Demis Hassabis Thinks We're in the 'Foothills of the Singularity'
demis-hassabis.why: He argues competitive pressure rewards labs that cut safety corners, so outside government involvement is needed.

ed-zitron.q: not because it’s all-powerful, sentient, conscious, or even “innovative,” but because it’s clear that the people running these labs are irresponsible and the people backing them don’t give a shit.
ed-zitron.work: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands
ed-zitron.why: He gives this as the reason outside safeguards are needed: the labs and their backers will not act responsibly on their own.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: This is a stupid state of affairs, and an undignified way for Earth to die, and the rest of humanity ought to step in at this point and help the industry solve its collective action problem.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: The Only Way to Deal With the Threat From AI? Shut It Down
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He argues the AI industry cannot stop on its own and outsiders must intervene.

elizabeth-warren.q: The recent calls by AI industry leaders to ‘pace the frontier’ are insufficient, and their suggestions that we must weaken antitrust protections in order to confront the AI threat are transparently self-serving.
elizabeth-warren.work: Senator Warren Calls for Pause in Advanced AI Development
elizabeth-warren.why: She rejects industry self-pacing as insufficient and demands outside guardrails.

elon-musk.q: You kind of need regulators to do that for all the teams in the game, otherwise the shareholders will ask: ‘Why aren’t you developing AI faster? Because your competitor is.’
elon-musk.work: Elon Musk Governor's Interview (NGA 2017, AI segment transcript)
elon-musk.why: He argues competitive and shareholder pressure keeps companies racing, so outside regulators are needed to make them pause for safety.

gary-marcus.q: We need serious regulation to prevent AI’s from running amok. Voluntary agreements between companies are not going to cut it.
gary-marcus.work: Why my p(doom) has risen, dramatically
gary-marcus.why: He argues that company self-regulation will not be enough and outside rules are needed.
