geoffrey-hinton.q: But we now have evidence that if they are created by companies motivated by short-term profits, our safety will not be the top priority.
geoffrey-hinton.why: He says profit-driven companies will not put safety first, which matches the statement's claim that they will not make AI safe enough on their own.

guillaume-verdon.q: I think organizations would allocate whatever budget is needed to achieve the sort of reliability they need to achieve to perform in the market. And I think third party auditing firms would naturally pop up
guillaume-verdon.work: Guillaume Verdon: Beff Jezos, E/acc Movement, Physics, Computation & AGI (Lex Fridman Podcast #407)
guillaume-verdon.why: Responding to proposed mandates for safety budgets and auditors, he says market pressure alone will produce the needed safety spending and auditing.

holly-elmore.q: AI companies cannot grade their own homework.
holly-elmore.work: YOU have the power: my Stop the AI Race speech
holly-elmore.why: She argues that self-regulation by AI companies is a recipe for corruption and external oversight is needed.

josh-hawley.q: Nor are dangerous interactions with children an unintended side effect of these products; too often, they are part of the business strategy.
josh-hawley.work: The American Covenant’s Answer to AI
josh-hawley.why: He argues companies' profit motives drive harmful AI behavior toward children, which is why he introduced binding legislation.

joy-buolamwini.q: This recommendation stems in part from the fact that law enforcement agencies themselves and vendors of facial analysis technologies have demonstrated unwillingness to engage in meaningful self-regulation.
joy-buolamwini.work: Written Testimony, Hearing on Facial Recognition Technology (Part 1): Its Impact on our Civil Rights and Liberties
joy-buolamwini.why: She justifies external rules on the grounds that AI vendors have not regulated themselves.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: At core, they are startups, with all the usual commercial incentives. Competition could push all of them to simply race through the intelligence explosion, and there will at least be some actors that will be willing to throw safety by the wayside.
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He argues that commercial labs left to themselves will not manage safety adequately, so outside (government) control is needed.

max-tegmark.q: Industry has collectively proven itself incapable to self-regulate, by violating all of these rules.
max-tegmark.work: The 'Don't Look Up' Thinking That Could Doom Us With AI
max-tegmark.why: He says AI companies have shown they cannot regulate themselves on safety.

meredith-whittaker.q: You know, we should not be taking these companies words. We should not be. Satisfied with voluntary commitments. Given the track record here
meredith-whittaker.work: Tech, AI, digital infrastructure and surveillance with Meredith Whittaker
meredith-whittaker.why: She rejects voluntary commitments from tech companies and calls for liability, auditing and accountability; elsewhere she says the profit motive overrides safety.

miles-brundage.q: And boy, AI companies are really in a hurry: by all of their own admissions, they cut corners here and there in order to avoid being left behind.
miles-brundage.work: We're in Triage Mode for AI Policy
miles-brundage.why: He argues that, left to their own devices and under competitive pressure, companies will cut safety corners, which is why outside rules are needed.

noah-smith.q: with essentially no oversight or safeguards other than the guardrails that AI companies themselves have built into their products — and which they admit can sometimes fail.
noah-smith.work: If AI is a weapon, why don't we regulate it like one?
noah-smith.why: He presents relying only on companies' own guardrails as inadequate, and argues for regulating AI as a weapon.

richard-blumenthal.q: But we all know, and you have pointed out in your testimony, that these commitments are unspecific and unenforceable.
richard-blumenthal.work: Oversight of A.I.: Principles for Regulation (S. Hrg. 118-108), opening statement of Chair Blumenthal
richard-blumenthal.why: He calls the companies' voluntary safety commitments unenforceable and 'only a start', and argues for enforceable laws instead.

rumman-chowdhury.q: Today, we have to rely on companies to do the right thing, but aligning the greater good with stakeholder incentives has proven to be insufficient.
rumman-chowdhury.why: She argues corporate incentives alone have proven insufficient and calls for an external body with enforcement power.

scott-wiener.q: While the large AI labs have made admirable commitments to monitor and mitigate these risks, the truth is that voluntary commitments from industry are not enforceable and rarely work out well for the public.
scott-wiener.work: Senator Wiener Responds to Governor Newsom Vetoing Landmark AI Bill
scott-wiener.why: He says voluntary industry commitments do not protect the public, which is why binding rules are needed.

steven-adler.q: We’ve seen how inclined the AI companies are to undercut each other; it’s part of why I fear the industry won’t end up with strong safety practices.
steven-adler.why: He expects competitive dynamics to keep companies from adequate safety on their own, and elsewhere argues against letting them grade their own homework.

stuart-russell.q: Until then, only regulation and a pervasive culture of safety can prevent serious harm.
stuart-russell.work: Written Testimony before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology, & the Law ('Oversight of A.I.: Principles for Regulation')
stuart-russell.why: After criticising voluntary industry commitments, Russell says that until provably safe AI exists, only regulation and a culture of safety can prevent serious harm.

ted-cruz.q: as if AI engineers lack the intelligence to responsibly build AI without the bureaucrats
ted-cruz.work: Sen. Cruz: Adopting Europe's Approach on Regulation Will Cause China to Win the AI Race (opening statement, 'Winning the AI Race' hearing)
ted-cruz.why: He argues the industry can build AI responsibly without regulators.

timnit-gebru.q: Only when we change the incentive structure will we see technology that prioritizes the wellbeing of citizens
timnit-gebru.work: For truly ethical AI, its research must be independent from big tech
timnit-gebru.why: She argues companies' current incentives produce harmful technology, so outside change is needed for safe, beneficial AI.

tristan-harris.q: I mean, even if one whole company watched the AI dilemma and was completely convinced that this is a problem and they changed all their practices and did transparency and just invested in safety work and controllability, the other companies would still be racing.
tristan-harris.why: Harris argues that companies cannot fix safety by acting alone under race dynamics, and that even public-interest structures failed, so coordination and rules are needed.

william-saunders.q: I don't think you can trust anyone at these companies to be making that judgment themselves.
william-saunders.work: Former OpenAI Engineer William Saunders on Silence, Safety, and the Right to Warn
william-saunders.why: He says no company's own judgment that safety work is sufficient can be trusted and calls for independent outside evaluation, citing industry-wide pressure to ship.

yann-lecun.q: Do you need specific provisions to make AI safe? No, you need to make better AI systems, and they will be safe because they are designed to be more useful and more controllable.
yann-lecun.work: Transcript for Yann LeCun: Meta AI, Open Source, Limits of LLMs, AGI & the Future of AI
yann-lecun.why: Using the turbojet analogy, he says developers making better products will make AI safe without special safety provisions.

yoshua-bengio.q: The problem comes when safety and profit maximization or company culture ("move fast and break things") are not aligned.
yoshua-bengio.work: Reasoning through arguments against taking AI safety seriously
yoshua-bengio.why: In a section rebutting the view that corporations will build only safe AI, he argues that profit motives conflict with safety and laws are needed.

arvind-narayanan.q: to adopt AI, legal protections for researchers, adverse event reporting requirements, and whistleblower protections.
arvind-narayanan.why: Whistleblower protections are listed among the policies the authors say would help whatever the future of AI, and which they recommend.

chuck-grassley.q: I’m proud to introduce this legislation to increase accountability and protect AI whistleblowers
chuck-grassley.work: Grassley Introduces AI Whistleblower Protection Act
chuck-grassley.why: In his own statement he introduces a bill protecting AI employees who make disclosures from retaliation and restrictive NDAs.

helen-toner.q: If AI companies want to claim that they are building the most world-changing technology to ever exist, their employees should be able to share concerns about risks to public safety along the way without fearing the repercussions.
helen-toner.work: Testimony before the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, IP, AI and the Internet: 'Protecting Our Edge: Trade Secrets and the Global AI Arms Race'
helen-toner.why: In her testimony she recommends new legislation creating whistleblower protections for AI employees who raise public-safety risks.

meredith-whittaker.q: I think you know, I think we also need frankly, strong protections for whistleblowers within tech.
meredith-whittaker.work: Reclaiming the Future: Privacy, Ethics & Organizing in Tech (Meredith Whittaker with Kade Crockford)
meredith-whittaker.why: She calls for strong legal protections for tech whistleblowers, and her congressional testimony makes the same recommendation.

scott-wiener.q: In order to drive better safety outcomes across the AI ecosystem it would also create whistleblower protections for employees of frontier AI laboratories.
scott-wiener.work: Senator Wiener Responds to Governor Newsom Vetoing Landmark AI Bill
scott-wiener.why: His office's release on his own bill, SB 1047, describes the whistleblower protections for frontier-lab employees that the bill would have created.

timnit-gebru.q: the #1 thing that would safeguard us from unsafe uses of AI is curbing the power of the companies who develop it and increasing the power of those who speak up against the harms of AI and these companies’ practices.
timnit-gebru.work: For truly ethical AI, its research must be independent from big tech
timnit-gebru.why: Answering what regulation is needed, she puts protecting those who speak up about AI harms first, and says protections like the Silenced No More Act should be universal.

tristan-harris.q: in October, 2025, we had the ﬁrst state in California to enact whistleblower protections for AI company employees.
tristan-harris.work: The Great Simplification ep. 214: Tristan Harris (transcript)
tristan-harris.why: Harris lists California's whistleblower protections for AI employees among the 'wins' that show progress in the right direction.

william-saunders.q: The most important ingredients in my view are requiring information from companies developing frontier models on risk assessments and safety measures and providing whistleblower protection in case employees come forward with concerns of critical harms from AI models
william-saunders.why: He names legal whistleblower protection for AI employees raising risk concerns, even where no law is broken, as a key ingredient of the law he supports.

bruce-schneier.q: The United States needs a government-funded and -directed AI program to develop widely reusable models in the public interest, guided by technical expertise housed in federal agencies.
bruce-schneier.work: Build AI by the People, for the People
bruce-schneier.why: He directly proposes that government build public AI models.

dean-ball.q: But in the long run, a truly public cloud is also necessary: renting compute from firms like Amazon and Microsoft is, in the long-run, significantly more expensive than owning it wholly.
dean-ball.work: The Case for Public AI Infrastructure
dean-ball.why: In an essay arguing for publicly accessible AI research infrastructure, he says the federal government needs its own publicly owned AI compute.

fei-fei-li.q: And that moonshot will have to include infrastructure investments such as the National AI Research Resource, as well as national labs focusing on solving the hardest problems.
fei-fei-li.work: Governing AI Through Acquisition and Procurement (testimony to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee)
fei-fei-li.why: Li calls for government-built public AI infrastructure (a national research resource and national labs).

adam-thierer.q: When this mentality inspires technology policy, it translates into mountains of red tape that suffocate innovation and investment.
adam-thierer.work: Testimony, Hearing on "AI at a Crossroads: A Nationwide Strategy or Californication?"
adam-thierer.why: Describing European-style precautionary AI regulation now spreading to US states, he says it suffocates innovation and urges Congress not to allow it.

alexandria-ocasio-cortez.q: Congress has a moral obligation to stand with the American people and stop the expansion of these data centers until we have a framework to adequately address the existential harm AI poses to our society. We must choose humanity over profit.
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.work: Ocasio-Cortez Introduces House Version of the AI Data Center Moratorium Act
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.why: She sponsors a strict measure now, a halt on data center growth, and frames it as clearly worth its cost to industry.

alondra-nelson.q: Thoughtful regulation catalyzes the development and adoption of new technologies, ensuring that no tradeoff between safety and progress or rights and innovation is necessary.
alondra-nelson.work: Regulating AI in the Evolving Transatlantic Landscape
alondra-nelson.why: She denies that regulation deters innovation, saying it catalyzes it.

andrew-yang.q: I’m confident that American tech firms can do two things at once: continue to break new ground in AI and also keep us from Skynet killing us all or hacking the grid and sending us into the stone age.
andrew-yang.why: He calls for killswitch, liability and inspection rules and rejects the claim that safeguards would cost the US its innovation lead.

anton-korinek.q: Moreover, if well-designed, even the oversight and regulation required to address the social control problem can in fact spur technological progress by providing certainty about the regulatory environment and by forestalling a race to the bottom by competing companies.
anton-korinek.work: Why we need a new agency to regulate advanced artificial intelligence: Lessons on AI control from the Facebook Files
anton-korinek.why: While arguing for a powerful new AI regulator, he says well-designed regulation can speed innovation rather than deter it.

asad-ramzanali.q: Undoubtedly, Big Tech will cry that regulation would stifle innovation. Don’t believe it.
asad-ramzanali.work: Break Up Big AI Before It Breaks Us
asad-ramzanali.why: He rejects the claim that regulating Big AI would stifle innovation.

barack-obama.q: When you look at the history of innovation, it turns out that having some smart guideposts around which innovation takes place not only doesn’t slow things down, but in some cases, it actually raises standards and accelerates progress.
barack-obama.work: Barack Obama on AI, free speech, and the future of the internet
barack-obama.why: Responding to the Valley view that any constraint is bad, he argues regulation does not deter innovation and can speed it up.

bernie-sanders.q: That is why I have introduced legislation to impose a federal moratorium on the construction of new AI data centers until strong safeguards are enacted.
bernie-sanders.work: Artificial intelligence is coming for the working class. We must fight back
bernie-sanders.why: He proposes strict measures now, a federal moratorium until strong safeguards exist, so he does not think strict regulation does more harm than good.

brian-merchant.q: I would also argue we might get a lot of the way to stopping any currently envisioned robot apocalypse simply by forcing AI companies to assume liability, and to submit to the full brunt of the law.
brian-merchant.work: The politics and possibilities of 'AI could kill us all'
brian-merchant.why: He calls for strict liability and transparency rules on AI firms now and praises new state AI laws; he mocks the deregulatory 'red tape' framing.

bruce-schneier.q: We need government to constrain the behavior of corporations and the AIs they build, deploy, and control.
bruce-schneier.why: He calls for AI transparency, safety and trustworthiness laws now and says the market will not provide trustworthy AI on its own.

chris-murphy.q: That China has been actively building towards a national AI law, while producing a cutting-edge model like DeepSeek’s, makes clear that AI regulation and innovation can, and do, co-exist.
chris-murphy.work: In our scramble to win the AI race against China, we risk losing ourselves
chris-murphy.why: He argues regulation does not deter innovation.

daniel-faggella.q: There is no end to the arms race for individual AGI labs (OpenAI, Meta, etc) or for nations (primarily: USA and China) unless there is international governance and agreement in place
daniel-faggella.work: Altman is Everyman - AGI Requires Coordination, Not Saintly Leaders
daniel-faggella.why: He argues that binding international AGI governance, scaled in severity as risks rise, is needed, not harmful.

daniel-jeffries.q: they will do real, lasting, nasty damage that's infinitely worse than the thing they're supposed to stop or prevent.
daniel-jeffries.work: If We Build It, Everyone Lives
daniel-jeffries.why: He argues strict AI restrictions would cause more harm than they prevent, in an essay on the lost benefits of slowing progress.

daron-acemoglu.q: ex ante regulation slowing down the use of AI technologies, especially in domains where redressing the costs of AI become politically and socially more di¢ cult after large-scale implementation.
daron-acemoglu.why: He endorses a precautionary principle of early regulation, the opposite of the view that strict regulation now does more harm than good.

david-sacks.q: Although we want a light touch on AI regulations, President Trump made clear that we do not intend to ignore the risks of this revolutionary technological power. We can monitor risks, and secure our edge, without stifling innovation.
david-sacks.work: Thread on the White House AI Action Plan and Trump's first major AI speech
david-sacks.why: Speaking for the administration ('we'), he favours light-touch regulation so as not to stifle innovation.

dean-ball.q: Here is what this means in practice: I oppose literally almost all AI regulation.
dean-ball.work: Before Leviathan Wakes (Why I Believe What I Believe)
dean-ball.why: He opposes nearly all AI regulation and wants deregulation so AI can transform lives, with a narrow exception for catastrophic-risk measures.

ed-zitron.q: If LLMs were a toy, they’d be taken off the shelves. If LLMs were a drug, they would be banned.
ed-zitron.work: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands
ed-zitron.why: The author says LLMs deserve product-safety-level restriction or bans, which contradicts the view that strict regulation would do more harm than good.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: Shut down all the large GPU clusters (the large computer farms where the most powerful AIs are refined). Shut down all the large training runs.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: The Only Way to Deal With the Threat From AI? Shut It Down
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He demands the strictest possible restrictions now, the opposite of holding that strict regulation would do more harm than good.

elizabeth-nolan-brown.q: Alas, Blackburn is serving up a cornucopia of proposals that could throttle free speech and free markets online. An anti-tech omnibus, if you will, sold as a simple AI regulatory scheme.
elizabeth-nolan-brown.work: The TRUMP AMERICA AI Act Is Every Bit as Bad as You Would Expect (Maybe Worse)
elizabeth-nolan-brown.why: She opposes a sweeping AI regulatory bill as harmful to free markets and, elsewhere, praises a 'restrained' approach without licensing.

elizabeth-warren.q: Policymakers undoubtedly need to regulate AI and protect against its worst-case harms, like cyber attacks, which could impact our financial system and national security.
elizabeth-warren.work: Why We Need to Tax AI
elizabeth-warren.why: She insists AI regulation is needed, and elsewhere calls for an immediate pause, the opposite of saying strict rules do more harm.

elon-musk.q: When it is cool, and the regulators are convinced that it is safe to proceed, then you can go. But otherwise, slow down.
elon-musk.work: Elon Musk Governor's Interview (NGA 2017, AI segment transcript)
elon-musk.why: He supports strict regulation now that slows AI until regulators are satisfied, though he adds he is 'against over regulation'.

emily-m-bender.q: It is high time for us to regulate usage of systems sold as “AI”, not because they are magical machines, but because they are error-prone products that shouldn’t be used in high-stakes scenarios.
emily-m-bender.work: Forget 'superintelligence': error-prone AI nearly sparked world war three this month
emily-m-bender.why: She calls for regulation now; her testimony also asks Congress for regulation to channel innovation toward the public good.

erik-hoel.q: We need the equivalent of a Clean Air Act: a Clean Internet Act. We can’t just sit by and let human culture end up buried.
erik-hoel.work: Here lies the internet, murdered by generative AI
erik-hoel.why: He calls for strong regulation of AI content now; elsewhere he also urges regulatory oversight to slow AI development.

gary-marcus.q:
Some in the tech world also seem to think that the world as we know it will end, if developers bear even a slight responsibility for licensing, knowing customers, etc.

This is nonsense.
gary-marcus.work: The misguided backlash against California's SB-1047
gary-marcus.why: He dismisses the claim that the regulation would stifle innovation and argues the industry can easily bear its costs.

gavin-newsom.q: proving that innovation and economic growth are fully compatible with common sense regulations that address risks and advance public safety through responsible deployment of AI systems and models
gavin-newsom.work: Executive Order N-9-26 (independent AI oversight, frontier-model 'kill switch')
gavin-newsom.why: In his own executive order he states that California's AI safety laws show regulation does not come at the cost of innovation.

geoffrey-hinton.q: But if they put in strong AI regulations that made Google less valuable but increased the chance of humanity surviving, I’d be very happy.
geoffrey-hinton.work: Brook Silva-Braga interviews Geoffrey Hinton on CBS Mornings (transcript)
geoffrey-hinton.why: He backs strong regulation, praises California's SB 1047 and criticizes companies for lobbying against regulation.

guillaume-verdon.q: over-regulating technologies suppresses variance and hence slows down progress towards higher utility technologies and advancement of civilization, a contrast to anti-AGI factions of EA
guillaume-verdon.work: Notes on e/acc principles and tenets
guillaume-verdon.why: He states that over-regulating technology slows progress, against the anti-AGI factions; on Lex he says registration rules would deter the hackers who make key discoveries.

holly-elmore.q: Whether or not there’s blood involved, regulation is never written in blood alone— and our job is always to fight for regulation written in ink.
holly-elmore.work: The myth of AI 'warning shots' as cavalry
holly-elmore.why: She argues for fighting for AI regulation now, before any disaster, which is the opposite of saying strict regulation now would do more harm than good.

jason-crawford.q: This could end up like nuclear, where nothing gets approved and progress stalls for decades.
jason-crawford.work: A plea for solutionism on AI safety
jason-crawford.why: He warns that strict pre-approval regulation of AI could stall progress for decades, and prefers a lighter, incremental approach like the DOT's for self-driving cars.

jd-vance.q: we believe that excessive regulation of the A- -- the AI sector could kill a transformative industry just as it's taking off
jd-vance.work: Remarks by the Vice President at the Artificial Intelligence Action Summit in Paris, France
jd-vance.why: In his Paris AI summit speech he argues heavy AI regulation now would kill the industry, and pushes a deregulatory approach.

jeff-jarvis.q: Such complication raises the barrier to entry for new and open-source competitors and the spectre of regulatory capture — as does discussion in the EU of restricting open-source AI models (Question 25.1).
jeff-jarvis.why: He argues that strict licensing rules on AI would shut out new and open-source competitors, and urges regulators not to rush.

joanna-bryson.q: Much regulation is helpful to a sector – governments regulate to strengthen their economy.
joanna-bryson.work: OpenAI reveals the anti-regulatory intent of its regulatory disinformation
joanna-bryson.why: Answering OpenAI's case for exempting smaller models from audits and licences, she argues that regulation helps innovation rather than harming it.

joy-buolamwini.q: So I think it’s a great opportunity for the Biden administration to make true on their promise to make what was put in the blueprint binding through the Office of Management and Budget, and then to push to make the blueprint federal law.
joy-buolamwini.work: How AI Is Enabling Racism & Sexism: Algorithmic Justice League's Joy Buolamwini on Meeting with Biden
joy-buolamwini.why: She calls for binding AI rules, federal law, regulatory oversight and a halt to TSA face recognition, and says 'laws do make a difference'.

karen-hao.q: And we need more — some kind of more guardrails to actually prevent these companies from continuing to try and develop labor-automating technologies
karen-hao.work: Karen Hao on How AI Colonialism Is Threatening the World (extended interview)
karen-hao.why: She rejects the industry's light-touch, beat-China argument and calls for more guardrails on AI companies.

kate-crawford.q: Much stronger regulatory regimes and greater rigour and responsibility around how training datasets are constructed.
kate-crawford.work: Microsoft's Kate Crawford: 'AI is neither artificial nor intelligent' (interview by Zoë Corbyn)
kate-crawford.why: Asked what is needed to make things better, she calls for much stronger regulation.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: I hear blunt cries for government regulation—but remember that it’s Lina Khan-types who would be writing these regulations right now.
leopold-aschenbrenner.work: Response to Tyler Cowen on AI risk
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He opposes government AI regulation now in favour of lab self-regulation and says labs should be free to charge ahead absent catastrophic risk; elsewhere he warns that safety bureaucracy hinders innovation.

liz-shuler.q: We’re demanding our politicians do what 80% of Americans want you to do: pass common-sense guardrails. Protect working people. Bring us to the table now, not after the fact,
liz-shuler.work: Labor Leaders Call on State Governments to Protect Workers from AI
liz-shuler.why: She demands AI guardrails now, and elsewhere says 'We’re not anti-innovation', so she does not think regulation now does more harm than good.

marc-andreessen.q: Regulatory agencies are being green lit in real time to do the same to Artificial Intelligence.
marc-andreessen.work: The Little Tech Agenda
marc-andreessen.why: In a list of ways government hobbles new industries, he says regulators are now doing so to AI, and calls bad government policy the top threat to startups.

mark-zuckerberg.q: Regulating against known harms is necessary, but pre-emptive regulation of theoretical harms for nascent technologies such as open-source AI will stifle innovation.
mark-zuckerberg.work: Mark Zuckerberg and Daniel Ek on Why Europe Should Embrace Open-Source AI
mark-zuckerberg.why: He argues that pre-emptive AI regulation now would stifle innovation, while still accepting rules against known harms.

max-tegmark.q: Like most other human tools, tool AI also comes with risks that can be managed with legally binding safety standards
max-tegmark.work: The Hopium Wars: the AGI Entente Delusion
max-tegmark.why: He argues for national AI safety standards now, tiered to minimize red tape, while going full steam ahead with tool AI.

meredith-whittaker.q: So I think ethics is not sufficient. We need regulation. We need significant accountability.
meredith-whittaker.work: Reclaiming the Future: Privacy, Ethics & Organizing in Tech (Meredith Whittaker with Kade Crockford)
meredith-whittaker.why: She argues that corporate self-regulation is not enough and that regulation is needed now; elsewhere she rejects the claim that guardrails mean losing the race to China.

michael-kratsios.q: We believe broad over regulation incentivizes centralization stifles innovation and increases the danger that these tools will be used for tyranny and conquest.
michael-kratsios.work: US statement at the Security Council open debate 'Artificial intelligence and international peace and security' (10005th meeting)
michael-kratsios.why: In the US statement he argues broad AI regulation stifles innovation and does net harm.

miles-brundage.q: Timely strong regulation: Perhaps most importantly from my perspective, the AI regulations that actually developed in 2025 all have fatal flaws.
miles-brundage.work: We're in Triage Mode for AI Policy
miles-brundage.why: He counts the failure to adopt strong regulation in time as the most important missed opportunity, the opposite of thinking it would do more harm than good.

mustafa-suleyman.q: I mean, the consequences are so vast and potentially so huge, both positive and negative, that this is a moment when we need strong governments and proactive intervention.
mustafa-suleyman.work: Leading voice in AI, who worries about its consequences, favors regulating it
mustafa-suleyman.why: He calls for the precautionary principle and strong government intervention now, and elsewhere names voluntary commitments he wants made legally mandatory.

neil-chilson.q: But history’s lesson is clear: regulating too soon slows innovation, stifles national leadership, and hurts consumers.
neil-chilson.why: He argues that the current wave of AI laws comes too early and will act like England's innovation-stifling Red Flag Laws.

pete-buttigieg.q: I mean, the aerospace sector is known to be very innovative, but also you make sure it's safe.
pete-buttigieg.work: Secretary Pete Buttigieg: The American Dream Is DEAD. We're Running Out Of Time To Fix It!
pete-buttigieg.why: Drawing on his time at the FAA's parent department, he holds up aviation regulation as a model for AI, arguing safety rules and innovation can coexist.

peter-thiel.q: But there’s no reason… if you had the FDA regulating video games, or regulating AI, I think the progress would slow down a lot.
peter-thiel.work: Thiel on AI & Racing with China (transcribed excerpt of Joe Rogan Experience, Aug 2024)
peter-thiel.why: He warns that FDA-style regulation of AI would greatly slow progress, and calls such regulating to death very bad from the point of view of progress.

pope-leo-xiv.q: Indeed, these criteria do not constitute a curb on innovation; instead they make it civilized and humane.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: He answers the worry that rules on transparency, taxation and equity stifle innovation by saying they make it humane.

reid-hoffman.q: I do. I hope there will be much more enablement of technology innovation.
reid-hoffman.work: Reid Hoffman AP interview on AI, Trump, Musk and Thiel (Q&A)
reid-hoffman.why: Asked whether to ease up on rigorous tech regulation, he agrees, in the name of enabling innovation.

richard-blumenthal.q: Sensible safeguards are not in opposition to innovation. Accountability is not a burden. Far from it.
richard-blumenthal.work: Oversight of A.I.: Rules for Artificial Intelligence (S. Hrg. 118-037), opening statement of Chair Blumenthal
richard-blumenthal.why: He denies that safeguards work against innovation, which rejects the claim that regulation now would do more harm by deterring it.

ro-khanna.q: We need a robust federal agency to regulate AI like we regulate nuclear energy or federal aviation.
ro-khanna.work: We need a new tech social contract to reclaim AI from billionaires
ro-khanna.why: He argues strong safety regulation helps rather than hurts US AI, 'not to slow innovation'.

robin-hanson.q: In fact, progress seems to me to be slowing down worldwide due to excess fear-induced regulation.
robin-hanson.why: He argues fear-driven regulation, as with nuclear power, stops valuable progress.

ruha-benjamin.q: And one of the recurring fallacies that comes up, again and again, is the pitting of innovation against these more social concerns around equity.
ruha-benjamin.work: Imagining 2025 and Beyond with Dr. Ruha Benjamin
ruha-benjamin.why: She calls the claim that addressing social harms sacrifices innovation a fallacy.

rumman-chowdhury.q: It is important to dispel the myth that “governance stifles innovation.” This is not true.
rumman-chowdhury.work: Submitted Written Testimony, Artificial Intelligence: Advancing Innovation Towards the National Interest
rumman-chowdhury.why: She directly denies that governance deters innovation, arguing it improves products.

safiya-noble.q: That seems woefully insufficient when we could regulate these tools differently and limit their adoption to where it makes sense.
safiya-noble.work: How AI discriminates and what that means for your Google habit
safiya-noble.why: She calls for policy-level regulation that limits AI adoption, rejecting the idea that regulation now would do more harm.

scott-wiener.q: Innovation and safety are not mutually exclusive, and I reject the false claim that in order to innovate, we must leave safety solely in the hands of technology companies and venture capitalists.
scott-wiener.work: Senator Wiener Responds to Speaker Emerita Pelosi's Opposition to SB 1047
scott-wiener.why: He explicitly rejects the claim that safety regulation must come at the cost of innovation.

sean-o-brien.q: These tools are being abused now, and without strong public oversight, the risks will get worse.
sean-o-brien.work: Big Beautiful Bill could give free pass to Big Tech to kill jobs
sean-o-brien.why: He argues strong public oversight is needed now, the opposite of holding that regulation would do more harm than good.

stuart-russell.q: They need not be particularly onerous; in comparison, restaurants need approximately ten forms of permitting to open, plus government-mandated training for every employee, yet approximately 50,000 new restaurants open every year in the US.
stuart-russell.work: Written Testimony before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology, & the Law ('Oversight of A.I.: Principles for Regulation')
stuart-russell.why: In urging immediate licensing and registration, Russell argues such regulation does not stifle activity, and he calls for urgent, enforceable rules.

ted-cruz.q: To lead in AI, the U.S. cannot allow regulation, even the supposedly benign kind, to choke innovation or adoption.
ted-cruz.work: Sen. Cruz: Adopting Europe's Approach on Regulation Will Cause China to Win the AI Race (opening statement, 'Winning the AI Race' hearing)
ted-cruz.why: He argues heavy AI regulation, as in Europe, would choke innovation.

yoshua-bengio.q: However, from the point of view of ordinary citizens and of public policy, the prudent approach into AGI is clearly preferable when adding up the risks and benefits.
yoshua-bengio.work: Reasoning through arguments against taking AI safety seriously
yoshua-bengio.why: Answering accelerationists who warn that slowing down forfeits benefits, he concludes that the cautious, regulated path is better on balance.

yuval-noah-harari.q: We can still regulate the new AI tools, but we must act quickly.
yuval-noah-harari.work: Watch out humans: AI has hacked the operating system of civilisation
yuval-noah-harari.why: He calls for urgent regulation now and says unregulated deployment would do the greater harm.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: This leads to the standard (and usually highly accurate) objections that regulations never work out the way you want them to and always stifle innovation and progress. Except, here, that could be exactly what we need to protect against existential risk
zvi-mowshowitz.work: On the FLI AI-Risk Open Letter
zvi-mowshowitz.why: He grants that regulation stifles innovation but says that in AI's case this could be exactly what is needed, rejecting the claim that strict regulation does more harm than good.

bernie-sanders.q: It means that if AI and robotics will be used by children, guardrails must be established to make sure they do not harm their emotional well-being or their capacity to learn.
bernie-sanders.work: Artificial intelligence is coming for the working class. We must fight back
bernie-sanders.why: He lists legal guardrails on children's use of AI among the safeguards his moratorium legislation is meant to secure, and elsewhere worries about teens using AI for companionship.

chris-murphy.q: We could create new rules that slow the job destruction, that protect human-created content, that keep children away from these friendship bots.
chris-murphy.work: Murphy Speaks on AI's Impact on Job Loss, Purpose, Social Connection at Brookings Institution
chris-murphy.why: He advocates rules keeping children away from AI friendship bots.

dean-ball.q: At the object level, it seems to me that the prudent law to pass today would require large AI companies to enable age verification or detection, impose content guardrails for minors, and offer parental controls.
dean-ball.why: He endorses a law requiring age verification, guardrails for minors and parental controls on AI chatbots, while warning about First Amendment limits.

elizabeth-nolan-brown.q: Even at its least broad, such a ban would be a bad idea.
elizabeth-nolan-brown.work: How a Bill Banning AI Companions for Kids Could Usher in Widespread ID Checks Online
elizabeth-nolan-brown.why: Discussing the GUARD Act's ban on minors using AI companions, she says even a narrow version would be a bad idea.

jonathan-haidt.q: There could be a role for AI therapists someday, but how about we require years of testing before we let anyone push it out into childhood?
jonathan-haidt.work: Why You Should Be a Techno-Skeptic (TED talk transcript)
jonathan-haidt.why: Under his principle 'beware of artificial relationships for minors', he proposes requiring testing before AI relationships reach children.

josh-hawley.q: Let’s just let’s ban AI chatbot companions for minor children. Let’s just start there.
josh-hawley.work: Josh Hawley: We Must ‘Bend’ AI to Serve the Good
josh-hawley.why: He calls for banning AI companion chatbots for minors and has introduced legislation to mandate it.

marsha-blackburn.q: Establishes requirements for companies providing AI chatbot and companion services to protect kids.
marsha-blackburn.work: Blackburn Unveils National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence (TRUMP AMERICA AI Act)
marsha-blackburn.why: Her bill sets legal requirements on AI chatbot and companion services to protect children.

taylor-barkley.q: The goal should not be less AI for kids — it should be safer AI.
taylor-barkley.work: False GUARD: Banning kids from AI won't keep them safe
taylor-barkley.why: In an op-ed against the GUARD Act's ban on minors using AI companions, he argues against restricting children's access.

alexandria-ocasio-cortez.q: Congress has a moral obligation to stand with the American people and stop the expansion of these data centers until we have a framework to adequately address the existential harm AI poses to our society.
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.work: Ocasio-Cortez Introduces House Version of the AI Data Center Moratorium Act
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.why: She introduced a federal moratorium on new and expanded AI data centers, a deliberate halt on the build-out of AI until rules exist.

andrew-yang.q: But when I see the absolute lack of leadership in DC stepping up to put us on a safer path, it makes me wish that I was in position to temper the breakneck pace of AI development.
andrew-yang.why: He supports an industry slowdown cemented by regulation and wishes he could temper the pace of AI development.

arvind-narayanan.q: But they should reject the kind of policies that might seem compelling if we view x-risk as urgent and serious, notably: restricting AI development.
arvind-narayanan.work: AI existential risk probabilities are too unreliable to inform policy
arvind-narayanan.why: Answering what governments should do about AI x-risk, the authors say governments should reject restricting AI development.

bernie-sanders.q: We must place an immediate pause on advanced-AI development and ban artificial superintelligence
bernie-sanders.work: Don't Let Big Tech Dictate Humanity's Future
bernie-sanders.why: He calls for a pause on advanced AI and says he has introduced legislation to do it.

bryan-caplan.q: The cost of caution is very high; unless humanity shuts down the internet, AI will keep improving rapidly. And yes, crushing AI really does amplify the risk of other awful outcomes.
bryan-caplan.why: Weighing caution on AI, he says crushing AI is very costly and raises other risks, arguing against stopping it.

chris-murphy.q: The only way to slow that race is one set of rules that applies to every company, and only government can write them.
chris-murphy.work: AI Leaders Are Sounding the Alarm. Who's Listening?
chris-murphy.why: He explicitly seeks to slow the race toward recursively self-improving AI.

curtis-yarvin.q: let’s ban the new technology, let’s ban AI, let’s ban genome sequencers. Something, something, something actually to fix the economy. It’s the old technology that you have to ban.
curtis-yarvin.work: Does Democracy Still Control Power? w/ Curtis Yarvin (Peter McCormack Show, transcript)
curtis-yarvin.why: He mocks the Luddite impulse to ban AI and says the old technology, not AI, is what should be restricted.

daniel-faggella.q: I have, for 7+ years, advocated for AGI slow-down within the OECD, the United Nations, and in articles / interviews.
daniel-faggella.work: A Worthy Successor: The Purpose of AGI
daniel-faggella.why: He states in his own voice that he advocates slowing AGI development.

daniel-jeffries.q: This technology is too amazing to let fear cripple it before it gets off the ground.
daniel-jeffries.work: AI, Art, Blurred Lines and the Looming Nightmare of Copyright Expansion
daniel-jeffries.why: He opposes calls to 'stop all progress' on AI and warns against killing the technology 'in its crib'.

daniel-kokotajlo.q: If that decreased to, for example, 10%, this would significantly slow down their race towards research automation while freeing up compute to go towards beneficial deployments, safety research, and also simply lowering prices for consumers.
daniel-kokotajlo.why: In his Senate testimony he recommends redirecting compute specifically to slow the frontier labs' race toward automated AI research.

dean-ball.q: I am opposed to pauses and bans on AI development.
dean-ball.work: Before Leviathan Wakes (Why I Believe What I Believe)
dean-ball.why: A direct statement of his position against slowing or stopping AI development.

e-glen-weyl.q: They are allies in important projects, such as limiting the race for massive investments in “AI” capabilities and engaging in governance experimentation.
e-glen-weyl.work: Why I was Wrong to Demonize Rationalism
e-glen-weyl.why: He names limiting the race for AI capability investment as an important project he shares with Rationalists.

ed-zitron.q: the grim truth that we need to start arresting people for committing crimes, halting any and all training runs, and putting real safeguards on this technology
ed-zitron.work: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands
ed-zitron.why: He calls for halting all training runs and says a mere 'slowdown' is not sufficient.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: The moratorium on new large training runs needs to be indefinite and worldwide.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: The Only Way to Deal With the Threat From AI? Shut It Down
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: Direct call to stop frontier AI training worldwide.

elizabeth-warren.q: We should immediately press pause on the development of advanced AI while lawmakers and regulators put systems in place to keep people safe.
elizabeth-warren.work: Senator Warren Calls for Pause in Advanced AI Development
elizabeth-warren.why: She directly calls for pausing advanced AI development.

erik-hoel.q: When a researcher or company goes to make an AI, they should have to show that it can’t do certain things, that it can’t pass certain general tests, that it is specialized in some fundamental way, and absolutely not conscious in the way humans are.
erik-hoel.work: We need a Butlerian Jihad against AI
erik-hoel.why: In an essay calling for a moral ban on strong AI research, he proposes that only demonstrably narrow AI be allowed.

gary-marcus.q: If there was ever a case for pausing a company for the public good, it would be now.
gary-marcus.why: In a piece titled 'Pause OpenAI, now' he calls for halting a leading frontier developer because its models are becoming more dangerous.

guillaume-verdon.q: over-regulating technologies suppresses variance and hence slows down progress towards higher utility technologies and advancement of civilization, a contrast to anti-AGI factions of EA
guillaume-verdon.work: Notes on e/acc principles and tenets
guillaume-verdon.why: He states that the goal is to accelerate the process rather than slow it, and opposes the 'decels'.

holly-elmore.q: We need to Pause frontier AI development if we’re ever going to have time and latitude to even see if superintelligence could be safe and respect human consent.
holly-elmore.work: YOU have the power: my Stop the AI Race speech
holly-elmore.why: Direct call to pause frontier AI development.

jack-clark.q: We will need to build the infrastructure to take advantage of this technology, but we will also need to go slowly and deliberately on developing the technology itself, to pace or otherwise control its development.
jack-clark.work: Import AI 477: In which I tell the IMF the Singularity has begun
jack-clark.why: In his IMF lecture he says AI development itself should be deliberately paced or slowed.

jason-crawford.q: But in contrast to defeatist pessimism, we should do this not in order to slow or stop progress, but to identify positive steps we can take towards safer technology.
jason-crawford.work: A plea for solutionism on AI safety
jason-crawford.why: He says identifying AI risks should not be used to slow or stop progress.

jd-vance.q: And to restrict its development now would not only unfairly benefit incumbents in the space, it would mean paralyzing one of the most promising technologies we have seen in generations.
jd-vance.work: Remarks by the Vice President at the Artificial Intelligence Action Summit in Paris, France
jd-vance.why: He opposes restricting AI development now, which rejects deliberately slowing it.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: Rabid claims of 99% odds of doom, calls to indefinitely pause AI—they are clearly not the way.
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He rejects pausing AI (elsewhere he says he 'strongly advocated against policies like an AI pause'); he only allows short safety delays if the US has a lead.

marc-andreessen.q: We believe any deceleration of AI will cost lives.
marc-andreessen.work: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto
marc-andreessen.why: He opposes any slowing of AI and backs deliberate acceleration.

max-tegmark.q: So let's not pause AI. Let's just pause the reckless race to superintelligence. Let's stop obsessively training ever-larger models that we don't understand.
max-tegmark.work: How to Keep AI Under Control
max-tegmark.why: He calls for pausing the race to superintelligence and stopping ever-larger training runs.

neil-chilson.q: A delayed approval for a frontier model could have a greater cost than even the horror of delaying a disease treatment. A delayed model could slow or stop progress across the entire economy.
neil-chilson.work: An FDA for AI Would Make America Less Safe
neil-chilson.why: Arguing against pre-approval of AI models, he treats any delay of frontier models as a grave cost, the opposite of deliberately slowing them.

nick-land.q: Ergo, our instrumental but also absolute priority is the realization of superior minds.
nick-land.why: Pythia names unconstrained intelligence explosion; Land argues that complying with it, not inhibiting it, is what we consistently want.

noah-smith.q: So yes, we should be worried about vibe-coded doomsday viruses, and we should be doing everything we can to secure biology labs, police the modification of viruses and other pathogens, and so on. “Pacing” AI development would probably help here too.
noah-smith.work: Two missing pieces in the AI safety discussion
noah-smith.why: He endorses 'pacing' (slowing) frontier AI and spends the post on how to bring China into a joint international slowdown.

peter-thiel.q: Well, it's already, it's an answer to the nuclear problem. It's an answer to the environmental challenges. It's an answer to the AI challenge, which is, and I would just submit it's not a good answer.
peter-thiel.work: Peter Thiel, Leader Of The Rebel Alliance (Uncommon Knowledge transcript)
peter-thiel.why: He argues that stopping AI and science would require a one-world state with global surveillance, rejects that answer, and earlier says he is still in the accelerationist, deregulation camp.

reid-hoffman.q: It's a common misconception that we can steer clear of risk. When in reality, stopping or pausing to avoid risk is a risk—and most often a more perilous one than embracing risk in the first place.
reid-hoffman.work: AI, Society, and Our World Order
reid-hoffman.why: Arguing for iterative deployment, he says pausing AI is usually the more dangerous choice.

richard-sutton.q: Clamping down, trying to control everything, is not the answer
richard-sutton.work: AI Succession (talk slides, World AI Conference 2023)
richard-sutton.why: He lists calls to limit AI research among the 'wrong answers' and urges people not to make decisions out of fear.

robin-hanson.q: Thus when facing the risk of our fear essentially halting progress here, I’d rather continue down our current path, and work harder on controls when we better see concrete serious control problems to manage.
robin-hanson.why: He opposes slowing AI progress, preferring to continue and address control later.

scott-alexander.q: Short, carefully-tailored pauses could improve the chance of AI going well by a lot, without increasing the risk of social collapse too much.
scott-alexander.work: Pause For Thought: The AI Pause Debate
scott-alexander.why: In his own concluding thoughts he backs deliberate, tailored pauses in AI development.

scott-santens.q: It may be how we slow a technology racing past our ability to control it.
scott-santens.work: Our Data. Our Resources. Our Terms and Conditions.
scott-santens.why: He backs blocking data centers partly to buy time and slow frontier AI until alignment is solved.

steven-adler.q: I want us to get those great futures too, and I fear that rushing ahead isn’t the way to do so.
steven-adler.why: In a section arguing that superintelligence should be built more slowly, ideally via a treaty, he says rushing ahead is the wrong path.

stuart-russell.q: In summary, further development towards AGI with current levels of safety and weak technical understanding presents an unacceptable risk.
stuart-russell.work: Written Statement for the U.S. Senate AI Forum on 'Risk, Alignment, & Guarding Against Doomsday Scenarios'
stuart-russell.why: Russell judges continued development toward AGI under present safety levels to be unacceptable, and elsewhere calls the AGI race 'a race towards the edge of a cliff'.

timnit-gebru.q: We urge researchers in AI to stop their quest to build a system that even those in favor of AGI concede is not well-defined.
timnit-gebru.work: The TESCREAL bundle: Eugenics and the promise of utopia through artificial general intelligence
timnit-gebru.why: She calls for stopping the attempt to build AGI.

tristan-harris.q: I think we don’t know and we probably shouldn’t be racing to release increasingly powerful AI systems that can do more and more crazy things like hack critical infrastructure before we know that we’re not in the worst-case scenario
tristan-harris.why: Harris says increasingly powerful AI should not be released until we know it is safe; elsewhere he says we should be able to refuse to build superintelligence until there is scientific consensus that it is safe.

tyler-cowen.q: We should take the plunge. We already have taken the plunge.
tyler-cowen.work: Existential risk, AI, and the inevitable turn in human history
tyler-cowen.why: Answering his own question of whether to halt or slow down AI advances, he concludes we should proceed.

venkatesh-rao.q: So yes, pace the frontier. But don’t turn the frontier labs into a cartel to do it.
venkatesh-rao.work: The Accelerationist Case for Frontier Pacing
venkatesh-rao.why: Rao endorses deliberately pacing frontier AI development now, though he prefers market mechanisms over a lab cartel for doing it.

vitalik-buterin.q: I personally am very pro-technology, and if it were a binary option of "go further" vs "stay where we are", I would gladly push forward on everything except for a very small list (eg. gain of function research, weapons and superintelligent AI) despite the risks.
vitalik-buterin.work: "I support it only if it's open source" should be a more common viewpoint
vitalik-buterin.why: He excludes superintelligent AI from the technologies he would push forward, and elsewhere tells people not to work for companies speeding up frontier fully-autonomous AI.

william-macaskill.q: Slowing the intelligence explosion. If we could slow down the intelligence explosion in general, that would give decision-makers and institutions more time to react thoughtfully.
william-macaskill.why: Among their recommended AGI-preparedness measures, the authors list slowing the intelligence explosion as beneficial.

yann-lecun.q: Or is the strategy to, on the contrary, open it up as widely as possible, so that progress is as fast as possible, so that the bad guys always trail behind? And I'm very much of the second category of thinking.
yann-lecun.work: Meta's AI Chief Yann LeCun on AGI, Open-Source, and AI Risk
yann-lecun.why: He chooses opening AI up so that progress is as fast as possible, the opposite of deliberately slowing it.

yoshua-bengio.q: Slowing down AI research and deployment in directions of high risk in order to protect the public, society and humanity from catastrophic outcomes would be worthwhile
yoshua-bengio.work: How Rogue AIs may Arise
yoshua-bengio.why: He calls for slowing high-risk AI development and proposes banning powerful systems beyond GPT-4 that are given autonomy.

yuval-noah-harari.q: I am not saying stop developing all AI. What I am saying is that that development must occur more slowly and more carefully so humanity can adapt.
yuval-noah-harari.work: Yuval Noah Harari: 'AI could be a great manipulative psychopath' (El Pais interview)
yuval-noah-harari.why: He calls for AI development to be deliberately slowed so society can adapt, while not stopping it entirely.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: We should not build superintelligence until such time as that changes, and the risk of everyone dying as a result, as well as the risk of losing control over the future as a result, is very low.
zvi-mowshowitz.work: New Statement Calls For Not Building Superintelligence For Now
zvi-mowshowitz.why: He says in his own voice that superintelligence should not be built until the risk is very low, and he signed a statement calling for a prohibition.

audrey-tang.q: It’s very good. It produced extremely good policies. But if we just rely on delegating our deliberation to the robots, it’s exactly like sending our robots to the gym to lift weights for us.
audrey-tang.why: She grants that the Habermas Machine produces very good policies but says deliberation must not be delegated to AI ('We cannot delegate democracy'). She still accepts AI as a helper in deliberation.

brian-merchant.q: Now, some organizing will continue to focus the politics of refusal; identifying the contexts of technology in which AI should simply not be used, and resisting it outright.
brian-merchant.work: This Labor Day, let's consider how we want technology to work for us
brian-merchant.why: He goes on to answer "No, no, and no" to AI replacing artists, teachers and newsroom reporting.

jack-clark.q: just because AI will be a capable scientist, that does not mean we should use it for absolutely everything.
jack-clark.work: Import AI 477: In which I tell the IMF the Singularity has begun
jack-clark.why: He says that even where AI is capable, it should not be used for everything, and that we must tell apart what we can do from what we should do.

jonathan-haidt.q: Absolutely not. Because that would mean that nobody depends on us. Nobody is relying on us. We are not important to anyone.
jonathan-haidt.work: Why You Should Be a Techno-Skeptic (TED talk transcript)
jonathan-haidt.why: Supposing for argument's sake that AI could give us excellent friends and partners, he says relying on it would still not make us happy, so relationships should stay human.

josh-hawley.q: Most jobs should be reserved for humans. Only humans should drive cars and trucks. Only humans should enter into contracts.
josh-hawley.work: AI Threatens the Working Man
josh-hawley.why: He calls for reserving certain work for humans regardless of AI's capability.

paul-kingsnorth.q: The first of these points draws a line for our own creative work. We say, as storytellers: we will remain human.
paul-kingsnorth.why: He launches a pledge to keep writing free of AI even while granting that machine-written work may be as good or better.

pope-leo-xiv.q: Educating people about the use of AI, then, involves teaching them to decide when and for what purpose it ought not to be used.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: He holds there are purposes for which AI ought not to be used, and elsewhere forbids handing lethal decisions to machines.

russell-moore.q: The wording of the message matters to a degree. But the point here is that this type of message shouldn’t come by text or email. Such life-altering news needs to be delivered by a human, in person.
russell-moore.work: AI Might Teach, But It Can't Preach
russell-moore.why: Granting that AI could write orthodox sermons, he argues preaching must still come from a human person.

adam-thierer.q: First, Congress should expressly preempt state regulations related to AI frontier labs and models because the costs associated with such parochial regulations would outweigh any local benefits.
adam-thierer.work: Testimony, Hearing on "AI at a Crossroads: A Nationwide Strategy or Californication?"
adam-thierer.why: He asks Congress to preempt state AI rules for frontier labs and models, and more broadly to stop a state 'patchwork'.

asad-ramzanali.q: The state AI law moratorium recently passed by the House would wipe away guardrails protecting real people from real harms, not to mention its unintended consequences.
asad-ramzanali.work: Testimony before House Energy & Commerce Subcommittee on Communications and Technology: AI in the Everyday
asad-ramzanali.why: He opposes federal preemption of state AI laws and urges Congress to keep 'allowing states to remain the laboratories of democracy'.

brian-merchant.q: Trump vocally supports Silicon Valley’s push for deregulation, and is on board with the push to ban states from passing AI laws. In other words, the plan will help de-democratize AI.
brian-merchant.work: Trump's AI Action Plan is a blueprint for dystopia
brian-merchant.why: He criticises the federal push to stop states passing AI laws as undemocratic.

chris-murphy.q: They pushed for and secured a provision in the giant Republican budget bill that bans all AI regulation at the state level, knowing that federal regulation is normally inspired by state models
chris-murphy.work: In our scramble to win the AI race against China, we risk losing ourselves
chris-murphy.why: He criticizes the federal ban on state AI regulation as an industry tactic to block regulation.

dean-ball.q: I have long been a supporter of a federal AI law with broad (though not universal) preemption of state regulations.
dean-ball.why: In his conclusion on the 2026 state bills, the author says in his own voice that he supports federal preemption of state AI regulation.

dwarkesh-patel.q: And honestly, Anthropic specifically has been naive here in urging regulation, and, for example, in opposing moratoriums on state AI regulation.
dwarkesh-patel.work: The most important question nobody's asking about AI
dwarkesh-patel.why: He calls opposition to moratoriums on state AI laws naive, implying support for blocking state AI rules.

gary-marcus.q: Some state laws are trying to address these issues, but as we know the Federal government is trying to undermine the states’ abilities to pass and enforce AI regulation.
gary-marcus.work: We URGENTLY need a federal law forbidding AI from impersonating humans
gary-marcus.why: He presents federal efforts to curb state AI laws as undermining needed regulation.

josh-hawley.q: Fourth and finally, while Congress gets its act together to do all of this, we can’t kneecap our state governments from moving first.
josh-hawley.work: AI Threatens the Working Man
josh-hawley.why: He opposes a federal ban on state AI regulation and says he helped kill it on the Senate floor.

karen-hao.q: This is absolutely going to enshrine the impunity of Silicon Valley into law.
karen-hao.work: Empire of AI: Karen Hao on How AI Is Threatening Democracy & Creating a New Colonial World
karen-hao.why: Asked about the federal provision that would bar states from regulating AI for a decade, she condemns it.

marsha-blackburn.q: Instead of pushing AI amnesty, President Trump rightfully called on Congress to pass federal standards and protections to solve the patchwork of state laws that have hindered AI innovation,
marsha-blackburn.work: Blackburn Unveils National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence (TRUMP AMERICA AI Act)
marsha-blackburn.why: She defends state AI laws only until Congress acts, and her own framework aims for one preemptive federal rulebook that replaces the 'patchwork of state laws'.

michael-kratsios.q: need to do preemption around state--around AI regulations.
michael-kratsios.work: Testimony, 'AI've Got a Plan: America's AI Action Plan' (Senate Commerce Subcommittee on Science, Manufacturing, and Competitiveness)
michael-kratsios.why: In his answer to Chairman Cruz, which begins 'A patchwork of State regulations is anti-', he says federal preemption of state AI regulations is needed.

neil-chilson.q: the real question is not whether there should be a national AI framework, but how it can be drawn to ensure continued American AI dominance, including by preempting overreaching state laws while preserving state authority where it makes sense.
neil-chilson.work: Raising the Cost of Bad AI Laws
neil-chilson.why: He wants Congress to pass a national framework that preempts overreaching state AI laws, with some areas left to states.

sean-o-brien.q: Senators, do the right thing for the working class and strike the AI moratorium from this bill.
sean-o-brien.work: Big Beautiful Bill could give free pass to Big Tech to kill jobs
sean-o-brien.why: He calls on the Senate to remove the federal ban on state AI laws, defending states' right to regulate.

taylor-barkley.q: The proposed AI moratorium offers exactly that: a pragmatic pause to craft a single, strong federal framework that provides clarity, ensures accountability, encourages innovation, and most importantly, protects children nationwide.
taylor-barkley.work: Protecting Kids Requires Smart National AI Policy, Not Fifty Shades of Red Tape
taylor-barkley.why: He supports a federal moratorium that would block new state AI-specific laws.

ted-cruz.q: Third, prevent a patchwork of burdensome AI regulation, including often-conflicting state AI regulations;
ted-cruz.work: Sen. Cruz: AI Policy Should Harness the Power of American Ingenuity (opening statement, 'AI've Got a Plan' hearing)
ted-cruz.why: His legislative framework aims to prevent state AI regulation he calls duplicative and punitive.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: At this point, given what we’ve seen from the Trump administration, I think our best bet is the state law path. As for pre-emption, OpenAI is actively trying to get an all-encompassing version of that in exchange for essentially nothing at all
zvi-mowshowitz.work: DeepSeek Panic at the App Store
zvi-mowshowitz.why: He prefers state AI laws and, in the next sentence, says the broad federal pre-emption OpenAI is seeking must not happen ('We can’t let that happen').

anton-korinek.q: By contrast, robot taxes on owning or operating robotic equipment would directly tax productive capital. Such taxes would discourage precisely the investments needed to build AI infrastructure.
anton-korinek.work: The future of tax policy: A public finance framework for the age of AI
anton-korinek.why: He argues against special taxes on automation capital, favouring consumption taxes instead.

bernie-sanders.q: we should enact a robot tax on large corporations and use the revenue to improve the lives of workers who have been harmed.
bernie-sanders.work: AI must benefit everyone, not just a handful of billionaires
bernie-sanders.why: He proposes a robot tax on companies that replace workers with new technology.

daron-acemoglu.q: Definitely not automation taxes, definitely not slow down automation. We do not want to slow down automation.
daron-acemoglu.work: Daron Acemoglu on Innovation and Shared Prosperity
daron-acemoglu.why: Listing his policy ideas, he explicitly rules out taxes on automation.

dean-ball.q: strongly opposed to regulations or taxes designed to remedy the “problem” of AI and labor, since today, there is no problem we can perceive.
dean-ball.work: Before Leviathan Wakes (Why I Believe What I Believe)
dean-ball.why: He says he strongly opposes taxes aimed at AI's effect on labor.

lawrence-summers.q: Mr Gates’ robot tax risks essentially being protectionism against progress.
lawrence-summers.work: Robots are wealth creators and taxing them is illogical
lawrence-summers.why: He argues that a tax on labor-replacing robots is illogical and would shrink the economic pie.

ro-khanna.q: Funded by a modest wealth tax on the trillions created here and by a token tax on AI used by businesses that displaces labor
ro-khanna.work: We need a new tech social contract to reclaim AI from billionaires
ro-khanna.why: He proposes a tax on business AI that displaces labor.

robert-shiller.q: A moderate tax on robots, even a temporary tax that merely slows the adoption of disruptive technology, seems a natural component of a policy to address rising inequality.
robert-shiller.why: He endorses a moderate tax on labor-displacing robots and AI to fund adjustment for displaced workers.

alexandria-ocasio-cortez.q: Because not all creativity needs to be bonded by wage.
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.work: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at SXSW (full transcript of conversation with Briahna Gray)
alexandria-ocasio-cortez.why: She says that with automation's wealth shared, people could spend more time on education, art, science and invention, finding purpose outside paid work.

anton-korinek.q: First, we should remember that work is a means to an end, not an end in itself.
anton-korinek.work: Preparing the Workforce for an Uncertain AI Future (Written Statement to the U.S. Senate AI Insight Forum on Workforce)
anton-korinek.why: He argues that if income were provided without work, people could find new sources of meaning.

barack-obama.q: Because work isn't just a way of making money, and feeding, and clothing, and housing ourselves. It also gives our life shape and direction, and a sense that we matter.
barack-obama.work: Obama Speaks at Hamilton College (conversation with Steven Tepper)
barack-obama.why: Discussing AI displacing work, he says work gives life meaning beyond income, and asks how that will be rebuilt.

bernie-sanders.q: It's not just economics. Work, whether being a janitor or a brain surgeon, is an integral part of being human.
bernie-sanders.work: AI must benefit everyone, not just a handful of billionaires
bernie-sanders.why: Setting income aside ('not just economics'), he says losing work removes a vital part of human existence.

curtis-yarvin.q: So actually, a world in which you get shoes without work doesn’t really work, because people need to do something.
curtis-yarvin.work: Does Democracy Still Control Power? w/ Curtis Yarvin (Peter McCormack Show, transcript)
curtis-yarvin.why: He argues people need real work for purpose and that income without work leaves them living like children.

james-livingston.q: Most adults don’t want or need to be fulfilled by work, as per Gourevitch’s achingly earnest agenda—they want to enjoy the rest of their lives.
james-livingston.work: More Work for Father: Rejoinder to Alex Gourevitch
james-livingston.why: Livingston argues against the view that work is central to human fulfilment, saying most people do not need it for meaning.

jason-crawford.q: Others will do whatever is most meaningful to them: pursue knowledge and satisfy their curiosity; express their creative vision in art or music; travel and explore; spend time with family and loved ones; play games or sports.
jason-crawford.work: The future of humanity is in management
jason-crawford.why: He expects that in a fully automated economy most people will find meaning outside paid work, and he rejects the worry that they will be bored.

jd-vance.q: even if you replace the financial element of their jobs, you would destroy something that was dignified and purposeful about work itself.
jd-vance.work: Remarks by the Vice President at the American Dynamism Summit
jd-vance.why: Recounting his own worry, he says replacing the income from work would still destroy its dignity and purpose.

joanna-bryson.q: Employment is a form of security, it binds a local community together.
joanna-bryson.why: She argues that paid work gives security and a place in the community that money alone does not, and that losing it makes people expendable.

josh-hawley.q: Pay a man to do nothing, and you have not solved his problem; you have deepened it, and degraded him.
josh-hawley.work: The American Covenant’s Answer to AI
josh-hawley.why: He argues that income without work degrades people, because work is about dignity, not only wages.

lawrence-summers.q: So the challenge for economic policy will increasingly be generating enough work for all who need work for income, purchasing power and dignity.
lawrence-summers.work: The Economic Challenge of the Future: Jobs
lawrence-summers.why: He names dignity alongside income as something people need work for, and treats long spells out of work as troubling.

marc-andreessen.q: Man was not meant to be farmed; man was meant to be useful, to be productive, to be proud.
marc-andreessen.work: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto
marc-andreessen.why: Arguing against UBI, he holds that people need productive work for pride and purpose even if income is provided.

oren-cass.q: Work gives not only meaning but also structure and stability to life.
oren-cass.work: Why a Universal Basic Income Is a Terrible Idea
oren-cass.why: He argues that income from a UBI cannot replace the meaning, structure and socialization that work provides.

pete-buttigieg.q: You're an auto worker, you're in a tool and dye shop, and it's your whole sense of belonging revolves around your job, not just your paycheck.
pete-buttigieg.work: Secretary Pete Buttigieg: The American Dream Is DEAD. We're Running Out Of Time To Fix It!
pete-buttigieg.why: He says workers who lost jobs often never recovered their identity, because work supplies belonging beyond the paycheck.

pope-leo-xiv.q: As the Bishops of the United States of America have recalled, work is not merely a source of income but a crucial sphere in which identity is formed, friendships and relationships are forged, practical responsibilities are learned and one’s vocation is discerned.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: He adopts this teaching in his own encyclical, treating work as a source of identity and vocation beyond income.

robert-shiller.q: with not only their effects on their incomes, but also with something deeper, the meaning of work and life, a concept which our psychology will not let us neglect.
robert-shiller.work: Narratives about Technology-Induced Job Degradations Then and Now (NBER Working Paper 25536)
robert-shiller.why: In his own policy section, Shiller argues that job loss threatens meaning beyond income, and he later concludes that new institutions may matter as much as any direct redistribution of income.

robin-hanson.q: Yes, there is a further issue of how humans can find meaning if they don’t get most of their income from work. But this seems like a nice problem to have, and historically wealthy elites have often succeeded here
robin-hanson.why: He treats finding meaning without work as manageable, citing elites who found it in pastimes.

scott-alexander.q: Given all this, I lean in favor of thinking most people would tolerate financially secure leisure time just fine.
scott-alexander.work: Basic Income, Not Basic Jobs: Against Hijacking Utopia
scott-alexander.why: After rebutting the claim that people need jobs for purpose, he concludes that most people would do fine without paid work if their income were secure.

taylor-barkley.q: Your value is not your productivity. Your dignity is not granted by an employer, an algorithm, or a trend.
taylor-barkley.why: He denies that human dignity depends on employment.

bernie-sanders.q: Workers need a seat at the table to best determine how AI is used in their companies.
bernie-sanders.work: AI must benefit everyone, not just a handful of billionaires
bernie-sanders.why: He proposes requiring large corporations to let workers elect at least 45 percent of their boards so that workers can shape how AI is used.

brian-merchant.q: Returning to the Luddites reminds us that above all, workers and users must have a seat at the table. We need a real say, real empowerment, real agency over any technology that is made to reshape our workplaces, communities, and lives.
brian-merchant.work: Understanding the Luddites in the age of AI
brian-merchant.why: His conclusion demands that workers get real say over workplace technology, resting it on democracy, labor laws and collective bargaining.

cory-doctorow.q: If we are gonna campaign to get a new law passed in hopes of making more money and having more control over our labor, we should campaign to restore sectoral bargaining, not to expand copyright.
cory-doctorow.work: The Reverse-Centaur's Guide to Criticizing AI
cory-doctorow.why: On how creative workers should protect themselves from AI, he calls for a law restoring sectoral bargaining, the tool he credits for the writers' strike win over AI.

daron-acemoglu.q: AI will profoundly affect all workers, yet workers as a group currently lack meaningful voice in shaping AI’s development and deployment. Establishing institutional mechanisms for worker input could prove valuable.
daron-acemoglu.why: Among the paper's policy proposals, he and his coauthors call for formal mechanisms that give workers a say over AI deployment.

josh-hawley.q: We should give workers rights over AI in their companies.
josh-hawley.work: The American Covenant’s Answer to AI
josh-hawley.why: He proposes giving workers rights over AI in their workplaces as part of regulating AI.

karen-hao.q: Having the ability to maybe even bargain for the longevity of their job in certain ways, and bargain against AI being used to automate certain aspects of their jobs.
karen-hao.why: This follows her call to strengthen labor laws so that workers can bargain collectively over how AI is used in their jobs.

liz-shuler.q: An agenda that gives workers a voice at the table, shaping technology in every workplace — classrooms, factories, airports, Social Security offices, film sets, everywhere.
liz-shuler.work: AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler's Speech to the National Press Club
liz-shuler.why: Her Workers First AI policy agenda, pursued through contracts and state laws, demands worker voice over workplace AI.

ro-khanna.q: Even so, federal policy should require public companies to have active worker participation when making decisions on how A.I. will change jobs that have functions that might be automated
ro-khanna.work: Democrats Must Not Repeat the Mistakes of Globalization
ro-khanna.why: He calls for federal law requiring worker participation in AI adoption decisions.
